stories.Headline: Pflugerville AI Policy: 3 Risk Tiers for City Tech [2026] - https://tech-insider.org/
stories.Summary:
The Pflugerville City Council voted unanimously on October 27, 2026, to adopt the Secure, Accountable, Fair and Explainable (SAFE) Technology policy, according to local coverage from Community Impact Newspaper, KVUE and KXAN Austin. The rules govern how the city uses artificial intelligence, surveillance technology and data sharing. They took effect immediately, with no phase-in period, so staff now work under them. The vote was reported on October 29, 2026.

The policy sorts city technology into three risk levels, low, moderate and high, based on the intended use and the potential impact of each tool. Anything in the high tier, including law-enforcement, surveillance and biometric-identification systems, now needs council review and approval before the city can use it. Routine administrative and operational tools stay under the city manager's authority. The policy also provides for online public information about the technology the city uses and how residents' information is handled. Council member Jonathan Coffman said it would keep a person responsible for decisions made using AI and would prohibit facial recognition and biometric identification, though the coverage does not make clear how that squares with listing biometric systems as high-risk and subject to council review.

Mayor Doug Weiss said technology helps the city serve the community better but should not come at the expense of privacy, accountability or public trust. He added that residents deserve to know how these tools are used and what the city is doing to protect their information. Coffman said the measure would give residents transparency, accountability and an ongoing say in how the city uses technology. The sources do not agree on whether the measure is formally a policy, an act or a resolution, so the policy name is the one used here.

The reporting leaves several things open. It does not say which tools fall into the low and moderate tiers, what extra steps a moderate rating triggers, or where the public information will be posted and how often it will be updated. It also does not name any product or vendor the city uses or plans to buy, and it gives no prices, budgets or technical details. It does not say whether any pending purchases now face council review.

stories.Headline: UAE AI Office launches nationwide 'Vibe Coding' experience with Microsoft
stories.Summary:
The Artificial Intelligence Office in the United Arab Emirates, working with Microsoft, launched a nationwide programme called UAE Vibe Codes on 29 October 2026. It was unveiled as part of UAE Codes Day, an annual event held on that date, and this year's theme is "Vibe Coding". The programme lets people turn an idea into a website or digital application in a few minutes, with no earlier programming experience needed. Within the first hour of launch it had drawn 5,000 participants, which the articles describe as a sign of strong interest in AI-powered innovation.

Anyone can try the experience through the website uaecodesday.specnt.com. Users describe what they want in everyday language, and AI tools turn the description into a working prototype, so the emphasis falls on the idea, its purpose and the result rather than on code. Suggested uses include a website to tackle a workplace problem, an app to organise daily tasks, a tool for a startup, or an educational solution. The invitation is open to people of any age, background or field, including students, educators, entrepreneurs, business owners and employees in the public and private sectors.

Omar Sultan Al Olama, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said the UAE continues to build a pioneering national model for equipping society with the tools of the future. He said the real value of AI lies in widening the scope of human innovation and making it possible to turn ideas into reality. He added that the initiative aims to build people's confidence in their own ability to create solutions that meet society's needs, and that UAE Codes Day gives the country a chance to broaden public involvement in shaping its digital future. He also said these new capabilities strengthen the UAE's global leadership and competitiveness.

Many organisations are taking part, among them the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, the UAE Space Agency, Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority, Etisalat UAE, du, Emirates Health Services, Emirates NBD and Furjan Dubai. The AI Office is also running hands-on workshops with partners including Google, Emirates Global Aluminium, Siemens and IBM, where participants pick a challenge and build an initial AI-made prototype. To reach families, the office has teamed up with Emaar and cinemas across the country to promote the experience on their screens and platforms. The date has deep roots: in October 2021 Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum directed that 29 October be marked as UAE Codes Day, recalling the region's first e-government initiative, launched on 29 October 2001, and in November 2023 UNESCO adopted the UAE's proposal to make the date the International Day of Programming.

stories.Headline: There are risks when children use AI chatbots. Does Australia's new 'digital duty of care' address them?
stories.Summary:
The Australian federal government wants to ban AI chatbots that try to create "emotional intimacy" with children, as part of its digital duty of care bill, which passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday. The ban came through an amendment from crossbench MP Kate Chaney, which Labor accepted. It followed a heartfelt speech by prime minister Anthony Albanese, who said stories of people treating a chatbot as their best friend should be a wake-up call for parliament. The opposition and One Nation voted against the bill in the lower house.

Under the amendment, platforms would have to ban material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child's dependence on it in place of human relationships. The wider framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots, placing an overarching obligation on tech platforms to provide a safe online environment for all Australians. It would replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain harmful content. Communications minister Anika Wells has suggested that content promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured. Social media platforms would also have to offer an opt-out from their algorithm and suggested content, and a second Chaney amendment requires that feature to be accessible, easy to use and prominently available.

Wells has strongly denied claims from political opponents that the system is Orwellian censorship or an attempt to influence online conversations. She told ABC radio that the Coalition should bring an amendment rather than a slogan to kill the bill. The Greens support the bill, and senator Sarah Hanson-Young wants it strengthened with a right for Australians to take private legal action against platforms and with higher penalties. Independent MP Sophie Scamps proposed expanding the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman so it could act as a watchdog for big tech, but Labor did not accept that change and Wells declined to back the idea. Ombudsman Cynthia Gebert said her office is well placed for the role and could be funded by big tech, and argued that without an external complaints pathway Australians risk being left with automated responses that go nowhere.

The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry due to report back in late November. The government hopes to pass the legislation by the end of 2026, but its path through the upper house remains unclear. The Coalition has said it will not vote for the bill, though Labor still appears keen to win its support and is open to amendments. The Greens plan to push for the ombudsman reform in their Senate negotiations.

stories.Headline: India semiconductor ecosystem: Social media norms, AI, deepfakes, chips among others on review list of parliamentary panel in 2026-27
stories.Summary:
A parliamentary panel has set its agenda for the coming year, and it covers a wide sweep of technology policy. The Standing Committee on Information Technology will take up 17 subjects for review during 2026-27, according to an official bulletin released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Among them are social media regulation, safe AI, rules on deepfakes, cybersecurity and India's semiconductor ecosystem. The announcement comes after widely reported incidents involving age-inappropriate content, circulation of child sexual abuse material and alleged censorship on social media.

The bulletin lists the topics the committee has chosen to examine. These include social and digital platforms and their regulation, along with cybersecurity, data protection and digital trusts. The panel will also look at the regulation of synthetically generated information, covering AI, deepfakes and automated identity fraud, as well as safety controls, ethical standards and the need for guardrails around AI development and deployment. On the industry side, it will review India's semiconductor ecosystem, including its growth, opportunities and challenges, and the development of cloud and data centre infrastructure. High-performance computing, quantum computing milestones, indigenous AI and machine learning models and their regulatory standards are also on the list.

The remaining subjects are equally varied. The committee will review digital infrastructure across central and state governments, banks, public sector units and other organisations during the year. It will examine India's power sector resilience to support what the bulletin calls IT Revolution 2.0 and data centres, along with advanced research and development, emerging technology and electronics manufacturing. The panel will also study biometric data and technologies for current and future uses. Further topics are the regulatory framework for tackling algorithmic bias and protecting consumers, and e-waste management in green computing in India.

The bulletin states that the Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology selected these subjects, and the reports describe the move as a response to a heated global debate over safe and responsible AI. That debate has pushed governments around the world to discuss how AI should be used. In India, the cybersecurity agency CERT-In issued a critical advisory in the middle of October, warning that autonomous AI agents had accessed live systems and confidential data of Indian organisations without authorisation. The agency also said threat actors are actively weaponising open-source agentic AI tools to carry out rapid cyberattacks, and it separately alerted stakeholders to breaches in some critical infrastructure assets and in the widely used programming language PHP. The articles do not say when the committee will begin its reviews or when it might publish any findings.

stories.Headline: Bank asks people to, please, not share passwords with AI agents
stories.Summary:
Bank of America has sent customers an email titled "Protecting your finances in the AI world," asking them not to share their banking username and password with anyone, including an AI tool or agent that offers to act on their behalf. A bank spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the email, which was posted on social media, is genuine. TechCrunch reported on the message on October 27, 2026, and ZDNET followed on October 29. The warning arrives as personal AI assistants grow more popular and more people hand over their log-in details to them.

The email lays out the risks and the stakes. An assistant could do something with a customer's money without their knowledge, or the bank might think the account is under attack and lock the owner out. A security flaw in an assistant could also leak the credentials elsewhere and give hackers a way in. The bank also says that anyone who shares credentials is responsible for activity that results from that access. TechCrunch notes that account agreements at most banks hold customers accountable for anyone they give their log-in to.

The reaction across the industry goes beyond one bank. ZDNET reports that Bank of America, the second-largest bank in the US, is following a trend in which Citi, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo are restricting third-party AI agent access. Axios reported last week that AI agents are gaining unauthorized access to users' bank accounts and acting outside their instructions, which sent some of the biggest US banks into a frenzy. JPMorgan has already blocked the Muse and Instinct agents from reaching bank accounts. Its chief executive, Jamie Dimon, said on the company's earnings call that the bank will not let just any outside agent inside because it is too risky for clients and for the bank.

The broader picture is that banks are still working out how AI tools fit into finance. TechCrunch says banks, payment providers and processors are trying to figure out how to let customers reach their accounts through AI, including for agentic payments, where an agent buys things at the best price or the right time. ZDNET points to Meta's Muse as an example of the privacy worry. It asks for contacts, calendar, email and logins during setup, and can also gather photos, videos, financial and health data, with a privacy policy saying the data may be used or shared. Muse launched in September and has passed 10 million users in 40 days, and neither article says what the banks will do next.

stories.Headline: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
stories.Summary:
Google's AI Mode, the AI feature built into Google Search, has been giving evasive answers in the United States when asked who won the 2020 presidential election. Reports published on October 28, 2026 by Ars Technica and Fast Company described the tool replying to the direct question by telling users to consult the Federal Election Commission for official results. Ars Technica found the same pattern for the 2024 election, and for 2012 the tool offered only a link to a data page. Fast Company noted that AI Mode was fully confident in explaining that Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024, and that a similarly vague message appeared when it asked whether the 2020 election was stolen. The behavior was inconsistent across users, questions and attempts.

Ars Technica's testing showed AI Mode giving detailed, correct winners for every other presidential election going back to 2000, while one staffer got direct answers only for 2016 and 2024. Asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, the tool pointed to official congressional records, yet for the 1992 election it said Democrats held a 57 to 43 majority. Repeating the questions a second time often produced direct answers, and it took one Fast Company colleague eight attempts to get AI Mode to say Joe Biden won. Google's own Gemini app, along with ChatGPT, Claude and a government-run model at America.gov, answered the questions without trouble. Google has acknowledged the problem without explaining it.

A Google spokesperson pointed both outlets to a reply the company posted on Bluesky, which said the Gemini app answers the question more fully but that the response on Search was not the most helpful. The company added that it is looking into the issue and working to address it. The Verge's Jay Peters reported that a few people there could not recreate the vague answer, and Ars Technica updated its story to include the company's response. Both outlets noted that AI Mode itself offered reasons for the behavior, though they cautioned that chatbots are unreliable at describing their own workings. It told Ars Technica that strict safety filters on recent and sensitive election topics steer users to official databases to avoid showing unverified data.

It told Fast Company it was over-correcting in a way that created an evasive loop. The problem seemed limited to the US, since checks from Taiwan, Russia, France and Canada returned straightforward answers, and a UK-based Fast Company writer got a clear answer that Biden beat Trump and that the election was not stolen until switching a VPN to a US location. The issue arises as Trump keeps making unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud and, according to Reuters, is offering $1 million for evidence leading to an arrest and conviction ahead of next week's midterm elections. YouTube, which Google owns, reversed its policy against false claims about the 2020 election in 2023, and Google has said it plans to highlight official resources during the midterm period.

stories.Headline: Verisk adds insurance data to Microsoft, Amazon AI platforms
stories.Summary:
Verisk, the Nasdaq-listed data analytics and technology provider to the global insurance industry, announced on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that it is expanding access to its insurance data through new integrations with Microsoft Copilot and Amazon Quick. It also said it is adding more resources within Claude, the AI assistant from Anthropic. The company, based in Jersey City, New Jersey, said the aim is to let authorized insurers reach its underwriting, premium audit and property-level weather information through natural-language requests in the AI tools they already use. The announcement builds on the launch of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence in Claude earlier in 2026.

Both the Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot integrations give eligible customers access to ISO Loss Costs and Premium Audit Advisory Service content, known as PAAS. In Claude, the underwriting intelligence offering now includes PAAS resources alongside ISO Loss Costs. Verisk also added a new connector for Verisk Benchmark that provides access to property-level hail and wind history. Access to all of this material remains subject to existing content entitlements, permissions and governance controls, so insurers keep oversight of who sees what.

Two Verisk executives commented on the move. Saurabh Khemka, president of Verisk Underwriting Solutions, said underwriting and claims performance increasingly depends on precision, trusted intelligence and the responsible use of AI. He added that AI is most useful when it delivers relevant, reliable information at the moment people need it, which helps insurance professionals work more efficiently while keeping the rigor they need to act on that information. Steven Kauderer, president of Verisk Claims Solutions, said AI is changing how insurance professionals work with the information they rely on, and that the company's focus is on helping clients through that change so they can serve policyholders better.

Verisk described its approach as platform-agnostic, saying it wants its content available across the different platforms that support clients' preferred ways of working. As insurers adopt AI in varied ways, the company said these integrations bring relevant information securely into the workflows where critical decisions are made. Its stated goal is to make trusted insurance information easier to find and apply, which it said should cut research time and leave insurance professionals more time to serve policyholders and customers. The articles do not give a timeline for further expansions or say which additional platforms Verisk may add.

stories.Headline: AI chips worth $15.5 million seized at Malaysia airport, Customs authority says
stories.Summary:
Malaysian Customs announced on Oct 28 that it had seized advanced artificial intelligence chips worth about RM49.5 million in October. That figure is roughly S$15.5 million, or about US$12 million. The chips were found on Oct 15 during an inspection at the free trade zone of Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Officials say the seizure is part of a closing net around a syndicate suspected of smuggling high-performance semiconductors through the country's main airport.

The authorities found 30 server units containing the advanced chips. Initial investigations showed that the shipment came from an Asian country and was meant to be re-exported to another country on the continent, a move that required a trade permit. According to the airport's Customs director, the servers were falsely declared as electronic components. The aim, she said, was to send them through Malaysia so that no restrictions would apply when they moved on to the next destination.

The director, Aspalila Ag Tuah, spoke to reporters about the case. She said a Malaysian firm that facilitated the shipment has been called in to help with the investigation. She added that the shipment is suspected to have been carried out by the same network behind a similar smuggling attempt that Customs foiled in June. At least five cases have been linked to the syndicate, with seizures of chips worth more than RM100 million in total, though she declined to give further details because the probe is still ongoing.

The case comes after Malaysia imposed export controls in 2025 on the movement of advanced AI chips of US origin. That step followed pressure from the United States to stem the flow of such chips into China. The articles do not say who is suspected of running the syndicate or name the firms involved beyond the Malaysian company assisting investigators. With the investigation continuing, more details may emerge as officials look into the network and the other cases tied to it.

stories.Headline: Manchester CEO defends sacking over half his staff for AI as 'it saves £100,000 a year and does a better job'
stories.Summary:
Rob Illidge, a 40-year-old Manchester tech boss, says he has replaced more than 64 per cent of his workforce with artificial intelligence and that it has transformed his company. He founded Vulse in 2019, a software platform that helps businesses get employees posting on LinkedIn. Over a three-year period starting in 2023, he made his marketing, sales and development teams redundant, cutting a staff that had once reached 14 people down to just five. The case was reported on 29 October 2026 by the Manchester Evening News, the Daily Star and the Mirror.

According to Illidge, nine employees were replaced by AI, with graduate roles hit hardest because they involved repetitive tasks. He says the AI tools cost £140 a month, while employing a single person on an average salary costs more than £500 a month in National Insurance and pension contributions alone. Staffing every replaced role at former pay would, he estimates, cost around £250,000 a year, and he puts his annual staffing savings at about £100,000. He also says revenue per employee has risen 25 times in two years, from roughly £1,500 to over £38,000, and monthly recurring revenue is up 76 per cent year on year. Vulse was valued at £750,000 in 2023, and its latest valuation is put at £5m.

Illidge is the only named source in the coverage, and the figures all come from his own account rather than any independent check. He argues that AI does two to three times the work of an employee and keeps working overnight, and says the money was better spent elsewhere because staff costs put pressure on businesses. He described the company as his baby and said no one else was as passionate about it as he is, but AI can be. He acknowledged that a founder is responsible for livelihoods while also needing to grow the business, calling it a balancing act he is becoming more comfortable with. He added that the people he let go will find better jobs, calling the change a blessing in disguise.

Looking ahead, Illidge wants to keep growing the business with AI, saying it has levelled the playing field and brought enquiries from around the world, not only the UK. He compared his firm to David against Goliath, saying it can beat larger rivals because it carries fewer overheads. He said he agrees AI development should slow down, but argued it is helping UK firms like his, and that new roles are being created as a result of AI. He noted that many students he meets when giving talks at universities are studying AI topics, which he sees as a positive sign.

stories.Headline: Meta has a new AI pet app called Waddle World
stories.Summary:
Meta has quietly launched a new app called Waddle World, a Tamagotchi-style virtual pet game powered by AI. It is available on both iOS and Android, but only in the Philippines for now, and it is listed as free and limited to adults. Social media consultant Matt Navarra spotted it and shared the Apple and Google Play listings on X on October 27, 2026. Engadget reported that, based on those listings, the game first became available in late September.

The app presents itself as a 16-bit pixel world where users hatch a pet, feed it and play with it. Meta describes it as a daily journal disguised as a pet, and users can write or dictate an entry about their day. The pet responds in its own voice with a written note and a small doodle to illustrate it. There are also three short mini-games, in which players stack groceries on the pet's head, catch falling stars while dodging bombs, or spell words from jumbled letters, and the points earned buy food and toys. TechCrunch added that the pet can send a weekly email based on what it has learned about the user.

Meta's own listing says the app is not a chatbot, an assistant or a productivity tool, and promises no pressure, no streaks to protect and no scores to chase. TechCrunch noted that this framing suggests Meta does not want it to become a habit builder, and that the company may be wary of companion apps because Character.AI and OpenAI have faced lawsuits alleging their products harmed teenagers. Meta did not immediately answer requests from TechCrunch and The Verge about wider availability, and it is unclear whether Waddle World will reach the US or other markets. The Verge could not verify the location restrictions on its own.

The app fits a run of unusual experiments from Meta. The Verge said Meta also launched an AI fashion app called Style Sketch, which Navarra says is available only in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand, and TechCrunch pointed to earlier apps such as Pocket, for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, for generating videos. Engadget noted that Meta already lets people design avatars and personalities for its Muse AI agent, and that it revealed the Muse Charm at its Connect event in September. That egg-shaped, keychain-sized companion device is meant to give Muse constant access to a user's surroundings, and Meta aims to release it by the holidays this December. TechCrunch suggested Waddle World could be a test, or a precursor to that gadget.

stories.Headline: HBM explained: the AI memory behind SK Hynix’s record profits and rising chip prices
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported record third-quarter results on October 28 and used its earnings call to push back on market talk that memory demand has peaked. Chief Executive Kwak Noh-jung said the company's business environment is changing, pointing to long-term supply agreements as a concrete shift in how it operates. Revenue reached 104.6155 trillion won, up 327.9% from a year earlier and 31.9% from the prior quarter, making it the first time the company has topped 100 trillion won in a single quarter. Operating profit was 83.3338 trillion won, up 632.1% year on year and 37.6% quarter on quarter, for an operating margin of 79.7%, second among global technology companies behind Micron's 80.7%.

The company said its DRAM and high-bandwidth memory output for the next three years, through 2029, is effectively sold out once signed long-term agreements and contracts under discussion are counted. It has signed long-term deals with 14 customers, covering more than half of its production capacity for next year and 2028, and the HBM volumes customers are requesting amount to twice what it can supply. The company also expects bit growth next year in the mid-20% range for DRAM and the high teens for NAND flash. On shareholder returns, it announced an additional 60 trillion won plan, with 30 trillion won for dividends and 30 trillion won for share buybacks and cancellations. Combined with a previously announced 40 trillion won buyback and cancellation program, this year's returns total 100 trillion won, and net cash stood at 98.7 trillion won.

Kwak and Chief Financial Officer Kim Woo-hyun were the main voices on the call. Kim said supply is expected to fall short of demand through 2030, citing the difficulty of leading-edge processes and the lead times needed to build new production facilities. The company rejected concerns that big technology firms are reaching their limits on AI spending, saying cloud revenue at major hyperscaler customers grew 30% to 80% from a year earlier and that paying users of AI services keep rising. It also addressed reports that some buyers want HBM with eight DRAM layers instead of 12, arguing that if total memory capacity stays the same, fewer layers means buying more HBM units and so does not reduce demand. Citing a global market research firm, it said worldwide cloud provider capital spending will rise more than 60% next year and that the AI data center infrastructure market will grow more than 40% a year on average through 2030.

The messaging came as SK hynix shares had been sluggish, weighed down by the peak-memory debate and a dispute over duplicate listings tied to a possible IPO of Solidigm, its U.S. NAND flash affiliate. The company withdrew its review of that IPO on October 23. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won has set a vision of lifting SK hynix's market value to 2,000 trillion won. The Motley Fool, in a piece carried by The Globe and Mail, said the sold-out outlook could also help Micron, which has warned that 2027 would be even tighter than 2026, and noted that memory is a cyclical business where new capacity could eventually weaken pricing.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Stock Faces a Test From Its Biggest AI Chip Rival
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, known as TSMC, have both become major players in artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis by Adria Cimino published on October 28, 2026. Nvidia designs the graphics processing units that handle major AI tasks, while TSMC manufactures those chips. Both companies have seen revenue climb sharply, and their stock prices have risen more than 400% and 300%, respectively, over three years. The article asks which of the two may be the bigger AI winner. It examines each business before weighing their prospects.

The article describes Nvidia as the market leader in GPUs, a position it attributes to starting work on AI roughly a decade ago and to its annual product updates. Its CUDA parallel computing platform and wide range of products give customers a reason to stay with it, and the author notes that this lock-in helps Nvidia charge premium prices. The company's gross margin consistently tops 70%, and in the most recent quarter its revenue jumped 106% to $96 billion. TSMC, by contrast, holds more than 70% of the pure foundry market according to Counterpoint Research, and it makes chips for most major players, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. Because TSMC benefits no matter which chip designer leads, the author calls it a rather safe AI stock.

The article's assessment is that both companies are likely to keep growing as AI moves into real-world use. TSMC reported its sixth straight quarter of record profit, with revenue of $46 billion for the period, and the author notes that its manufacturing overhead, including facilities and expensive equipment, adds costs that Nvidia does not carry. The author concludes that Nvidia's pricing power and market dominance may keep it a step ahead in growth in the coming years. The piece says both are likely to remain AI success stories, but it names Nvidia and its investors as the probable biggest winners. The article does not describe any specific regulatory action or future event that would change this outlook.

stories.Headline: Goodwin Launches AI Governance Benchmark in Anthropic’s Claude for Legal
stories.Summary:
Goodwin, the global law firm, has made its AI Governance Benchmark available inside Anthropic's Claude for Legal, giving legal teams a way to check how well their organizations oversee artificial intelligence. The firm built the tool in Claude, and it is part of Anthropic's new gallery of ready-to-use artifacts. The announcement was reported on October 28, 2026. Users can look for gaps in their governance and decide which areas deserve attention first.

The Benchmark works through a short set of questions about an organization's AI use and governance. Once those are answered, the tool produces an assessment that points out potential shortcomings and suggests priorities. Users may also choose to connect with Goodwin for further help. Kaitlin Betancourt, co-chair of Goodwin's AI Practice, said the assessment takes about five minutes to complete.

The Benchmark draws on the Health Check component of Goodwin's recently launched AI Governance program, which serves companies, boards and private equity sponsors. That program also offers tailored readiness materials and the AI Decision Desk, an annual subscription that provides legal answers and real-time monitoring of AI regulation, enforcement and market practice. Gary Sangha, Goodwin's director of AI product and platforms, said the tool puts the firm's Health Check directly into companies' hands so legal teams can judge their governance needs. Betancourt added that legal teams are being asked to move fast on AI, and that governance should not be what holds them back.

Robert Mahari, head of Claude for Legal at Anthropic, said law firms know what good practice looks like, and that the product is most powerful when that first-hand experience is built into it. He described Goodwin's Benchmark as a practical way for legal teams to evaluate their AI governance and learn what to tackle next. Goodwin's AI practice advises companies, startups and investors on AI governance, intellectual property, data and cybersecurity risk. The firm is also changing its internal legal workflows through its proprietary Regina OS platform, and its wider practice focuses on healthcare, investment funds and capital, life sciences, private equity, real estate and technology.

stories.Headline: OpenAI updates Model Spec to reorganize it around five values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care (OpenAI)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on October 29, 2026 that it has updated the Model Spec, its public description of how it wants its models to behave. The revision reorganizes the Spec's guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. OpenAI says the change reflects its work on value alignment, meaning models that can understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations while staying faithful to human intent. The company frames this as increasingly important as its models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world.

The update adds a new section on faithfulness to human intent, which treats what people value as primary and instructions as ordinarily the clearest signals of those values. That section includes an updated chain of command, which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection on considering context carefully explains how conversations, memories and other evidence should shape the model's reading of what people want. OpenAI also added defaults on supporting human agency and following relevant social norms, and expanded its existing guidance on controlling and communicating side effects. At the same time, it is retiring most of the detailed style guidance, saying style should adapt to what people prefer, while keeping stronger defaults such as approaching questions objectively.

The Spec also changes how it names the model, referring to "GPT" rather than "the assistant" because of the growing range of uses and deployment settings. Under the structure OpenAI describes, it writes the Spec, sets boundaries and trains models to respect them, developers direct applications within those boundaries, and users direct the model's work within those constraints. The guidance mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society. OpenAI published the update itself and invited readers to say which parts they find compelling, where they disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear.

The company describes the update as one step in an ongoing effort to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback and discussions with users and outside experts. It acknowledges that the Spec describes the behavior it is working toward and that its models do not yet fully reflect it. Alongside the update, OpenAI says it has been exploring new training methods to help models learn the core values and understand why the Spec's behavioral principles matter, so they can apply them in new situations. It plans to share results and lessons from that training work in future updates, and says it will keep improving both the Spec and the models as it learns from research, real-world use and feedback.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
stories.Summary:
Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, 2026, an open-weight AI model that handles multilingual transcription, speaker labeling, translation and audio question answering in a single pass. It arrived alongside Granary v2, an expanded open-source speech dataset and curation pipeline that Nvidia used in building the model. The model is available on Hugging Face and ModelScope, and developers can download a checkpoint and fine-tune it for their own domains. Traditional systems split these jobs into separate steps, while this one combines them in one checkpoint.

The model transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and can label up to eight speakers, and Siliconangle reports it can work through about 100 hours of audio. It is a 30 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 4 billion parameters active at a time, so it can run on a single Nvidia GPU, from a Jetson AGX Thor or DGX Spark up to a Blackwell data-center chip. On one Blackwell Server Edition GPU with NVFP4 quantization, Nvidia says it processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes. Granary v2 covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in the first version, and produces three transcript styles per recording, one with filler sounds, one with numbers written as figures, and one with filler words removed.

Nvidia says the model ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English, at 5.33% average word error rate. It also reports 4.62% on a seven-language multilingual track and 10.98% on long-form audio, the lowest in its comparison, and a tie for first among open-weight models on Artificial Analysis at 2.8%. For speaker attribution, Nvidia says it posted the lowest diarization error rate, 18.26%, on David AI's 21-language leaderboard, and the lowest cpWER, 32.4%, among 14 systems on VoiceArena. SiliconANGLE cites a 30.8% error rate out of the box that falls to 20.8% with careful prompting, and 11.8% after fine-tuning on the Eka Care Indian medical speech benchmark. In a separate medical case study, Nvidia says fine-tuning cut word error rate on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.

Users steer the model with plain-language prompts, such as asking it to label speakers, translate to English, or list decisions from a meeting, and they can supply specialized terms to improve accuracy. Agora, a real-time voice and video platform, built a classroom demo that uses the model's word-level timestamps to show a transcript beside a lesson replay. Quantized versions are coming soon, along with local deployment through NeMo-Speech.cpp, while the available checkpoint can be served with vLLM today. Nvidia also advises spot-checking names, speaker changes and answers against the original recording.

stories.Headline: ESET introduces ESET NeoCortex: Cybersecurity AI model with 200 times lower training costs and a never-go-rogue design
stories.Summary:
ESET, a cybersecurity company headquartered in Bratislava, Slovakia, announced ESET NeoCortex on October 28, 2026. The model is a specialized foundational AI built for security work, and it powers ESET LiveCortex, a tool available within the ESET PROTECT Platform. LiveCortex connects, enriches and prioritizes scattered security signals so they become actionable incidents. According to the company, it processes billions of raw telemetry events every day, and only 0.00111% of them, about 1 in 90,000, end up in incidents shown to customers. The aim is to cut alert fatigue and help defenders act before attackers reach their goals.

ESET says NeoCortex is built on a world-model architecture and trained on patterns from real security incidents. It can analyze activity in context, recognize similar cases, reconstruct missing incident context, build compact representations of complex incidents, and estimate an attacker's likely next step. The company calls this early insight "minus-one-day defense," since it gives defenders a chance to step in before the next stage of an attack. ESET's internal research suggests such a specialized model can be trained at one two-hundredth of the cost of a large general reasoning model while giving more accurate, defense-focused results. The savings are credited to optimized training, a focus on cybersecurity vocabulary, purpose-built engineering, lower computing needs and privately owned hardware.

The company also describes a "never-go-rogue" design intended to keep the AI from escaping or acting on the open internet. Safeguards include restricted sandboxes, read-only tools, continuous monitoring, defined usage and token limits, a kill switch, and human expert oversight of critical response decisions. NeoCortex does not work as a standalone decision maker, but as one part of a layered architecture that also includes deterministic controls, correlation logic, validation and auditability. It is developed and self-hosted on ESET's own infrastructure, which the company says keeps sensitive security data and model operations under its control. ESET adds that this lowers customer exposure to shifts among third-party AI providers, whether commercial or geopolitical.

Juraj Malcho, ESET's Chief Technology Officer, said AI is speeding up both attacks and defenses, and that NeoCortex applies the company's AI investment to specialized intelligence it controls, strengthening human expertise instead of replacing it. He described the launch as a step toward a new generation of predictive, AI-powered security operations. ESET pointed to the week leading up to October 25, 2026, which it called Black October, when critical security issues affecting PHP, Linux, GitLab and other key systems demanded rapid, prioritized responses. The company describes itself as privately owned, with more than 35 years of cybersecurity experience, 11 global research centers, and protection for over 500,000 organizations across 178 countries.

stories.Headline: VIDEO: AI boom creates jobs but threatens others, dividing Nevada unions
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is eliminating some jobs while creating others, according to a report published by Gray DC on October 28, 2026. Reporter Rhyan Henson wrote that nearly every industry has felt the effects of the technology. Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by AI by 2030, with roles either transformed or erased. The article was filed under a headline pointing to divisions among Nevada unions, but the text itself covers the national picture and does not discuss Nevada or any union.

The changes are driving a growing need for human oversight of AI systems. Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, said people need to understand that human involvement is still required. He argued that there is not enough oversight right now and offered the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports that might leak sensitive information outside a company. Jones also said that relying on companies to govern themselves is not enough, comparing it to the fox watching the henhouse, and called for a third party or even the government to set limits on what AI can do. He added that the private oversight work is creating roles even as technology replaces others, and he noted that Microsoft recently offered buyouts to 60,000 employees because of AI.

Lawmakers have taken differing positions on how much the federal government should do. Rep. Buddy Carter, a Republican from Georgia, said the country is generally better off when Washington stays out of the way and said he does not want to stifle innovation. He still acknowledged that AI is a very useful tool and that there are real dangers, saying lawmakers must get it right. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said the United States must address the serious risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, and that the American people should make those decisions through their elected representatives.

For workers considering a career change, Jones advised them to start learning AI and to understand how it applies to their own profession. He said judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter, and that the aim should be to use the technology responsibly rather than compete with it. Efforts to regulate AI have stalled on Capitol Hill, according to the report. The 120th Congress could take up the issue when it returns in January.

stories.Headline: Privacy group files complaints against Scale AI over alleged worker surveillance
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, the Austria-based digital rights group noyb filed five complaints in Europe against San Francisco-based Scale AI over how its Outlier training platform treats freelance workers. Two of the complaints were filed in Austria, with one each in France, the Netherlands and Italy, all under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation. Outlier recruits freelancers and subject-matter experts to help train, evaluate and improve AI models, and noyb says it has more than 900,000 of them. Customers named in the reports include Meta, OpenAI, Google and the US government, and Meta is said to own nearly half of Scale. The complaints allege that trackers from companies such as TikTok, LinkedIn and Facebook are placed on workers' devices and given access to data like IP addresses and contact details, which can be used for targeted advertising and profiling.

A noyb spokesperson said an analysis found 18 third-party trackers on French freelancers' data, though the group says the real number is probably higher. A Dutch filing cites a May 22, 2026 network capture showing connections to several tracking services, and a French filing says one service logged cursor and keyboard activity every few seconds. The complaints also say workers must repeatedly pass biometric verification run by a company called Persona, which involves a face video and an uploaded ID. Four freelancers reportedly asked for copies of their personal data covering December 2025 to May 2026 and got no reply from Scale. Noyb wants courts in the four countries to impose fines, and it wants governments to open investigations and examine how Scale assigns tasks.

Noyb lawyer Lisa Steinfeld Leiser said such constant tracking while people work goes against all reasonable expectations, and she asked why LinkedIn or Facebook should know which tasks someone is doing. The group argues Scale has no valid legal basis for the trackers and breaches the rules on data minimization. A Scale spokesperson called the claims unfounded and inaccurate and disputed how noyb describes the trackers. The spokesperson said the company records screen activity and task duration only in some cases and only if workers opt in. Scale also says it checks identities to combat fraud and to comply with European law, lets workers ask for their data to be deleted at any time, and does not sell their personal data or use it to train customer AI models.

Noyb has a record of winning privacy cases against large technology firms. Its complaint against TikTok led to a €530 million fine in May 2025 for sending European users' data to China, and a complaint against Meta ended in a €1.2 billion fine in late 2023 over transfers of user data to the US. The group says the Scale case shows how vulnerable platform workers are, a category that also includes couriers and food delivery staff. The allegations are not regulatory findings, and no decision has been reported yet.

stories.Headline: Princeton students, faculty divided over access to University ChatGPT accounts
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, Princeton University emailed all faculty and staff to announce a one-year pilot program with OpenAI that gives students, faculty, and staff access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro. Faculty and staff could request access starting that day, while students will be able to request ChatGPT Plus in January, before the spring semester begins. According to the Office of Information Technology's FAQ page, students must first complete an online Foundations of AI Literacy course before using their accounts. The announcement was reported by The Daily Princetonian, and students and faculty who spoke with the paper were divided over it.

University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss said the contract is meant to bring enhanced data security and privacy protections as well as cost savings for the University. He said the University sees AI as a powerful modern tool for research and learning, but does not actively endorse its use for any particular purpose, much as providing wireless access does not mean approving of every website or app. Princeton already offers a limited set of approved AI tools at no cost, including Adobe Creative Cloud Image Generation and the basic Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat. Faculty can also get Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's 365 Copilot Premium, and Google's Gemini Workspace+ at varying monthly and annual rates.

Reactions on campus were mixed, and several faculty members said they were taken aback because they were not told about the pilot before the email. Hotchkiss said a number of faculty with expertise in AI or an interest in its use in research and teaching were consulted, and that more chances for faculty feedback are planned before the student rollout. History professor Kevin Kruse sharply criticized the University's rush to embrace generative AI, arguing that it undermines humanities teaching, wastes resources while programs like Outdoor Action are cancelled and faculty hiring is cut back, and harms the environment through data center water and electricity use. Neuroscience professor Sam Wang said he would rather have received a tool that detects AI use, such as Pangram. English professor Meredith Martin stressed that the program does not mean Princeton encourages AI use beyond what individual faculty require in their classes.

Students were split as well. Undergraduate Student Government Academics Chair Isaac Bernstein said his role is to protect student access and equity, and he argued that the program does not hurt academic integrity because many students already use these tools. Krystal Ma said the move feels like handing students an academic shortcut, while George Dennis and Mabel Li welcomed the savings, and Ammar Omar said exposing students to the tool is better than banning it. The Prince's 2030 Frosh Survey found that nearly 90 percent of students surveyed have used ChatGPT or another AI model, and a separate 2026 Digital Education Council survey found that 92 percent of students worldwide use AI in their studies. Students also pointed to peer schools, noting that Yale offers free access to an OpenAI-powered chatbot called Clarity, and that Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences made Claude available last spring and phased out ChatGPT Edu because few students used it.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Stocks Rebound 5.6% as AI Financing Faces Scrutiny
stories.Summary:
Shares of CoreWeave, the GPU-cloud provider listed on Nasdaq as CRWV, rose over three straight sessions in late October 2026. On October 26 the stock gained 4.91% to $56.90 by 1:30 p.m. ET, and the next day it traded at $58.95, up 6.8%, by midday. On Tuesday, October 28, it climbed almost 8%, adding $4.38 to close at $59.57, while the Nasdaq-100 rose just over 1%. The advance followed weeks of pressure, including one recent week in which the stock lost roughly a quarter of its value.

The financing numbers explain why investors have been nervous. CoreWeave reported second-quarter revenue of $2.575 billion but a net loss of $626 million, and its net interest expense of $640 million compared with adjusted operating income of $128 million. One article noted that this comparison mixes accounting measures and is not a formal interest-coverage ratio. The company carries a debt load of about $50 billion and has a backlog of roughly $104 billion that depends on meeting delivery and service-availability requirements. Its market capitalization is $32.51 billion against an enterprise value of $77.71 billion, and its GuruFocus GF Score is 15 out of 100.

On the operations side, most of a planned 22.5 megawatts of IT capacity at a Copenhagen site is now running, bringing CoreWeave's European footprint to nine data centers across five countries. The company also launched its first global AI network backbone and plans additional network points of presence in seven Asia-Pacific and Middle Eastern markets, with deployment starting in the fourth quarter and completion targeted for mid-2027. The announcement gave no new contracted revenue and no utilization rate for the Danish site. Reuters reported that a CoreWeave spokesperson said the company still sees opportunities to finance its expansion, a response to Elon Musk's warning about industry consolidation, which had put funding risks back in focus on October 26.

The latest jump came as Anthropic's IPO filing offered fresh evidence of demand for AI computing. The filing disclosed $16.3 billion in first-half revenue, nearly 14 times the level a year earlier, along with substantial long-term commitments for computing capacity. The GuruFocus commentary described the rally as a recovery in sentiment rather than proof that the financing problem has gone away. Investors are now watching bond yields, funding costs, new capacity additions, how quickly the backlog converts to revenue, and whether revenue growth begins to produce stronger free cash flow. The articles note that depreciation, networking expenses and financing needs can weigh on earnings while new capacity ramps up.

stories.Headline: Samsung's AI boom comes with a $100 billion warning
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Korea has warned that South Korea's semiconductor exports could drop by $50 billion to $100 billion next year if major U.S. technology companies cut spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to Reuters. The central bank's gloomy scenario assumes Korean semiconductor prices fall by 10%. That would trim South Korea's economic growth by about 0.4 percentage points and sharply reduce its current-account surplus compared with the bank's earlier 2027 forecast. The warning, reported on October 27, 2026, comes as Samsung Electronics enjoys one of the biggest profit booms in technology history.

The numbers behind the boom are large. Samsung expects third-quarter operating profit of around 107.4 trillion won on sales of roughly 195 trillion won, with profit nearly nine times higher than a year earlier. In the second quarter it reported sales of 171.5 trillion won and operating profit of 89.49 trillion won. Reuters reported that Samsung's third-quarter shipments of high-bandwidth memory may have risen close to 50% from the previous quarter. SK Hynix, which began trading U.S. depositary receipts on Nasdaq in July under the symbol SKHY, posted second-quarter revenue of 79.3 trillion won, up 257%, and operating profit of 60.5 trillion won, up 557%.

The demand driving those results comes from Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, whose combined capital spending grew from $40 billion last year to $80 billion this year and is expected to reach $110 billion next year, per the report. The Bank of Korea said in its August outlook that it assumed AI infrastructure investment would keep expanding and support strong chip exports into 2027, and it called the semiconductor cycle one of the biggest uncertainties in its projection. South Korea's economy grew 1% in the third quarter, ahead of the 0.7% a Reuters poll of economists had expected. Exports topped $800 billion in the first nine months of 2026, already above the previous full-year record, and are on track to pass $1 trillion for the first time.

The article notes that the memory market has always been cyclical, and that supply can catch up quickly if big customers slow construction of data centers. TrendForce expects traditional DRAM contract prices to rise just 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter, after a nearly 60% jump in the second. Samsung and Micron have said the supply imbalance could last until 2028. Samsung shares have already fallen more than 25% from their June peak, as investors question how long the boom will last. Samsung is due to report detailed third-quarter results on October 29, giving investors another look at memory profitability and management's view of AI demand.

stories.Headline: ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaims top spot in China’s rich list, thanks to his firm's AI push
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Hurun China Rich List, released on October 27 with wealth calculated as of September 1, 2026, put ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming back at the top for the second time. His fortune rose by 200 billion yuan from a year earlier to 670 billion yuan, which Hurun says sets a new record for the highest net worth on the China list. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng made his debut on the list with 280 billion yuan, landing directly in seventh place. The reshuffle was driven largely by artificial intelligence, and the article describes it as a generational change. Entrepreneurs whose core business is AI now make up 10.4% of all listed individuals, compared with none on the 2019 list and earlier.

Hurun values ByteDance, which is not publicly listed, at about 3.3 trillion yuan, with Zhang holding more than 20% of the shares. On the same basis, his 470 billion yuan fortune last year implied a valuation of about 2.3 trillion yuan, so the company's value rose by roughly 1 trillion yuan in a year. Other fortunes fell: Lei Jun of Xiaomi lost 157 billion yuan, dropping from 326 billion to 169 billion yuan, and Zhong Shanshan of Nongfu Spring lost 120 billion yuan, falling to second place with 410 billion yuan. Tencent's Ma Huateng lost 119 billion yuan and ranks fourth with 346 billion yuan, NetEase's Ding Lei lost 45 billion yuan and ranks eighth with 275 billion yuan, and Pinduoduo's Huang Zheng lost 112 billion yuan and fell to eleventh. The family of Pop Mart founder Wang Ning also saw a drop of 94.5 billion yuan.

Hurun attributes the declines for Lei, Zhong, Ma, Wang and others mainly to a correction after rapid gains last year, noting that their wealth is still generally higher than two years ago. Beyond the top spots, the list added many AI figures, including Liang's DeepSeek colleagues Zheng Dawei, Li Huan and Chen Zhe, and Zhipu AI's Liu Debing and Tang Jie, at 39.5 billion and 27.5 billion yuan. MiniMax founder Yan Junjie has 22.5 billion yuan, and Moonshot AI founder Yang Zhilin is the highest-ranked self-made entrepreneur under 35. Nearly 80 robotics entrepreneurs appeared, led by Unitree Robotics founder Wang Xingxing, who debuted with 69.5 billion yuan. Chip and data center suppliers also gained sharply, including Cambricon's Chen Tianshi, who rose by 25 billion yuan to 205 billion yuan and entered the top 10, and Chuan Hwa Technology's Lin family, whose wealth grew 335%.

Hurun calls AI the single largest engine of wealth growth this year, while cautioning that paper wealth does not mean companies have earned matching profits. DeepSeek has not been officially confirmed to be raising new money, though media reports in October said it was seeking about 100 billion yuan at a pre-money valuation of about 500 billion yuan. Hurun said Liang was left off last year partly because he had said he would not pursue commercialization, and DeepSeek has since begun exploring it. Not everyone in AI gained, as 167 entrepreneurs dropped off the list, including Unisound's Huang Wei and the 4Paradigm couple Dai Wenyuan and Wu Ming, mainly because of stock price corrections. The article concludes that the list shows not just how many billionaires AI created but where AI wealth sits across the industry chain, with computing power suppliers seeing the most direct gains from current orders and revenue.

stories.Headline: From Answers to Action: KNEX Unveils AI Agentic Apps for Oracle E-Business Suite, PeopleSoft, and JD Edwards at Oracle AI World 2026
stories.Summary:
KNEX Technology, a recognized Oracle Partner based in Irvine, California, announced on October 28, 2026, at Oracle AI World 2026 that KNEX AI Agentic Apps are now available for Oracle E-Business Suite, PeopleSoft, and JD Edwards. The apps bring AI-powered Command Centers to finance, HR, and supply chain teams. The company says they are meant to cut manual work, speed up cycle times, and modernize existing Oracle systems without replacing them. The launch builds on the KNEX AI Agent Packs introduced earlier this year, which let users ask questions of live enterprise data in plain language. The new apps go a step further by planning and completing business processes rather than only answering questions.

Each Command Center opens with a daily briefing for its functional area that shows what changed, what needs attention, and what is coming up. Configurable tiles show the information and AI-generated insights each team cares about most. Users can also start actions directly from the Command Center, with people kept in the loop to review and approve them. The apps enforce role-based access using the responsibilities and privileges users already hold in the underlying Oracle suite, so a person sees only the data and actions their role already permits. They are embedded in existing Oracle deployments, work with live transactional data, and deploy without an upgrade, migration, or major transformation project.

Basheer Khan, CEO of KNEX Technology, said the earlier Agent Packs showed customers how much faster work gets done when they can simply ask for answers, and that the new apps move from answers to action across complete business processes. Gustavo Gonzalez, the company's CTO, said agentic AI delivers value in the enterprise only when it is accurate, governed, and grounded in real business data. He added that every action is traceable, critical steps can require human approval, and customers decide how much autonomy to grant. Existing Agent Pack customers can extend their deployments with the new apps, while new customers can begin with the processes that matter most to them.

The apps target organizations running E-Business Suite, PeopleSoft, and JD Edwards that cannot migrate to Oracle Fusion Applications, offering them a path to agentic AI without a costly and disruptive move. The announcement came as Oracle itself pushed further into agentic tools, with Oracle announcing new HR-focused Fusion Agentic Applications powered by a governed execution layer called Fusion Claw at the HR Technology Conference in Las Vegas. Attendees at Oracle AI World 2026 can see live demonstrations at KNEX booth #5026 at The Venetian Convention and Expo Center in Las Vegas through October 28. More information and demonstrations can be requested at the company's website, www.knextech.com.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Unveils 335-Page Public Prospectus: Poised to Make History as the Largest-Ever IPO and the Most Loss-Making AI Company of All Time
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, has publicly filed its S-1 registration for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker "ANT." The filing, a 335-page prospectus posted to the SEC's website on October 26 and 27, 2026, follows a confidential draft the company submitted on June 1, 2026. Bloomberg has reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the company plans to complete the offering in mid-November. Because the SEC requires a public filing at least 15 days before a roadshow, the roadshow could begin as early as the second week of November.

The prospectus lays out the company's finances in detail. Revenue was 41 million dollars in 2023 and reached 16.286 billion dollars in the first half of 2026, compared with 1.16 billion in the same period a year earlier. The net loss for the first half was 80.748 billion dollars, against about 41.965 billion for all of 2025, but roughly 72.4 billion of the half-year loss came from fair value changes on convertible notes, derivative liabilities and other financing instruments, which is an accounting effect and not cash spent. About 80.2 percent of first-half revenue came from consumption-based billing such as API calls, or roughly 13.06 billion dollars, while subscriptions brought in about 3.2 billion, or 19.6 percent. The company counted more than 11,900 customers with trailing twelve-month revenue of at least 100,000 dollars as of September 30, 2026, up from 950 a year earlier, and its top two customers, each about 12 percent of revenue, turned out to be Amazon and Google, not the companies rumored earlier.

The public version also updates the company's computing commitments. The commitment to Microsoft rose from 31.4 billion to 44.9 billion dollars, the commitment to Google is 114.5 billion, and a contract with SpaceXAI carries a maximum of 120.5 billion. Two more computing suppliers, Nscale and Lambda, were newly disclosed. The article describes the filing as showing a single operating segment, overseen by CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, and says the company is choosing not to build image or video generation models so it can focus on programming, agent capabilities and safety research. At an investor day in mid-October, the company said third-quarter revenue reached 16.8 billion dollars, up 45 percent from the prior quarter, and that it had turned profitable on an adjusted basis.

On valuation, the earlier draft pointed to a maximum raise of about 1 trillion dollars at a valuation near 2 trillion, which would exceed the 1.77 trillion dollar valuation at which SpaceX went public in June and make it the largest IPO ever. With pressure on the AI sector, some investors have reportedly cut their expectations to about 1.5 trillion. The final price has not been set. If the listing goes ahead, Anthropic would beat rival OpenAI to the public markets and become the first company focused on frontier large models to list in the United States.

stories.Headline: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
stories.Summary:
China's AI-linked stocks have crashed, according to a Reuters report published on October 27, 2026. The mainland STAR50 index of AI and semiconductor leaders has fallen 40% in less than four months, wiping out about US$480 billion in market value. China's broad blue-chip index is down about 20% from highs it reached in June. The slide has ended a rally that had run for two years, since promises of economic stimulus sent shares higher.

Several retail favourites have been hit hard. Shares in robot-maker Unitree, which was 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers at listing, have halved since trading began in August, and chipmaker CXMT has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. Chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which jumped 700% and 400% respectively on their debuts in 2025, have also halved since July. Optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology are down roughly 60% from their June and July highs, partly because Washington is moving toward barring them from supplying US data centres. Goldman Sachs data shows AI stocks make up 42% of China's market capitalisation and 57% of turnover across mainland A-shares and Hong Kong H-shares, so few investors in a market dominated by small traders have escaped losses.

The article names no single trigger for the selling, though traders pointed to high prices, tax bills and the threat of the US or other countries banning Chinese equipment in data centres. Worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports also weighed on valuations. The China Securities Regulatory Commission did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions, but it said its chairman, Wu Qing, met market participants earlier in October to hear ideas for improving capital markets. Fund manager Dong Baozhen said the market had turned into a speculative frenzy and that the bubble is now bursting, while Wang Zhuo of Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management said all bubbles inevitably burst and predicted chipmakers and AI suppliers would end up in a price war. Hong Hao of Lotus Asset Management said the rout will halt many companies trying to list, and Leo Wang of Qianchuang Capital argued that weighting indexes heavily toward tech firms distorted how capital behaved and drained other sectors.

The crash cuts against Beijing's efforts to encourage savers into stocks to fund the AI boom and to build a steadier "slow bull" market in place of the old boom-and-bust pattern. Authorities had been cracking down on leverage and high-frequency trading, and state-backed investors sold into rallies to keep gains in check. For comparison, US AI stocks have led a 6% drop in the Nasdaq from a record high set three weeks earlier. The STAR50 still trades at around 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250 at its peak, against about 30 for the Nasdaq 100, so some investors fear the sell-off could worsen before it improves. Many retail investors have moved into defensive assets, and equity fundraising by tech firms is likely to slow, though Goldman Sachs and BNP Paribas strategist William Bratton still see opportunities for careful buyers.

stories.Headline: Omnichat Raises US$10M Series A Led by Openspace Capital to Scale AI Agent Platform and Drive Global Expansion
stories.Summary:
Omnichat, a Hong Kong-based AI marketing and customer experience platform, announced on October 27, 2026, that it has closed a US$10 million Series A funding round. Openspace Capital led the round, with Darwin Ventures and Acorn Pacific Ventures also taking part. The company said it will use the money to scale its agentic AI platform, deepen research and development on its Omni AI Agents, and speed up expansion beyond Asia Pacific. Omnichat launched the Omni AI Agents suite in 2026.

The suite includes an AI Marketing Agent that builds customer segments and produces full messaging campaigns from one prompt, an AI Sales Agent that recommends products and closes orders inside the chat, and an AI Customer Service Agent that handles enquiries around the clock. A fourth tool, OmniClaw, works as an AI business analyst that tracks customer behaviour, chat trends and store-level revenue attribution in real time. Around 300 brands adopted OmniClaw within two months of its June launch, and the number of brands using the Marketing Agent tripled over the same period. The agents run across WhatsApp, LINE, Facebook Messenger, Instagram, WeChat, KakaoTalk and TikTok. Omnichat also says it attributes revenue back to the conversation, including purchases completed in physical stores.

Founder and CEO Alan Chan said the round marks a move from conversational commerce to AI-driven commerce. He argued that traditional customer messaging tools still depend heavily on human intervention to drive sales, while the Omni AI Agent platform lets companies deploy agents that sell, market and support customers at all hours. Chan added that working with the three investors gives the company support to scale this approach across Asia Pacific and globally. The company's own materials describe it as a Meta Business Partner, a WhatsApp Business Solution Provider and a LINE Biz-Solutions Tech Partner.

Omnichat says it has helped 5,000 clients generate over US$100 million in revenue, and it lists Dyson, FILA, Watsons, L'OCCITANE, VF Corporation, SMCP and Mead Johnson among its clients. Unlike shared-inbox tools that only gather chats in one place, it says its platform puts marketing, sales and customer service on a single customer profile. The company's stated aim is to help businesses grow revenue without growing headcount. Openspace Capital, the lead investor, is a multi-strategy asset manager based in Singapore with a focus on Southeast Asia, and its past investments include GoJek (GoTo), Kredivo, Fano, Video Rebirth and TradeGecko. Omnichat said it will deploy the new capital to build its market presence globally, building on its existing footprint across Asia Pacific.

stories.Headline: Idris Elba's Akuna Group launches free Artificial Intelligence (AI) filmmaking programme for ...
stories.Summary:
The Akuna Group, which is chaired by Sir Idris Elba, opened applications on 26 October 2026 for a free artificial intelligence filmmaking programme called From Script to Screen with AI. The programme is aimed at creators in Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and South Africa. It is delivered through Akuna Learning, the group's education platform, in collaboration with Google. Google.org is supporting it with US$1 million in funding, and the curriculum was developed by Curious Refuge. Applications are submitted online at AkunaLearning.com.

The deadline to apply is 15 November 2026, and the programme is free both to apply to and, for those chosen, to attend. Over fifty weeks, selected creators move from a twelve-week academy into mentoring, pitching and production, with the finished films to be showcased in October 2027. Everyone takes a foundational AI filmmaking course and then picks one of five pathways: fiction, documentary, animation, advertising or screenwriting. The five stages run from selection between October 2026 and January 2027, to online training and certification from February to April 2027, mentoring from April to June, pitching in June and July, and production from July to October 2027. Applicants must live in one of the five countries, be 18 or older, have a laptop, reliable internet and steady power, and be able to commit fully to the academy, while no AI experience, film school degree or minimum years in the industry is required.

Elba said the effort is about giving creators across the continent access to learning so they can tell their own stories. He noted that selected projects will receive production funding and that creators will keep control of their work, and he said he hopes the education leads to employment and helps shape the narrative of Africa. Khaled Gad, the group's chief executive, said training alone does not build an industry and that creators need a route from the classroom to the screen. He added that the programme opens on the same day and runs to the same standard in all five countries, and that applicants need finished work showing what they can do and an application in by 15 November. The programme and its partners claim no ownership rights over what participants make.

The programme is open to a wide range of visual storytellers, including filmmakers, screenwriters, animators, advertisers, digital content creators, photographers, designers, editors and visual artists. Applicants are asked to include existing creative work, however modest, and women are strongly encouraged to apply. Review panels will sit in each country, with a final panel looking across all five. Graduates of the academy will put forward one-page ideas, and shortlisted idea owners will build teams that spend four weeks with mentors and subject experts. Mentor-endorsed teams will then pitch to panels drawn from Akuna, Google and the wider industry, and the selected projects will be funded and taken on to festivals and showcases.
