stories.Headline: Fujifilm plans 5x production boost of 100TB magnetic storage tapes driven by skyrocketing AI storage demand
stories.Summary:
Fujifilm plans to raise its magnetic tape production capacity fivefold to meet demand driven by artificial intelligence, according to Nikkei Asia, which reported the plan on October 28, 2026. The Japanese company would make the investment in order to supply offline storage media used for critical data. The expansion is described as Fujifilm's largest investment in the medium in roughly 20 years. The reporting came from sources familiar with the plan, and the article's figures are the ones the sources gave.

Magnetic tape is used by data center operators, financial institutions and research organizations to back up data, and the report says AI has revived interest in it. The article presents the plan as a response to that rising need for storage rather than a change to the product itself. The headline describes the tapes as 100TB units, though the body text provided does not add further detail on capacity per cartridge. No specific dollar cost, timeline for completing the buildup, or new facility locations appear in the material available.

Fujifilm is the company responsible for the plan, and the reporting attributes the information to sources rather than to a formal public statement from the company. The article notes that Fujifilm has been raising its profile in other areas, while the magnetic tape business is the focus of this expansion. The reporting does not include a direct on-the-record comment from the company in the text provided. Nikkei's account is the basis for the plan as described here.

The wider context is a broader push across the storage and electronics sector to keep pace with AI infrastructure demand. The article places the Fujifilm plan within a period in which data centers are scaling up and older storage technologies are finding new use. The available material does not say how competitors are responding or what regulatory steps, if any, are involved. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan partners with Dutch company Wonderful on AI solutions
stories.Summary:
Azerbaijan's Ministry of Digital Development and Transport and the Dutch company Wonderful signed a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in artificial intelligence and related digital technologies at a ceremony in Baku on 29 October 2026. Deputy Minister Rashad Hasanov, Farid Osmanov, chairman of the Innovation and Digital Development Agency, and a delegation led by Wonderful co-founder and CEO Bar Winkler attended the signing. The memorandum sets up a framework for exploring the use of AI solutions built on the Wonderful platform across ministries, government agencies and state-owned enterprises. The articles do not say how much the arrangement is worth or set any deadlines for putting it into practice.

The agreement is meant to fit Azerbaijan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy for 2025–2028 and its Action Plan for Accelerating Digital Development for 2026–2028. It also supports the ministry's wider work on building a modern public sector that serves citizens and relies on data. Separately, the Innovation and Digital Development Agency announced on the same day that companies offering cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, robotics, and ICT training and consulting services can now register as technopark residents. Until now only ICT firms focused mainly on system integration and software development could do so. Osmanov said registration will no longer depend on a physical location, so ICT companies in other regions can register digitally and gain resident status.

Osmanov made the technopark remarks at a media briefing on legislative amendments in technology and innovation, and he presented the expansion as a broadening of the existing incentive scheme. stories.Headline: First Humanist Wins Religious Exemption From AI at Work. Could You?
stories.Summary:
A humanist from Kentucky has become, by the American Humanist Association's account, the first humanist granted a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence at work. David Durman, a 45-year-old research administrator at the University of Kentucky, objected when the university began asking employees to use AI tools in their workflow, including Microsoft Teams Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT. He argued that using such tools would undercut his ability to think through his work and ethics, which he sees as part of developing himself as a moral person. With help from the American Humanist Association, he requested an accommodation under Title VII, the federal law that lets employees seek changes to work requirements for religious reasons, and in a letter dated September 25 an Office of Equal Opportunity senior manager said the request was granted.

The accommodation means Durman is excused from personal use of AI to complete his tasks, though he may still be expected to attend meetings or submit materials through sites that use AI. Staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens of the American Humanist Association said officials found no undue burden on his department and granted the request promptly after a collegial meeting. Durman's letter cited his personal beliefs and the 2003 Humanist Manifesto, which stresses freedom of conscience and human flourishing. Federal courts have ruled that humanism qualifies as a religion, so humanists receive the same Title VII protections as other faith groups, according to Huiskens. Legal scholar Douglas Laycock noted that such requests depend on whether the belief is sincere and analogous to a religious commitment, a question an employer would normally investigate.

The case comes amid wider skepticism about AI from religious leaders and the public. Pope Leo XIV warned in his recent encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas" that AI could weaken democracy and human dignity and concentrate power among a few elites. A Washington Post-ABC News-IPOS poll released this week found that 57 percent of Americans said AI is bad for society, and two-thirds opposed building the data centers needed to run it. Durman said he worries AI use harms society at a broader level, and his request was partly inspired by Erin Maus, a Unitarian Universalist software engineer who received an exemption from her employer over religious concerns about AI. Durman said he hopes his example and those of others seeking accommodations will prompt more people to think through the implications of AI use.

stories.Headline: AI at Wake Forest: What the AI Task Force is doing and how you can help shape what’s next
stories.Summary:
Wake Forest University's AI Task Force, chaired by William Fleeson, associate provost for AI initiatives and Hultquist Family Professor of Psychology, shared a question-and-answer update on its work on October 28, 2026. The group's main job this year is to develop an overall academic strategy for AI, and it is also supporting three pilot programs under an initiative called AI for Human Flourishing. Members come from academic affairs, research, the library, information technology, and personal and career development, and include Andy Chan, Anne Hardcastle, Kim McAllister, Mur Muchane and Lauren Pressley. Separately, Cleveland Clinic's Cancer Institute formalized a strategic approach to evaluating emerging AI technologies, according to an article dated October 26, 2026. At Wake Forest, the three faculty-led pilots are already underway.

The AI Teaching Studio, directed by Fleeson, is working across 12 priority areas covering faculty development, course design, departmental engagement and institutional planning. AI Compass, led by Ana Iltis, has funded 17 research and scholarship projects on how AI affects human identity, health and societal well-being. The AI Impact Clinic, a new computer science and business course designed by Shannon McKeen, Paul Pauca and Errin Fulp, has 57 students this fall, and selected students will work with faculty in the spring to build AI solutions for clients. The task force said it is not writing a University-wide policy on AI use in individual classrooms, because faculty are best placed to decide given differences among disciplines. The existing Guidelines for Academic Use and Guidelines for Administrative Use stay in effect, and schools and departments have been asked to develop their own approaches this year.

The strategy is still in its early stages, and early ideas will be shared at three town halls hosted with the Faculty Senate: Monday, Nov. 2, 4 to 5 p.m. in Tribble Hall A110, Monday, Nov. 16, 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. in Benson 409, and Wednesday, Dec. 16, 2 to 3 p.m. in Carswell 111/Annenberg Forum. Faculty and staff can also answer the second-year campus AI survey by November 2, which enters them in a drawing for a $100 or $50 gift card at the Deacon Shop, or send feedback to Fleeson directly.

At Cleveland Clinic, the new Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy is led by Dr. Paul Thambi and Dr. Louis Williams. It vets proposals from AI companies, weighing their effect on operations and care delivery and their fit with enterprise goals. Current uses include personalizing radiation doses for lung cancer patients, cutting notetaking time by up to 75%, and streamlining patient referrals. Williams said AI will be fundamental to running the institute, and that it must reduce barriers to adoption while keeping proper governance. The enterprise AI Task Force, which Williams compared to an institutional review board for non-research applications, checks safety, bias and data security, and monitors models for changes in performance over time.

stories.Headline: OpenAI now lets you text your Dot.
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has begun rolling out a feature that lets users text their Dot, its AI agent, through iMessage or RCS. The company said the feature is arriving in preview for US Pro users, after it had promised the capability for its AI agents. The Verge reported the news on October 28, 2026, noting that the feature is now available. The article itself is short and focused on the launch rather than on details about pricing or wider availability.

Separately, a Vocal Media piece published on October 28, 2026 reported that OpenAI is introducing an invisible watermark for text generated by ChatGPT and Codex. The system, called textGrain, slightly shifts word choices to embed a statistical pattern that is undetectable to readers but can be identified by a detector. It is set to apply by default only to users in the European Union, so a user in Munich would generate watermarked text while a user in Malaysia would not, unless a developer opts in through the API. The watermark does not identify the individual user, and it survives basic copying and pasting.

OpenAI itself acknowledged that the watermark is fragile, according to the article. In internal testing, replacing 10% of words in a 400-token passage with synonyms dropped detection accuracy from 92% to 66%, and swapping 25% of words reduced it to 17%. Detection is also weaker on short passages, math answers, and translated text, and OpenAI is limiting access to the detector to approved researchers and expert organizations for now. The company cautioned that a missing watermark does not prove human authorship, and a present watermark does not show how much human editing shaped the output.

The article places the move within a wider industry effort to establish AI provenance ahead of regulatory deadlines, including the EU AI Act's transparency rules that took effect on August 2. Google uses its SynthID watermark, Meta uses Content Seal, and Microsoft and Adobe back the C2PA standard, while Anthropic announced in August that it would watermark Claude text worldwide and faced user backlash. The article notes that open-source models can generate unwatermarked text and that each company's detector typically recognizes only its own mark. It concludes that text watermarking remains a probabilistic tool rather than definitive proof of authorship.

The company's results showed that Google's artificial intelligence is driving more search queries, according to a statement from Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai. Even so, revenue generated from search came in lower than analysts had expected. The drop in the share price followed that gap between usage growth and earnings.

Pichai framed the quarter around the growth in search activity tied to AI features, which he presented as a sign the products are gaining traction with users. The figures in the coverage, however, show that the money coming from search did not keep pace with that increase in queries. Investors had been expecting search revenue to be stronger, so the shortfall weighed heavily on the stock. The articles do not provide the specific revenue figures or the size of the expected and actual numbers.

The coverage attributes the outcome to Alphabet and its leadership, with Pichai speaking for the company in its statement about the quarter. The company has not, according to the reporting, offered a detailed explanation in these pieces for why AI-driven search activity has not translated into the revenue analysts projected. The articles were published as the broader conversation about the AI economy continued on Here & Now, where Scott Tong spoke with Ali Velshi about Google and that wider economy. stories.Headline: Cadence Brings AI Design and HPC Expertise to DOE Genesis Mission Consortium
stories.Summary:
Cadence, the electronic design automation and digital twin company, announced on October 29, 2026, that it has joined the Genesis Mission Consortium, a U.S. Department of Energy public-private partnership that uses artificial intelligence to speed up scientific discovery. The company said it will contribute AI-enabled design and simulation technology along with engineering expertise to work with DOE National Laboratories on priorities including advanced microelectronics, quantum and superconducting systems, data center energy efficiency and AI-driven scientific workflows. The consortium was launched by Executive Order in November 2025 and is led by DOE Under Secretary for Science Dr. Darío Gil. Its stated goal is to double the productivity and impact of American science and engineering within a decade by linking supercomputers, AI systems, experimental facilities and datasets across the 17 DOE National Laboratories.

Tom Beckley, senior vice president of Strategic Technology Programs at Cadence, said the company has long believed AI-driven design and physics-based simulation will reshape how critical systems are built. He described joining the consortium as a way to put Cadence's AI-enabled electronic design automation and system design and analysis technologies toward America's scientific leadership. Beckley said the company looks forward to working with the national laboratories, consortium partners and the research community on discoveries that bolster U.S. competitiveness, energy security and innovation. The announcement was issued as a press release through Business Wire and carried on HPCwire and Yahoo Finance.

Cadence's participation builds on existing work with several national laboratories, including Sandia, Fermi, Oak Ridge, Lawrence Livermore, Argonne and Brookhaven, as well as NASA Ames Research Center. Dr. Jeffrey S. Vetter of Oak Ridge National Laboratory said the Genesis Mission offers an extraordinary opportunity to accelerate discovery through AI, high-performance computing and advanced design tools. He said the collaboration with Cadence would bring advanced engineering capabilities into research workflows. The company plans to contribute subject-matter expertise, provide access to its AI-enabled EDA, system design and analysis, multiphysics simulation, digital twin and advanced packaging tools for pilots, and help integrate its workflows with laboratory HPC environments. It also plans to work with laboratories and academic partners on training and curriculum for AI-enabled engineering.

stories.Headline: Palantir defense chief says AI advances may force China to invade Taiwan
stories.Summary:
Palantir's head of defense, Mike Gallagher, said on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that advances in artificial intelligence have made it more likely that Chinese leader Xi Jinping will try to take control of Taiwan. He spoke at a defense policy event in Indiana alongside Republican Senator Jim Banks. Gallagher is a former Republican congressman who once led a House committee on US strategic competition with China, and he joined Palantir later in 2024 after leaving Congress. Gallagher argued that Taiwan has become so important to AI development that Beijing may feel pressed to act on its plans for the island. He said that if the United States pulls ahead in AI, Xi may see a window he cannot count on later, since China may be unable to catch up.

Taiwan is home to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's leading producer of advanced AI chips, which Gallagher said gives the island strategic weight. He warned that a Chinese takeover could let Beijing control or disable that company and hold the rest of the world's economy hostage. China has long claimed Taiwan as its territory, and Xi has promoted peaceful unification without ruling out military force, while Taiwanese officials have rejected those claims. During a September summit with President Donald Trump, Xi asked the United States to change its position on the island and oppose Taiwanese independence. A US intelligence assessment in March concluded that an invasion would be extremely challenging and carry a high risk of failure, a shift from earlier warnings that China might have invasion capability by 2027.

Chinese forces have also increased coast guard patrols off Taiwan's east coast, in addition to their regular military drills in the area. Gallagher also said that AI companies increasingly discuss the point at which models begin to improve themselves, and he compared the technology to nuclear weapons in the 1940s. Palantir supplies the Pentagon with tools including its Maven Smart System, which uses artificial intelligence for surveillance and targeting and has been used by US forces in operations against Iran. The article does not report any response from Beijing or Taipei to Gallagher's remarks, nor any scheduled follow-up.

The letter contains four pages of questions and asks for "exhaustive responses" by Nov. 3, before the AI company goes public. The company is reportedly planning an IPO that could bring in up to $100 billion. According to the Journal, the filing sets up a stock market debut as early as the week ahead of Thanksgiving. In the filing, Anthropic said its technology could reshape programming, research and everyday tasks, and might help cure serious illnesses. The company also cautioned that AI might help produce novel bioweapons and could destabilize the geopolitical order.

Warren wrote that the risks posed by the company's AI technology demand greater scrutiny before they become intertwined with public capital markets, the Journal reported. She is one of several legislators urging the AI industry to slow work on advanced systems so tougher rules can be put in place. The article notes that Warren previously asked the Securities and Exchange Commission to halt SpaceX's IPO, citing its target valuation, a governance structure that concentrates power in CEO Elon Musk, and changes to stock index rules. That SpaceX offering went ahead as planned in June, according to the Journal. stories.Headline: MP Spurious Liquor Case: Accused Used AI to Learn Brewing Methods
stories.Summary:
Police in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district say an arrested man used artificial intelligence to learn how to brew liquor at home by mixing chemicals and water. The fake liquor was blended with real alcohol and poured into empty licensed bottles bought from scrap dealers, then sold mostly in rural areas. Police arrested 10 people on Monday, October 27, and seized six cartons of country liquor, according to Dewas Kotwali Police Station in-charge Shashikant Chaurasia. Police said the arrested man, Ajay Rathore, had been using AI since September to look up home-brewing methods. Reports also say he ordered chemicals through a private firm in Indore, though the officials did not name the chemicals.

Investigators say Rathore collected empty licensed bottles from scrap dealers between October 2 and 7 and prepared the fake liquor with help from other accused. Among those arrested are two managers and two salesmen from three licensed liquor shops in Dewas and Indore districts, who allegedly supplied alcohol illegally. Police say the adulterated liquor was sold to local residents between October 6 and 12. The Indore warehouse of the private firm that supplied the chemicals has been sealed, and relevant provisions of the Excise Act have been added to the FIR. Viscera samples from the two deceased, along with the recovered liquor, have gone to the Forensic Science Laboratory, and the cause of death will be confirmed once the report arrives.

Police say two other employees of a licensed liquor shop are also involved, and a search for them is underway. Villagers in Chandana, Binjana and nearby areas of Dewas claim at least 10 people died after drinking poisonous liquor between September 27 and October 16. State Congress President Jitu Patwari alleges that 22 people died and at least 40 lost their eyesight over the past month. The district administration first dismissed the death claims. After the controversy grew, the state government formed a five-member high-level investigation team to probe the matter.

The reports note that the death toll claims remain under investigation and that the forensic findings are still awaited. Police have not confirmed how many of the deaths were linked to the adulterated liquor. Each account is based on statements from police officials and local claims as reported by PTI. The next step is the forensic report, which will determine the cause of the deaths, along with the work of the state investigation team.

stories.Headline: Human in the loop is not yet an AI agent recovery plan
stories.Summary:
Keeping a human in the loop is a common way enterprises govern what AI agents do, but a new study suggests that approval alone does not prepare organizations to recover when things go wrong. Krista Case, principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research, discussed the findings with Dave Vellante, co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, during a broadcast tied to the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit on October 28, 2026. The research examined how organizations are governing agent actions and preparing for incidents. Case said companies are still leaning heavily on human approval to secure AI actions while pushing to move faster at machine scale. The study drew on 25 enterprise technology and security leaders, 19 of whom had agents in production.

None of those 19 allowed agents to carry out high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. Vellante compared the gap to organizations that test failover in disaster recovery but never test failback. Case explained that restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, so recovery may require rebuilding the sequence of actions the agent took.

Eleven of the 25 practitioners said they lacked full ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems. Speed makes the problem harder, according to Case, because agents can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute. The research also found a counterintuitive pattern: organizations that let agents perform low-risk actions on their own were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios. Case described this bounded autonomy as a sign of a more mature security program.

Twelve of the 25 respondents had not addressed, or did not plan to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. Vellante said these are the capabilities needed if human-in-the-loop controls break down. Case expects the field to change quickly, saying it is very volatile and will likely look far more advanced within a year. The discussion was part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the summit, and Dell Technologies sponsored that segment, though neither Dell nor other sponsors have editorial control over the content.

stories.Headline: AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
stories.Summary:
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, a meteorologist in Alabama called emergency management expert Laura Myers about a problem. A local emergency manager had published a graphic warning that the storm might bring a "sting jet" of high winds to the Alabama coast, but he had made the graphic with an AI chatbot, and it was not meteorologically accurate. Myers, who directs the University of Alabama's Center for Advanced Public Safety, said the official had asked the tool to help him draw attention to local risk, and it produced what he asked for rather than what the weather data supported. Most emergency management agencies do not allow staff to use generative AI, yet the experts interviewed agree that it is likely already widespread in state and local disaster departments. Hundreds of companies are selling AI tools to emergency managers, and public communication is among the areas where officials and startups show the most interest.

Public alerts are a natural target for these tools because emergency managers often struggle to communicate clearly. They tend to use jargon, leave out information they assume people already know, and include details that distract from urgent instructions. Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who built a dashboard of alert templates, said many agencies have too few staff and little time, so they treat communication as a priority only after a failure reveals its importance. Emergency managers at the state and local level form the first line of defense after an extreme weather event, and they often say that trust is their currency, which they build or lose through what they tell the public. Poor communication has already caused harm in past disasters.

In 2016 adjacent California counties issued a "voluntary" and a "mandatory" evacuation for the same wildfire, and in 2019 Australian officials used a "Watch and Act" phrase that the government later admitted caused significant confusion. The most serious case cited is Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire, when a heavy rainstorm weeks later produced a deadly mudslide. Santa Barbara County sent alerts to residents in the voluntary evacuation zone, telling them to stay alert and be prepared to leave immediately, and many people treated the notice as optional, while others had no wish to leave a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others. Sutton describes this pattern as warning fatigue, and she warns that governments issuing poor warnings risk losing the public's trust.

Advocates of AI argue that large language models could help here, since they can review large volumes of alerts and research in minutes and then revise a draft in seconds. Rob Dale, who runs emergency management in Ingham County, Michigan, said an inexperienced official facing a chemical plume could likely do better with AI help than with memory of training taken years earlier, though he would still want to control when an alert is sent. Some companies say the technology is already good enough, and the startup EM1 says its in-house model can match or exceed most human emergency managers on benchmark tests. When Sutton ran a flood alert from a New Mexico county through the model, it produced a much clearer message that named the sender, specified the location, told residents what to do, and pointed them to updates, though it still needed human review.

EM1 has contracts with about a hundred agencies and school districts, but none uses it to automate extreme weather alerts yet. Experts believe many officials are already using personal or free chatbot accounts to draft messages, even if they do not say so. Still, researchers warn that AI-generated content can seem inauthentic to a skeptical public, and that faster alerts could add to warning fatigue. For now, the experts say, the software is only as good as the person using it, and it has not yet reached the point of working without a human expert involved.

stories.Headline: Teens often turn to AI when feeling distressed; report flags mental health risks
stories.Summary:
A new report from The Jed Foundation, a youth mental health organization, links some uses of artificial intelligence with poorer mental health among teenagers. The group surveyed thousands of middle and high school students and found that more than 80% use AI in some capacity. It did not find a link between overall AI use and worse mental health, but it did find associations among students who used AI for schoolwork, problem-solving advice, companionship, or help when they were emotionally struggling. The report was published this week as a follow-up to a Capitol Hill briefing the researchers held over the summer.

Students who used AI for schoolwork reported higher levels of loneliness and a greater lifetime history of suicidal thoughts. Those who turned to AI for relationship or problem-solving advice showed greater symptoms of anxiety and depression, more loneliness, and higher suicidal risk. Students who used AI for friendship or companionship, or who sought help from it when emotionally struggling, had greater anxiety and depression symptoms, more loneliness, and a history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. They also reported lower resilience and flourishing. Most students, 58%, said they use AI for schoolwork, while 12% said they use it for friendship or companionship.

The report's author, Kayla Anderson, JED's vice president of research and evaluation, said the way adults talk with young people about AI matters a great deal. She noted that 57% of students said they use AI when they feel sad, stressed, lonely or overwhelmed, though only 8% said they specifically sought help with their feelings from it. Anderson said AI should never replace human counsel and connection for young people. She also cautioned that the study found an association rather than a cause, and that it is still unclear how much AI itself drives worse outcomes. She said it is plausible that already struggling kids lean on AI more, and that such use could also worsen their problems.

Anderson said the issue needs to be addressed at the systems level, with tools designed specifically for safety. For parents, she said the first advice is not to let young people use AI as a friend or companion, since AI companions are associated with worse mental health in teens. She added that families should have early and frequent conversations about what young people use AI for, so that they do not hand too much of their thinking and relationship work to the technology. Anderson stressed that such work should stay in human spaces.

stories.Headline: Likely 40 Tesla Robotaxi in Each of Houston, Tampa, Miami and Orlando
stories.Summary:
Brian Wang, writing on NextBigFuture.com on October 29, 2026, argues that Tesla's robotaxi fleet in Houston, Tampa, Miami and Orlando is likely much larger than the figures tracked publicly. He estimates about 40 vehicles in each of these cities, and roughly 75 to 140 across the three Florida cities alone, instead of the 38 that a crowdsourced tracker had recorded in Florida. His estimate for Texas and Florida combined is between 1,155 and 1,220 robotaxis, compared with 1,080 registered vehicles in Texas. The piece is built on weekly unsupervised mileage and ride counts rather than on direct confirmation of vehicles.

The reasoning rests on the idea that the tracker has undersampled the service. Wang notes that Tampa, Miami and Orlando reported similar weekly driverless miles, roughly 5,600 to 6,100 each, and similar service areas of about 24 to 31 square miles, yet logged very different numbers of rides and identified cars. He says Miami had recorded no rides in the prior month even though it reported about 20,000 miles and 7,000 rides, which he treats as proof that the sampling is incomplete. Converting miles to fleet size at an assumed 200 to 1,000 miles per active vehicle per week, he suggests 25 to 45 vehicles per Florida city. He cross-checks the method against Waymo's published figures, which imply about 900 to 1,000 miles per vehicle per week, and says that fits his mid-range assumption.

Wang does not attribute the gap to any particular cause in Tesla's operations, and he presents the estimates as his own calculations from public data. He calls the crowdsourced tracker's coverage the likely source of the undercount and says a proper statistical test, with error bars and a comparison against a more active city such as Austin, would be needed to firm up the numbers. The article does not include a statement from Tesla, and it does not say whether Tesla has disclosed fleet sizes for these cities. The piece is an analysis rather than a report of a confirmed change, and it offers no timetable for any further data or corrections.

stories.Headline: California Enacts AI Spokespeople, Chatbots and Content Disclosures Laws - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
California's governor recently signed three artificial intelligence bills into law, and the articles say two take effect January 1, 2027 while one took effect immediately. The first, SB 1000, amended the California AI Transparency Act and took effect on signature, September 30, 2026. It covers providers of publicly accessible generative AI systems in California and removes the former threshold of more than a million monthly visitors or users. Systems designed primarily as assistive technology are exempt until January 1, 2029. The bill also requires covered providers, where technically feasible, to embed a latent disclosure in images, video, and audio their systems create or alter.

That disclosure must name the provider, the system and version, the creation or alteration date and time, a unique identifier, and whether the system made or changed the content. It may be given directly or through a link to a website with the information. Covered providers must also offer a free, publicly accessible disclosure verification tool, directly or through a qualifying third party. The tool must let users assess whether content is AI-generated or AI-altered, show the system provenance of the content's data, and avoid outputting personal data unless the person concerned gave informed consent. The second law, SB 1050, was signed by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 16, 2026, and takes effect January 1, 2027.

SB 1050 covers synthetic performers, which may be visual replicas or synthetic voice-over narrators, in advertisements for products or services. Under it, anyone who creates and publishes an advertisement in California that prominently features a synthetic performer must include a clear and conspicuous disclosure near the performer, visible and held long enough for a reasonable consumer to understand it. The articles define a synthetic performer as a digital figure, voice, or representation made wholly or partly with artificial intelligence, machine learning, or similar techniques, which appears human and cannot be based on or intended to depict a specific identifiable person. The articles note this differs from laws in New York, Tennessee, and Washington, which focused on deepfakes and digital replicas of identifiable people. The third law, AB 1609, was signed September 28, 2026, and also starts January 1, 2027.

AB 1609 applies to large private businesses with more than $500 million in national gross annual revenue that serve California customers. Those businesses may not represent that an AI customer service chatbot is human, and must disclose the chatbot's nature in the interaction's medium whenever a reasonable person could believe they are talking to a human. They must also offer a simple way to request a human agent during at least regular business hours, make a good-faith effort to connect the customer with a human within 15 minutes of the request, and, if that is not possible, let the person schedule an appointment within one business day. The authors, attorneys Liisa M. Thomas and Kathryn Smith of Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP, say these laws signal a trend in AI and privacy regulation and expect more to follow quickly. They advise companies to review how adaptable their privacy and AI governance programs are to coming changes in this and other state laws.

stories.Headline: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Ohio State University have built an artificial intelligence framework that could help plan future trips to the moon. Developed by Gokce Inal, a PhD candidate in civil, environmental and geodetic engineering, the system is meant to help scientists judge possible lunar landing sites, flag hazards that future crews could face, and search new areas for valuable geologic features. The work was presented this month at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society. Inal said the findings were shared as part of a broader effort to bring together artificial intelligence and planetary science.

The system, called LUMINA, is an extension of an earlier lunar model known as LLaVA-LE, which could describe lunar terrain and answer science questions. LUMINA adds the ability to plan and carry out multistep analyses, evaluate candidate landing sites, and explain the evidence behind its recommendations. Early results show it can make complex lunar observations and produce meaningful commentary on landing sites, which could help planners find areas rich in water ice and other resources. Inal designed the tool as a decision-support system rather than a semi-autonomous machine, so that it works alongside mission planners who make the final calls.

She described the goal as an active scientific assistant rather than a passive tool that only answers questions. Alper Yilmaz, a co-author and professor in the same department at Ohio State, said the approach could also apply to other planetary bodies, including Earth, Mars and some asteroids. He noted that few GPT-like map models currently exist for space exploration, and that the team aims to make its model generalizable to other surfaces. Yilmaz added that as datasets grow more advanced, efficient tools will be needed to sort through them, since finding the best landing spots would otherwise be like searching for a needle in a haystack.

He also said such a system could act as another set of eyes to verify and question findings in a harsh environment. The team plans to test LUMINA on new high-quality lunar data and to further evaluate how well it supports mission planning as the system develops. Inal noted that NASA's Artemis program creates important opportunities for this research, and that new lunar data could improve systems like hers. Reporting on the work came from Ohio State News and Newswise, which both credited the research to the university.

stories.Headline: Otto Group and Sereact Bring NVIDIA-Powered Physical AI to Returns Processing
stories.Summary:
Otto Group and robotics software company Sereact announced on October 28, 2026 a two-phase program to test AI-controlled robots at Otto Group's logistics center in Poland. The robots will inspect and sort returned customer orders, a task that is hard to automate. Ten dual-arm systems will be deployed first, and 15 more robotic arms are planned for a second phase, bringing the total to 25. The companies are developing the technology together, and Otto Group will evaluate a wider rollout across its logistics network if the second phase succeeds.

The robots run on Cortex, Sereact's Physical AI model, which can handle items it has never seen before without product-specific training or a fixed catalog. Returns are difficult because items arrive folded, crumpled or repackaged, and the product mix of a multi-category retailer keeps changing. Cortex decides in real time how to grasp each item, assess its condition and route it. Sereact trains and validates the model with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, NVIDIA Isaac Lab and NVIDIA Cosmos, turning real picks into simulated variants so that fixes can reach the robots within days rather than weeks.

Sereact operates and maintains the systems under a Robotics-as-a-Service model. Employees will move away from repetitive grasping and lifting and toward supervision, handling exceptions and making final quality decisions. The robots will be introduced in stages, and each stage will produce operational feedback that the partners will use to improve the systems. The companies say this process will show whether the technology meets the reliability, flexibility and quality standards needed for broader use.

Martin Umland, Group Vice President Supply Chain Management at Otto Group, said the project will show at real scale how far Physical AI can go in making returns faster and the supply chain more flexible. Sereact CEO and co-founder Dr. Ralf Gulde said a robot that knows only yesterday's catalog is of little use in a returns center and that each handled return improves the model. The partnership is part of Otto Group's medium-term commitment to invest €350 million in technology and AI, and it follows the group's earlier robotics investments across its logistics operations. Sereact, founded in Stuttgart, raised a $116 million Series B in 2026 and counts Zalando, IKEA, DHL and BMW among its customers.

stories.Headline: Using AI to improve lives: UTulsa students advance prosthetic research - The University of Tulsa
stories.Summary:
Students at The University of Tulsa are using artificial intelligence to study how prosthetic limbs affect the comfort and confidence of people who wear them. The work takes place in the biomechanics laboratory of John M. Henshaw, department head of mechanical engineering and Harry H. Rogers Endowed Chair in Mechanical Engineering. Students combine engineering, healthcare and machine learning to find out why one prosthetic device may feel more comfortable than another. The article reports that the project brings students from several disciplines together.

Maddie Fulk, a master's student in mechanical engineering, and fellow student researcher Maura Wahl analyzed data collected from people with below-the-knee amputations as they walked with different prosthetic devices. Motion sensors placed across the body recorded hundreds of measurements tied to gait, balance and movement. Using machine-learning techniques, the students looked for the measurements that best separated one device from another. The article says the model consistently flagged movement near the pelvis as one of the strongest indicators, which suggests changes near the body's center of mass may reveal how users experience different prosthetics.

Henshaw described the model as very successful and said it revealed patterns that would have been hard to find with traditional methods alone. Wahl said many people may not know that a better option exists, and that some wear prosthetics that do not work well with their bodies. The team is now investigating whether sensors in smartphones could eventually gather similar movement data during everyday activities. The article notes that such an approach could make prosthetic evaluation more accessible and scalable.

Andreas Polycarpou, dean of the College of Engineering & Computer Science, said the project reflects the kind of hands-on experience that sets a UTulsa education apart. He said students are working with faculty mentors on real-world problems using technologies such as AI. The article adds that the experience is shaping career plans, with Fulk aiming for medicine and Wahl considering graduate study in prosthetics and biomedical engineering. The article is a university feature, so it describes the research as ongoing rather than reporting final outcomes.

stories.Headline: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.
stories.Summary:
Karen Hao, an award-winning journalist and author of Empire of AI, gave a talk at Lorimer Chapel at Colby College as part of the Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence's Distinguished Lecture Series. In the talk she compared today's largest AI companies to historic empires and argued that ordinary people can push back against them. The audience, which included students from Bowdoin College, gave her a standing ovation when she finished. Stacy Doore, Clare Booth Luce Associate Professor of Computer Science, introduced her. Doore called Hao a powerful ally for advocates of ethical AI.

Hao said that companies such as OpenAI are pursuing a scale-at-all-costs approach that consolidates economic and political power. She drew parallels with past empires, saying these companies claim resources that are not theirs, exploit large amounts of labor, monopolize knowledge production, and justify their actions with a moral and existential imperative. She warned that training ever-larger models risks eroding intellectual property and requires data centers that use large amounts of energy, freshwater, and minerals for computer chips. Her alternative was to build smaller, task-specific systems, which she likened to bicycles rather than rockets. She cited AlphaFold by DeepMind, which predicts protein structures, as an example of a tool trained on a curated dataset that does not need supercomputers to run.

Hao pointed to grassroots resistance as proof that the trend is not inevitable. She described Tucson, Arizona, where Amazon proposed a $3.6-billion data center called Project Blue, and where residents formed the No Desert Data Center Coalition to fight it. She said the coalition packed city hall on a day when temperatures reached 114 degrees Fahrenheit, and the council voted 7-0 to stop the project in its current form. Her message to the audience was that individuals can resist the idea that giant AI companies are all-powerful. She summed up her view by saying that when people rise, empires fall.

Articles.Title: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.

stories.Headline: Body Sensors and AI May Lead to New Kinds of Learning
stories.Summary:
Researchers at NJIT have proposed a concept called Minds and Machines: A Neuro-Adaptive AI Learning Companion, which combines physiological sensors, AI and extended reality to help students stay on track in their studies. The idea was reported on October 28, 2026, by NJIT News, with Evan Koblentz as the writer. Under the concept, students would wear a wrist device or headset that detects bodily signs of distress, such as overloaded brain waves measured by electroencephalogram, during lectures or other lessons. The article presents this as a way to spot students who may be falling behind or who are highly engaged and ready for harder material. The project is funded by a $50,000 university grant.

When those signs appear, an AI system would choose a different way to present the topic, drawing on preprogrammed knowledge of educational best practices and student motivation. The new material could be delivered in real time or later, and it could use augmented or virtual reality to make concepts more vivid. The approach could also extend beyond classrooms into hands-on settings such as NJIT's makerspace. Jessica Simon, a neuroscientist and pedagogical and instructional innovation specialist at the Center for Educational and Innovation and Excellence, is joint principal investigator with Zhifeng Kou, associate chair of biomedical engineering. Simon said personalized teaching has been shown to raise performance by at least two standard deviations, though the article notes the field of neuroscience-informed education is still young.

Kou said his interest grew from years of using AI for biomedical imaging analysis, and that when large language models emerged, he saw a way to help students learn. The team now faces the main hurdle of making the parts work together in a live classroom rather than only in a laboratory. They must separate useful body signals from background electrical noise and handle several signals while customizing instruction in real time. The researchers must also decide whether students are comfortable sharing body data and make sure that data stays private. Once the technical problems are solved, they plan to turn the research into a product that could be shared with other universities.

Several other faculty members are co-principal investigators on the project: Nicole Bosca, Elisa Kallioniemi, Bryan Pfister, Mengjia Xu and Lin Zhao. Kou emphasized that the goal is to build something practical and impactful, not only scientific. The article does not give a timeline for when the product might reach students or describe any results from testing with students. It frames the work as an early-stage effort in a growing field that combines education and neuroscience.

stories.Headline: MATRIX AI director joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing
stories.Summary:
Dhireesha Kudithipudi, founding director of the MATRIX AI Consortium at UT San Antonio, has been named a member of the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Next-Generation Computing. She is one of only 19 global experts selected to advise global leaders on emerging computing technologies. The appointment, reported by the university in late October 2026, recognizes her leadership in transdisciplinary research. The university says the role positions MATRIX as a contributor to international discussions on the next era of technology.

The Forum's Global Future Councils form a knowledge network of 37 thematic groups with more than 700 experts. Kudithipudi will serve alongside figures from IBM Research, SandboxAQ, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, UC Berkeley, the University of Toronto, Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation and the European Space Agency. The council's work feeds into its Next-Generation Computing Framework, released in October 2026 with the Forum, which guides governments and organizations on the technologies and strategic priorities shaping computing. Kudithipudi also received a special invitation to attend the Forum's Quantum Economy Day in Geneva, Switzerland, in October.

Kudithipudi's own research focuses on neuromorphic AI, artificial intelligence modeled on the brain, with an emphasis on reducing energy use. The article explains that conventional computing separates memory and processing, which contributes to the high energy demands of many AI models, while neuromorphic systems aim to learn and adapt at much lower energy cost. In January 2025 she was lead author of a review in Nature that brought together international experts to examine how neuromorphic computing might scale. She has said her work aligns with the council's concern that computing grow more powerful while staying sustainable and centered on human needs.

MATRIX has grown under her leadership into a network of nearly 90 scientists across three organizations, with expertise in engineering, neuroscience, ethics, medicine and computing. The consortium works on healthcare, energy, cybersecurity and smart cities, and Kudithipudi leads national research efforts. She serves as institutional lead for two Centers of Excellence and contributes to six in total. The university also launched THOR: The Neuromorphic Commons this year, which the article describes as the nation's first open-access hub for brain-inspired computing, funded by the National Science Foundation. The university says the appointment will expand its role in international discussions and create new collaborations.
