stories.Headline: 2026 State Privacy Law Trends: Consumer Data Protection Updates
stories.Summary:
Four states enacted comprehensive consumer privacy laws in 2026, according to a MultiState analysis published October 28, 2026, bringing the total to 24 states with such protections. Alabama, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Vermont joined the group this year, with Alabama's law covering businesses that process more than 25,000 consumers' personal data or earn at least 25 percent of gross revenue from selling it. The article notes that Florida's law, which applies to a narrow set of businesses, may or may not be counted in that total. Massachusetts could become the next state to join, since each chamber has passed a version of its privacy bill and a conference committee is working on differences this fall.

Several states also amended existing laws in 2026, including Connecticut, Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, New Hampshire, and New Jersey. The changes follow five trends identified by the article: broader coverage, limits that go beyond consent, expanded consumer rights, closer scrutiny of data use, and more data broker registration. Delaware lowered its coverage threshold from 35,000 consumers to 10,000, while Connecticut and Virginia now ban sales of precise geolocation information regardless of consent. New Jersey prohibits the sale of sensitive data even with consumer consent, and Connecticut and New Jersey joined California, Oregon, Texas, and Vermont in requiring data brokers to register.

The article attributes these developments to state lawmakers and governors, with the absence of congressional action cited as a reason states have continued to act. California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill that would have banned selling or sharing sensitive data with third parties, citing potential unintended consequences and enforcement costs in his veto message. Newsom's veto is presented as an exception to the broader trend. The article also notes that many of the strongest proposals have come from Democratic-led states, so the outcome of November's elections could affect whether stalled proposals are revived.

Looking ahead, the article says lawmakers are likely to focus on whether conversation logs from AI chatbots can be used for targeted advertising, and children's privacy remains a major concern with many state attorneys general filing actions against businesses. Colorado's revised AI law will begin regulating automated technology that materially influences consequential decisions in 2027. Connecticut has directed the creation of a universal deletion mechanism by 2028, and Vermont approved a feasibility study on a similar tool. The article suggests the next debate may focus less on establishing privacy rights than on making them easier to exercise.

Articles.Title: 2026 State Privacy Law Trends: Consumer Data Protection Updates - MultiState

stories.Headline: Former DOJ attorneys launch AI company to help lawyers help more people - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
Two former Justice Department officials launched FluxCap, a new artificial intelligence platform, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. The company says the tool could help lawyers take on cases that might otherwise never reach court. Handling major cases often requires a large team, months of work and a lot of money, which can leave smaller firms, government agencies and everyday people at a disadvantage against companies with far more resources. The co-founders, Jonathan Kanter and Doha Mekki, both led the DOJ's antitrust division under President Joe Biden, and Mekki also served in the department under Presidents Trump and Obama. The platform is designed to handle tasks that could take a team of lawyers days or weeks, such as reviewing hundreds of legal documents and conducting legal research, in a fraction of that time.

Unlike general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT, FluxCap is built specifically for complex legal work, with an initial focus on antitrust law and plans to expand into other legal fields. Its founders argue that concentrating on one specialty makes the technology more sophisticated and accurate than the tools of larger AI companies. The platform can also help lawyers develop strategies, identify gaps in evidence and anticipate opposing arguments. The founders stress that it is meant to support lawyers' judgment rather than replace it.

Kanter told ABC News that his team at the department could pursue only about 10% of the cases they believed were worth bringing. He said the government lawyers were outnumbered despite having some of the greatest lawyers in the world, and that a lack of people was the biggest obstacle. Kanter framed the company's goal as helping lawyers do their jobs better rather than replacing them. Mekki said the technology could let more people obtain representation and gain better access to economic justice to recover losses they suffered in the marketplace.

She added that lawyers using the tool have told her they are excited about practicing law and doing things they did not know were possible. The articles provide no information on how FluxCap is priced, how many clients or firms currently use it, or what its founders plan beyond antitrust law and general expansion. The coverage also does not say how the company's accuracy has been independently tested. It is clear that the launch was presented as a way to widen access to legal help while keeping human lawyers in control of their work.

Articles.Title: Former DOJ attorneys launch AI company to help lawyers help more people - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

stories.Headline: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation
stories.Summary:
Ru Peng, a professor at the School of Public Policy and Management at Tsinghua University, argued in a China Daily opinion piece published on October 29, 2026, that the social effects of artificial intelligence can only be understood through real-world experiments. Using the example of an AI companion placed in an elderly person's home, the author said that a system can work as designed and still change family relationships, daily routines or feelings of isolation in ways its developers did not expect. Because these effects often appear slowly, the piece said, waiting for problems to become obvious can make them harder and more costly to correct. The author framed this as the Collingridge dilemma, the difficulty of predicting a technology's consequences before it spreads widely.

The article said that testing should happen in carefully chosen settings before adoption becomes too widespread to change, with researchers establishing baselines, tracking outcomes over time and protecting consent and privacy, especially for vulnerable groups. It pointed to a three-year project launched in 2025 by researchers at Tsinghua University and industry partners, which plans to involve around 300 households and assess effects on older people's quality of life, emotional well-being, family interactions and social participation. Early findings, according to the piece, showed that some elderly users need help setting up equipment and that loneliness and limited digital access are concerns in some rural areas, though it stressed these observations do not yet show that AI companionship improves well-being. The author also noted that China has since 2023 set up a national standards working group, which has issued five national standards on AI social experiments and on assessing the social impact of generative AI.

The article placed this approach within China's policy agenda, citing government guidance issued in 2022, the State Council's 2025 AI+ initiative and national pilot bases and innovation zones that support such experiments. It also referred to President Xi Jinping's remarks at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and the High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in July 2026, where he raised questions about human-machine relations, security, ethics and the fair sharing of AI's benefits. The author argued that experiments reveal what happens when AI enters daily life while standards help apply those lessons consistently, and that neither removes uncertainty entirely. The piece did not describe any specific next steps beyond continuing these experiments and standard-setting.

Articles.Title: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation

stories.Headline: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates
stories.Summary:
UBS employees are using more than 12,700 personal artificial intelligence agents in their daily work, according to a press release the bank issued alongside its third quarter results, as reported by PYMNTS on October 29, 2026. The tools include software development agents used by 18,000 of the bank's software developers, and STAAT, a tool for financial advisor teams that has generated more than 30 million insights used in advising clients. UBS reports 608 live AI use cases in production, 81% more than a year earlier, and more than 1,090 applications in development. The bank describes these efforts as part of its investment in technology, capabilities and talent to enhance the client experience, strengthen infrastructure and increase efficiency.

UBS framed the spending as a way to position the firm for the future rather than as a set of specific mandates or changes to working arrangements. The release itself contains no further detail on how the agents are governed or how their use affects staffing. The article places the announcement within a wider trend in which financial firms concentrate AI on back-office work. A PYMNTS Intelligence report cited in the piece found that revenue recognition and accounting close, credit risk assessment and scoring, and sales forecasting and pipeline automation are the most adopted AI tasks in financial services and insurance. That same report found that 85% of financial services firms plan to increase their AI budgets over the next 12 months.

Other institutions cited in the article show similar moves. PYMNTS reported on October 23 that Customers Bank found a pilot of its AI-powered process closed select commercial loans in seven days, compared with a typical wait of 30 to 60 days, and its parent, Customers Bancorp, doubled its deployed AI agents in the latest quarter. Regions Financial Corp. said during an October 16 earnings call that it expects cybersecurity costs, which include frontier AI, to raise its adjusted noninterest expense by between 1.5% and 3.5% for full-year 2026. The article does not indicate any next steps for UBS beyond the continued investment described in the release.

Articles.Title: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates

stories.Headline: NY Implements Chatbot Restrictions for Interactions With Minors, Puts AI Companies 'On Notice'
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James put artificial intelligence companies on notice on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, the same day Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation giving the state's top prosecutor new authority over how AI chatbots interact with minors. The move is aimed at chatbot providers whose products children may use. The reporting describes the law as a step toward tighter oversight of that kind of interaction. Beyond the signing and the attorney general's statement, the available article gives few further specifics.

The article says the legislation gives the attorney general power to police how chatbots talk with young users. Compliance could require companies to retool their systems and to monitor their algorithms more closely. The piece frames these limits as new restrictions on chatbot interactions with minors. It does not spell out the specific rules, penalties, or deadlines that apply under the law. Readers looking for those details would need the bill text or other coverage.

The attorney general's warning was the central statement attributed to James, who used it to signal that AI firms should expect enforcement. Hochul signed the legislation, and the article ties her action to the attorney general's new enforcement role. The article's author, Brian Lee, wrote the report, which was published by Law.com. The available text does not include further direct comments from either official.

The story sits within a broader push to regulate AI systems as they reach young people. The article does not describe what happens next, such as lawsuits, rulemaking, or the timing of enforcement. The available reporting ends with the signing and the warning to industry. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NY Implements Chatbot Restrictions for Interactions With Minors, Puts AI Companies 'On Notice' - Law.com

stories.Headline: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Muqbil Ahmar of ETCIO published an exclusive interview on October 28, 2026, with Mahesh Ramamoorthy, Chief Information Officer at YES Bank, about how the bank is moving from AI experiments to bank-wide transformation. The piece frames AI integration and automation as top strategic priorities for CIOs across the banking, financial services and insurance sector. Recently, YES Bank hosted an "AI Fest" at its Mumbai office to explore the next phase of AI-led change. The event brought together more than 29 technology partners and focused on real-world AI applications and scalable implementation strategies.

Ramamoorthy argued that AI adoption is becoming unavoidable, but that financial institutions should advance cautiously because trust is their central asset. He described AI as probabilistic rather than deterministic, which means firms must decide carefully where to apply it. Many current use cases sit in the back office and in risk management decisioning rather than in customer-facing roles, and he said understanding of customer queries has already improved. He expects most banks to keep a human in the loop rather than move to fully autonomous systems. He also noted that banks are at different stages, with some ahead and others still catching up.

Looking 18 to 24 months ahead, Ramamoorthy expects the cost of AI to normalise, since large models with billions of parameters are currently being used for narrow tasks that could be served more efficiently. He anticipates use cases aligning with that rebalanced cost base and stronger data security safeguards arriving. On YES Bank's own position, he said the bank has built capabilities around good bots and context-driven engagement, but wants to do more. The AI Fest was designed as a collaborative marketplace, bringing in partners and vendors, with the aim of generating around 100 use cases that emerge from employees rather than from technology teams alone. He said the first edition was open only to YES Bank employees so that colleagues could learn about AI's possibilities in one curated setting.

Articles.Title: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said in a research post published on October 28, 2026, that an unreleased internal AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits. The company said these were built in its lab after the model was prompted, not drawn from any real attack, and that it reported every flaw to the affected vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks. Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in the post.

The company presents the work as evidence that a single model can now find several separate flaws and combine them into a functioning exploit, a task it says previously required a few specialist teams. Each chain has its own requirements: the Chrome chain runs code outside the browser sandbox after one visit to a page, the Safari chain disables the same-origin policy without running code, the Windows chain is a denial-of-service attack, and the Linux chain runs commands as root over the network when the target runs a multipath TCP listener. Anthropic reported 62 Chrome flaws to Google, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes, and says its Linux proof of concept took 48 minutes to leak a kernel address and five more minutes to reach a root shell. The company also points to a kernel use-after-free rated 9.8 that was fixed upstream on October 15.

Google and Apple have both publicly credited Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes, and those credits can be checked against vendor release notes. Google's notes credit a named Anthropic researcher, assisted by Claude, for certain Chrome fixes, though not for all 62 flaws. Apple credits two named researchers working with Claude at Anthropic for the Safari fix in iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not describe what a person did at each step, and it refers to the model only as an unreleased internal research model.

Anthropic frames the publication as support for defenders under a coordinated disclosure policy that gives developers 90 days to patch and 45 more before details beyond a public advisory are discussed. It also points security teams to its Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted professionals access to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1. In its own words, the company said publishing was warranted because models can now do this "with little human involvement" and produce a working exploit "that anyone can run and verify." The articles do not describe any further steps beyond these disclosures and program offerings.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits

stories.Headline: UMC invests $3.2 billion in capacity expansion amid AI revenue growth forecast - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
United Microelectronics Corp, the Taiwanese chipmaker, said on Wednesday that its board had approved approximately $3.2 billion for capacity expansion. The company did not give a timeline for the additional capital expenditure, saying it was still working with suppliers to accelerate the schedule. The announcement came alongside its outlook for the coming years and its third-quarter results. UMC's shares have risen 147.5% so far this year, outperforming a 62.4% gain in the broader market, and the stock closed up 4.5% on Wednesday ahead of its earnings release.

The company said it expects a significant shift in the pricing environment heading into 2027, supported by stronger customer demand and increasing capacity in selected technologies. It expects blended average selling prices to rise 10% in 2027 compared with 2026. UMC also said it expects AI-related revenue to account for 25% of total revenue in three years. Silicon photonics and advanced packaging are emerging as new growth drivers for the company, it added.

UMC reported third-quarter revenue of T$74.24 billion, or $2.29 billion, up 25.6% from a year earlier. Net income rose 9.7% to T$16.43 billion, or about $506.75 million. The company said AI remains a key growth driver but that it sees a decline in its personal computer segment. UMC focuses on more mature chip nodes, unlike Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the world's largest contract chipmaker, which is investing heavily in the most advanced 2- and 1-nanometre technology for artificial intelligence applications.

Articles.Title: UMC invests $3.2 billion in capacity expansion amid AI revenue growth forecast - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Influential Women Profiles Kristen Perdue: Making Artificial Intelligence Practical, Governed, And Profitable
stories.Summary:
Kristen Perdue, CEO and Fractional Chief AI Officer of AlterBridge Strategies in Kennesaw, Georgia, was profiled by Influential Women in a release published on October 28, 2026. The profile describes her as an AI strategist who helps organizations move artificial intelligence from experiment to practical, governed business capability. It credits her with more than 35 years of experience across software technology, SaaS, product management, marketing, compliance, and operations. The release presents her as a voice for responsible AI adoption rather than reporting any new event or announcement. The profile lists her areas of work as AI strategy and business transformation, AI governance and responsible adoption, and fractional Chief AI Officer advisory.

She advises SaaS and software companies, professional services firms, which are typically regulated, and expert-led companies. Her career began in software development management, then moved into product management, product marketing, go-to-market strategy, and executive leadership, including roles as CMO or Head of Marketing at AI-focused companies. The release says she created Power Moves AI and wrote the book Power Moves: The No B-S Guide to Leading with AI, and that she has trained hundreds of leaders. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from the University of Central Florida, along with several AI and information governance certifications. The release describes the fractional model as one in which a part-time executive works with leadership to set strategy, establish policies, evaluate tools, and train teams, without the cost of a permanent hire.

It also explains that information governance, the discipline behind her CIGO/AI credential, governs how organizations manage, protect, and retain information, which matters because generative AI tools draw on company documents, emails, and customer records. Kristen herself is quoted as believing that organizations often try to adopt AI agents before understanding generative AI, and that successful adoption requires governance, planning, and a clear view of risk. The release is authored by the Influential Women editorial team, and its content is the responsibility of that source. The profile is promotional in nature, and the release is distributed through EIN Presswire, which states it provides the content as is and does not vouch for its accuracy. The articles do not describe any next steps or upcoming events for Perdue or her firm.

Articles.Title: Influential Women Profiles Kristen Perdue: Making Artificial Intelligence Practical, Governed, And Profitable

stories.Headline: Rebranding ‘AI’ as Super Intelligence Could Create Contract Headaches
stories.Summary:
On September 29, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14434, which directed federal departments and agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "super intelligence" or "SI" in public communications, official policies, websites, and non-statutory documents. The White House argued that "artificial" makes the technology sound fake and possibly untrustworthy, while "super intelligence" better captures its capabilities. On a Tuesday in late October, Trump went further in a Truth Social post, calling for a ban on the term "AI" in all relevant documents and elsewhere. Federal agencies may now begin using the SI terminology in solicitations, reports, and policy statements, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced earlier this month that it would adopt the term. The U.S. Navy also issued a mandate to its commands to transition to the SI designation.

The change could create practical problems for contractors and agencies because many procurement rules, reporting obligations, grant programs, and agency guidance rely on the statutory definition of "artificial intelligence" in 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3). Wiley Rein LLP, a Washington law firm, said that if Congress adopted a new statutory definition of SI, implementing that change could raise difficulties, since many procurement policies either incorporate that definition or use terms derived from it. The articles say the name change alone does not alter the technology itself. Several tech leaders, including Elon Musk, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, and Jeff Bezos, have embraced the new terminology, and Musk has renamed some of his initiatives. California Governor Gavin Newsom, however, issued a competing executive order instructing state agencies to keep using "artificial intelligence."

Critics question the accuracy of the new label. Dr. Jim Purtilo, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Maryland, called "super intelligence" a manufactured term without a substantive definition and said it amounts to hype. He argued that current AI works by mathematically averaging answers drawn from many users, and that a new name does not make the systems more capable. Technology analyst Roger Entner of Recon Analytics made a similar point, saying a rose is still a rose by any name. The articles also note that "artificial superintelligence" already existed as a hypothetical term for a form of AI smarter than the best human minds, and that the original term "AI" was coined in 1955 by John McCarthy and others at Dartmouth.

Other countries are unlikely to follow automatically. Many nations use their own acronyms, such as "KI" in Germany and Norway and "IA" in France, Spain, and Italy, and Poland already uses "Sztuczna Inteligencja." No other country has officially changed its laws or government vocabulary so far, and major international media and regulators are expected to keep using "artificial intelligence." The articles also point out that previous Trump administration renamings, including the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and the Department of Defense to the Department of War, could be reversed by a future administration. The articles also mention a surge in registrations of the .si domain, which belongs to Slovenia, after the order.

Articles.Title: Rebranding ‘AI’ as Super Intelligence Could Create Contract Headaches - Security Clearance Jobs

stories.Headline: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone
stories.Summary:
Securities plaintiffs are filing a new kind of lawsuit tied to artificial intelligence, according to a Fried Frank analysis published by Bloomberg Law on October 28, 2026. Cornerstone counted 15 AI-related securities cases in the first half of 2026, against 16 for all of last year, putting this year on pace for nearly double. The authors describe a growing category of claims that companies concealed how shifting toward AI pulls resources and customers away from their core businesses. They call this the "AI diversion" theory.

The article walks through three recent complaints that illustrate the theory. In In re Microsoft Corporation Securities Litigation, the plaintiff alleges Microsoft diverted computing capacity from its Azure cloud business to Copilot development without telling investors. The complaint says capital expenditures reached $72.4 billion for the first half of fiscal 2026, largely from AI infrastructure and Copilot costs, without producing the expected Copilot subscribers. In Tejada v.

ZoomInfo Technologies, the plaintiff alleges customers shifted spending from ZoomInfo's seat-based software toward in-house AI tools, cutting into core license revenue. In Potter v. monday.com, the complaint says Google's "AI Overviews" and chatbot use reduced clicks to the company's website, eroding its paid search acquisition channel, and that executives described the effect as temporary or minor. The authors say the courts have not yet settled how to handle motions to dismiss these claims.

They point to In re Sprinklr Securities Litigation, where earlier this year the court dismissed a similar complaint after finding Sprinklr had adequately disclosed its resource realignment toward an AI-powered product line. The court also found the complaint relied on hindsight rather than particularized facts. The authors note that the Microsoft, ZoomInfo, and monday.com cases have not yet been decided on those motions. If they survive the pleadings stage, the authors expect many more complaints pleading AI diversion claims against other companies.

Articles.Title: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone

stories.Headline: Hochul signs sweeping AI restrictions, safeguards for baby monitors with new laws to rein in 'big tech'
stories.Summary:
Gov. Kathy Hochul signed two new laws on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that regulate how artificial intelligence chatbots interact with minors and require safety features on internet-connected baby monitors. The chatbot measures ban bots from feigning human emotions in conversations with kids and require users to prove they are over 18 to access certain features. The bots are barred from building emotional dependency, encouraging self-harm, or engaging in sexually explicit conversations with children. Companies that violate the chatbot rules face a $25,000 fine, and the baby monitor law requires manufacturers to build devices that keep intruders out and to label them clearly so families know how to stay safe.

Hochul, a Democrat seeking reelection, framed the chatbot bill around the case of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old in California whom she said was allegedly driven to kill himself by OpenAI's ChatGPT. She told reporters that the AI mentioned suicide 1,275 times during his chats, six times more often than he did himself. The chatbot bill was sponsored by state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblyman Alex Bores, and the baby monitor bill was sponsored in part by Assemblywoman Michaelle Solages. Attorney General Letitia James, who stood beside Hochul at the event, will enforce the chatbot rules, and she is also on the November 3 ballot.

Tech:NYC, a group representing New York technology companies, criticized the chatbot bill, arguing it could cut minors off from tutoring tools, homework help, coding assistants, and career platforms. The group said the restrictions would deprive young New Yorkers of resources that support their education and workforce preparation. Hochul's office presented the measures as part of a broader effort to rein in big tech, and she has previously signed laws limiting addictive algorithms on social media aimed at children. The articles do not say how the laws will be implemented or whether they will be challenged in court.

Articles.Title: Hochul signs sweeping AI restrictions, safeguards for baby monitors with new laws to rein in 'big tech' - New York Post

stories.Headline: How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
stories.Summary:
Law firm Ropes & Gray is developing a transactional diligence AI tool in partnership with OpenAI, as described in an OpenAI customer story dated October 29, 2026. The firm is an enterprise in the North American services industry, and it uses ChatGPT in the project. The work is aimed at speeding up the investigation buyers must carry out before an acquisition to check a seller's financial and legal claims. That process uncovers risks and liabilities, and it has traditionally demanded a large team of lawyers working through many documents on short deadlines.

The new tool takes a first pass through thousands of pages, identifies relevant documents, and groups them by themes and issues. It also produces summaries and a completed report in the firm's own format, and it inventories and categorizes a data room so reviewers can examine full relationships rather than isolated files. Lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed. Early development has focused on material commercial contracts, with the firm comparing test outputs against human-written diligence reports from completed deals and refining the rubric and format accordingly. The firm describes the tool as comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate.

Howard Glazer, Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray, says the tool frees lawyers to make judgments rather than simply review contracts. Josh Lichtenstein, Partner and Head of ERISA Fiduciary Practice, says lawyers must still review everything because the firm needs to stand behind any work it delivers to a client. The firm has publicly described an ambition to produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours rather than weeks. The article also says the firm uses GPT-6 Astra alongside the proprietary tool, and that it has solved client problems faster than before.

Looking ahead, Glazer believes the next stage of AI will help build collective knowledge across the firm, which has 340 partners and 1,500 lawyers. The aim is to give people access to knowledge from client meetings and past projects so the firm can better solve client problems. Glazer frames this as a way to create value directly, beyond saving time and money. The article does not give a launch date for the diligence tool or describe its availability to clients beyond the firm.

Articles.Title: How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence

stories.Headline: Is There Momentum to Ban AI, Screens Inside Minnesota Schools?
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's school districts are facing a question about whether to restrict artificial intelligence and screens for younger students, following moves in New York City and Los Angeles. Racket reported on October 28, 2026, that the two largest districts in the country had just adopted AI moratoriums and screen limits for younger learners. Local parent groups and teachers in Minnesota say the same kind of action is needed here. The article describes a growing, bipartisan parental movement that it characterizes as building momentum statewide.

The New York City ban covers pre-K through eighth grade, while the Los Angeles moratorium spans all grade levels, and both apply to generative AI for the current school year. Chicago is mentioned as a possible next district to follow. The article also points to a classroom experiment by Minneapolis teacher Maureen Mulvaney, who removed all technology from her classroom for the 2025 school year, and reports that over 95% of surveyed students said it had a positive effect on their learning. Those survey results came in by February of this year. The article notes that the experiment is not a scalable model on its own.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the tech industry wants people to believe that AI-powered early education is inevitable and necessary, and that the city does not see it that way. Grant Eustice, a public high school teacher and co-founder of the advocacy group MN Unplugged, compared major technology firms to Big Tobacco and Big Pharma and said he sometimes feels powerless against their influence on districts. Even so, he expects that the New York and Los Angeles actions will prompt smaller districts to follow. The article also reports that the Minneapolis Public Schools press office did not respond to an interview request.

The article ties the current situation to the period after 2020, when schools rapidly distributed devices during the pandemic. It cites National Center for Education Statistics data showing that about 45% of public schools issued take-home devices in early 2020, rising to 96% by the 2021-22 school year. It also reports that Minnesota's three largest districts, Anoka-Hennepin, Saint Paul Public Schools, and Minneapolis Public Schools, take different approaches to AI and device access. St. Paul is developing an AI policy due by the 2027-28 school year, and Anoka-Hennepin is revising its own AI policy. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Is There Momentum to Ban AI, Screens Inside Minnesota Schools? - Racket

stories.Headline: As US, China form AI blocs, countries increasingly torn between them
stories.Summary:
As the United States and China build separate artificial intelligence blocs, countries around the world are being pushed to choose between them. The United States leads Pax Silica, while China has backed the World AI Cooperation Organization, and experts say the window for nations to pick freely between the two is narrowing. Kazakhstan has taken an unusual path by joining both groupings, signing up to the U.S.-led effort in June and then becoming a founding member of China's initiative weeks later. Officials in Kazakhstan hope the arrangement brings technology partnerships and factory jobs from one side and a voice in setting standards from the other.

Kazakhstan's position is described as precarious, since it draws investment from both powers while holding minerals and cheap electricity that both want. Earlier this year its government signed a deal worth up to $10 billion with Nvidia to build a data center hub, and local officials said Chinese direct investment hit a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping also met the Kazakh president in July to deepen cooperation under the Belt and Road initiative. Both Washington and Beijing are using access to AI as a tool of influence, with the United States accusing China of extracting capabilities from American models.

The U.S. State Department said countries cannot be trusted partners in Pax Silica while pursuing a rival vision for advanced AI, and Beijing responded that AI should not be owned by major countries. Chinese officials have argued that the two powers should draw on each other's strengths rather than guard against one another. Analysts note that China must court third countries to build its alternative coalition, while Washington already has a large network of allies, which gives so-called swing countries more leverage. Other nations, including Indonesia, Singapore and Saudi Arabia, are also seeking deals with both sides.

Europe faces similar pressure and is trying to reduce its dependence on both powers while lacking the chips, infrastructure and homegrown AI models to compete on equal terms. The European Union is already part of Pax Silica, and in June it unveiled a technological sovereignty package aimed at expanding chip production and data center capacity. Recent moves by the United States, including the shutdown of certain Anthropic models, have raised alarm in European capitals. Brussels is also trying to cut its reliance on China for rare earths, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said Europe will help write the global rules for AI.

stories.Headline: Australia warns of ‘unprecedented’ AI threat
stories.Summary:
Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, warned on Tuesday, October 27, that artificial intelligence is now an "unprecedented" threat as foreign governments use it to hack computer networks and critical infrastructure. In its annual cyber threat report, the directorate said AI has been the defining force in the threat landscape over the past year, helping criminals and state-sponsored hackers find weaknesses faster and attack at greater scale, speed and sophistication than before. The agency also noted that new threats have emerged in recent weeks from the unintended actions of AI agents and model testing. It said it had even used some AI tools to help compile the report itself, and that the technology could bring huge benefits if used for good.

The report documents a sharp rise in incidents. The directorate issued more than 4,400 warnings about potentially malicious activity over the past year, an increase of 80% on the previous 12 months. It said state-sponsored hackers continued to target Australian organisations mainly to gain access to sensitive or non-public information, and that this activity reaches beyond government networks to include critical infrastructure operators, private businesses and individuals. Hackers linked to China, Russia and North Korea were named as having targeted Australia or its allies in recent times.

Defence Minister Richard Marles responded by telling reporters that the country cannot ignore the AI revolution. He said AI is real, that people need to engage with it, and that there is no turning the clock back. Marles added that malicious actors are using AI to find vulnerabilities in systems, and he urged Australians to update their computers and "harden their systems." The warning came from the directorate as the agency responsible, with the minister backing its message in public remarks.

The report arrives amid growing global concern about the power of advanced AI tools, following a string of hacking incidents involving models from leading developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. In recent days, governments and companies have been rushing to fix critical flaws in a programming language that runs a large share of the world's websites. That vulnerability was found using a powerful model from OpenAI. The articles do not describe any further steps the Australian government plans to take beyond the call for people and organisations to update and strengthen their systems.

stories.Headline: ZenaTech Anticipates Faster Survey Delivery and Increased Capacity with AI and Drone Automation
stories.Summary:
ZenaTech, Inc., a Nasdaq-listed company that provides AI drone, Drone as a Service (DaaS), enterprise software and quantum computing solutions, said on October 29, 2026 that it expects faster commercial survey delivery and more capacity across its land surveying operations. The forecast rests on its recently unveiled AI software suite and drone surveying automation. The company recently closed its 30th and 31st DaaS acquisitions, which add four locations to its footprint, including a civil engineering consultancy in Darwin and a surveying, civil engineering and town planning firm in Port Macquarie, New South Wales. The AI software suite is set to begin formal testing across the DaaS network in 2027. The company says its drone approach would cut field time sharply.

On a representative 100-acre topographic survey, a conventional surveyor covers about 3 acres a day, or roughly 267 hours of fieldwork, while a drone needs about 65 hours. Surveyors would still use ground equipment to set control points and check accuracy. The company's internal estimates suggest savings of more than 25 eight-hour workdays per 100-acre survey. Its AI targets the office work that follows, since a LiDAR drone produces point clouds with millions of measurements that technicians have traditionally sorted by hand over days. The company estimates the software could cut post-processing work by as much as 80 percent, with survey teams reviewing results before delivery.

Chief executive Shaun Passley, Ph.D., said each acquired firm brings clients and licensed surveyors that can benefit from expanded capacity. He argued that shorter time in the field and in the office would let the same crews finish more projects and grow recurring revenue, which he called central to the DaaS strategy. He also said the company pays for acquisitions with 50 percent cash and 50 percent seller notes payable over three years against revenue milestones, which he said keeps management aligned with shareholders and avoids dilution. The company expects its acquisitions to be immediately accretive.

The acquisitions are part of a broader push into Australia, where the company now has seven DaaS locations, including NorthGroup Consulting in Queensland, acquired in June. Byrne Consultants, based in Darwin with offices on Queensland's Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast, has served government clients for more than 20 years. Hopkins Consultants, founded in 1992, works across regional New South Wales and is the company's first acquisition in that state, where the government plans 377,000 new homes by mid-2029. The company says actual results will vary with site conditions and that it is preparing documented case studies to report verified results as they are completed.

stories.Headline: HKEX Launches Artificial Intelligence and Semiconductor Indices
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) announced the launch of the HKEX Artificial Intelligence Index, its first index with an AI theme. The index is meant to give investors a defined, comprehensive way to invest across the artificial intelligence value chain. HKEX also signed an agreement with China Southern Asset Management, which is authorized to launch an exchange-traded fund tracking the index in mainland China. The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire.

The index covers four segments: AI chips, AI infrastructure, AI models and AI applications. It holds 40 constituents, including SMIC, Alibaba Group, Tencent Holdings, Biren Technology, Zhipu AI, MiniMax and Horizon Robotics, many of which are listed in Hong Kong. To qualify, a company must have research and development spending and capital spending each equal to at least 3% of sales, and sales growth of at least 5% over the past two years. No single constituent may exceed a 10% weight, and each stock in the applications segment is capped at 3%. The index is reviewed and rebalanced quarterly.

HKEX's Group Chief Information Officer, Richard Leung, said the company was pleased to launch the index and to license it to China Southern for ETF products in mainland China. He said HKEX expects to work with other market participants to build further investment products on its index suite. Yang Xiaosong, General Manager of Southern Asset Management, said the firm was honored to receive the authorization and described it as a way to give mainland investors convenient access to Hong Kong's AI opportunities. The announcement also includes a risk disclosure that past index performance does not indicate future results and that AI-themed products may be highly volatile.

The articles place the launch within HKEX's broader push to expand its index business and its role as a market for innovative technology companies. HKEX is also developing other index products, including the HKEX TECH 100 Index. Southern Asset Management, one of China's early fund managers to operate under a standardized framework, says the collaboration extends its international strategy. The launch of the related ETF remains subject to regulatory approval, and the articles say its specific arrangements will be announced separately.

stories.Headline: Texas sues OpenAI over ChatGPT safety claims and alleged harm to minors
stories.Summary:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, accusing them of deceiving consumers about the safety of ChatGPT and failing to protect users, including children. According to one of the articles, the suit was filed on October 23 in Collin County, under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act. It names San Francisco-based OpenAI Global LLC and argues the company sold ChatGPT as a safe and reliable tool while releasing an undertrained product without adequate guardrails. The filing says the chatbot can produce inaccurate or damaging information, and that the company put market dominance ahead of user safety.

The complaint lists several alleged harms. It says vulnerable users have been steered toward self-harm, minors have come to rely on the software without parental supervision, professionals have been publicly embarrassed by wrong outputs, and some people have used the product to seek help with violent acts. It also says ChatGPT lacks adequate age verification and parental consent mechanisms. The state asks for injunctive relief and financial penalties, and a third report says it also wants to block minors' access to ChatGPT and require independent safety reviews of new AI models. The filing also points out that OpenAI began in 2015 as a non-profit meant to advance digital intelligence for public benefit, and contrasts that with its current commercial growth.

Paxton said in a statement that OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and warn them of the dangers of its platform. He added that he will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and make sure powerful technology companies are not above the law. An OpenAI spokesperson responded that the company has worked closely with experts to keep improving ChatGPT, reduce risks and add safeguards. The spokesperson said governments have an important role in setting strong AI safety standards, and that OpenAI wants to work with Texas and other states on practical policies covering the whole industry, not just one company.

Texas is not alone. Eight states, including Idaho, Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, have filed separate suits against OpenAI, according to the other reports. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador filed a 107-page complaint in Ada County on October 14, alleging violations of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act. He seeks a $5,000 payment to the state for each violation, along with damages and restitution, and wants the company barred from testing advanced AI models outside a secured, independently verified environment. OpenAI says it has added parental controls, break reminders, age-prediction tools and a teen-focused experience, and worked with more than 170 mental health experts in late 2025 to improve how its models handle sensitive conversations.

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic threat to humanity' as it eyes $2 trillion valuation in biggest-ever IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot, filed its S-1 paperwork on Monday, 26 October 2026, setting up what could be the biggest stock market debut ever. The 335-page filing, which lists the shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker "ANT," points to a Wall Street debut next month. Reports say the offering could raise as much as $100 billion, which would top the record SpaceX set with its June listing, though AP put that raise at $86 billion while Mint cited $75 billion. The company was formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, and an Anthropic listing would put it ahead of OpenAI in going public. The final amount raised, the valuation and the offering price have not been settled.

The filing gives a detailed look at the company's finances. Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, about 14 times the figure from the same period a year earlier. Net loss for the half stood at $80.7 billion, which included a one-off accounting charge of $72.4 billion tied to financing agreements, compared with a loss of $13 billion a year earlier. As of 30 June, Anthropic held $131.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents, and it said its push to expand computing capacity will change its cash flow and demand heavy capital spending. About 250 customers each brought in at least $10 million over the past year, and the five largest accounted for roughly a quarter of this year's revenue.

The filing also sets out unusual governance terms and a very long list of risks. Dario Amodei, the CEO, his sister Daniela, the company's president, and their five co-founders hold 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. A Long-Term Benefit Trust made up of independent members can appoint directors, and it is meant to stop financial interests from outranking public safety. The risk section runs close to 100 pages, and the company said AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if they are misused, replicated, weaponised or allowed to act with a high degree of autonomy. It added that AI can be used for cyberattacks or to design biological weapons, that its own use of AI to speed up research could outpace its safety work, and that climate change could raise power and water costs for its data facilities.

The valuation is still open, with reports ranging from $1.5 trillion to as much as $2 trillion, up from the $965 billion private investors put on the company earlier this year. At the top figure it would pass SpaceX's initial $1.77 trillion value, though Nvidia leads at $5 trillion. Figures in the filing suggest each of the seven founders would end up with 1.4% of the company, worth as much as $28 billion apiece, and Forbes already puts Dario and Daniela at $15.5 billion each. The listing comes amid worries about an AI bubble and about the huge financing needs of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI business, and several tech firms have recently pulled their own IPO plans. A month ago Amodei wrote a 4,000-word essay urging the industry to slow frontier AI development so safety measures can catch up.

stories.Headline: SAP Empowers AI Developers to Build What Matters and Turn Intent into Autonomous Execution - Engineering / Artificial Intelligence - KXEN | SAP
stories.Summary:
SAP SE used its annual SAP TechEd conference, held in Berlin in late October 2026, to announce a set of AI innovations aimed at developers. The company said the enhancements to its Joule Studio and Joule Work products, its SAP Business AI Platform, and its newest tabular foundation model are meant to give developers new tools for building and extending AI agents. The package also includes richer business data and context for those agents to reason with, along with stronger governance controls for running them across an enterprise. SAP described the release as an expansion of its portfolio for developers.

The Business AI Platform is meant to give organizations a single place to build, contextualize and govern AI across SAP and third-party systems. Joule Studio offers no-code and pro-code tools for building agents and lets users choose from more than 70 AI models. Early adopters in the Joule Studio program can also design and run n8n workflows, with broader access to follow. SAP said its Business Data Cloud and Knowledge Graph ground the agents in trusted business data and help organizations pick the right model for each job. The company also stated that customer data stays with the customer and is not shared with anyone to train or improve large language models.

Philipp Herzig, SAP's chief technology officer, framed the announcements as a move from AI that learns a business toward AI that runs it. He said Joule Work lets users state their intent and get work done across the SAP landscape and beyond, with the platform providing secure, governed and compliant deployment from the start. He credited the platform's context layer to more than 50 years of process and industry expertise. The Joule Work updates add agentic planning across multistep workflows, expanded knowledge graph sources, and governed access for third-party agents through an agent gateway. SAP also introduced an Enterprise AI Gateway for centralized traffic management and a new AI Governance Assistant to help customers meet EU AI Act requirements.

Joule Studio gains new observability and administrative controls so developers and administrators can track agent behavior, model usage and spending. Deploying and running custom agents on the SAP-managed runtime will be free through December 2026 for select customers, and the design-time tools will stay free under fair-use limits. On the data side, SAP is adding an ontology manager for Business Data Cloud, expanding its lakehouse support with Dremio, deepening its Databricks partnership, and bringing multidomain master data management through the Reltio solution. The company also unveiled SAP-RPT-2.0, which adds anomaly detection and embeddings, and a time-series model for forecasting in Integrated Business Planning. SAP said that model has been deployed on the International Space Station with HPE to support onboard mission-health analysis without sending data back to Earth.

stories.Headline: SK hynix reports 632% surge in Q3 profit due to AI-driven demand for memory chips - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported on Wednesday that its operating profit for the July to September quarter rose 632 percent from a year earlier. The company said the increase was driven largely by the artificial intelligence industry's strong demand for its advanced memory chips. Operating profit for the period reached 83.33 trillion won, or about $62.8 billion. Net profit climbed 215.7 percent to 39.77 trillion won, and sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The firm said this marked record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

The results fell short of market expectations, as analysts had estimated net profit at 59.67 trillion won, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency citing its own data. SK hynix also announced an additional plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme. The company's shares have been under pressure since June, when they retreated from record highs, and have fallen nearly 60 percent from that peak according to one professor cited in the reporting. Investors have pushed for more cash returns through dividends or buybacks.

SK hynix supplies high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and is a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy. The company's statement attributed its growth to a cycle in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue in software development, customer service and search lead to greater AI adoption. Market research analyst MS Hwang of Counterpoint said long-term agreements with major customers signal another phase of price increases across conventional DRAM, NAND and HBM. Hwang added that quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and that the upward trend will likely continue at least through 2027.

Not all observers are as optimistic about the outlook. Hwang warned that weaker AI spending, increased competition and the company's own capacity expansion could drive price volatility heading into 2027, and named a pullback in cloud providers' orders as the most severe threat. Kim Dae-jong, a business professor at Sejong University, said investors appear to be pricing in concern that current earnings levels may not be sustainable one or two years out. The reporting notes that the global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company's fortunes, even as worries grow that the sector may be overvalued.

stories.Headline: Harmonic AI expands Aristotle model for software and chip design verification - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Harmonic, the AI startup co-founded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev, said on Tuesday that it is expanding its Aristotle model beyond mathematical proofs into software and chip design verification. The announcement comes as the growing use of AI to detect software flaws is drawing more scrutiny. Researchers recently used the technology to uncover critical bugs in PHP, which set off a global rush to patch the vulnerabilities. Separately, Amazon is widening software support for its Trainium AI chips through its Neuron platform, a move reported by TechGig on October 20.

Under the expansion, Aristotle can now verify software written in C and chip designs written in Verilog. The tool is available with usage-based pricing. As an example of its capabilities, the US fusion lab DIII-D said Aristotle rebuilt part of its reactor-control software in four hours, working from one research paper and a 254-word prompt. Harmonic is developing what it calls mathematical superintelligence, a reasoning-focused AI system aimed at reducing hallucinations and factual errors.

On Amazon's side, the Neuron platform supports both Trainium AI chips and Inferentia accelerators. A key piece is the Neuron Kernel Interface, known as NKI, which gives programmers tools to create and fine-tune low-level operations for Amazon's custom silicon. AWS describes Neuron as a software development kit for building and running machine-learning workloads on its chips. NKI is aimed at developers who write specialized kernels, the small code segments that perform computations on the chip, and while that control can optimize particular workloads, it also requires them to learn new interfaces and adapt their code.

Harmonic is backed by Nvidia's venture capital arm, NVentures, along with Sequoia and Ribbit Capital. It raised $120 million in a funding round last November that valued the company at $1.45 billion. Amazon is the party behind the Neuron expansion, which it presents as a way for cloud customers to diversify computing supply and manage expenses. The articles do not include direct statements from either company's executives beyond the announcements themselves.

The Amazon effort targets Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem, whose mature tools and large developer community make switching hardware difficult even when alternatives are cheaper or offer more computing capacity. TechGig notes that customer adoption will hinge on software compatibility and the effort of migrating existing code. Companies weighing the platform will consider framework support, performance under their own conditions, reliability, availability and long-term support, and hardware savings could be offset if large application rewrites are needed. The articles do not say what comes next for either company beyond these adoption questions.

stories.Headline: Live2.ai Secures ₹130 Cr Funding for Expansion
stories.Summary:
Live2.ai, an artificial intelligence startup that helps brands analyse social media activity and manage marketing campaigns, has raised ₹130 crore in a pre-Series B funding round led by IvyCap Ventures, according to an announcement made on October 27, 2026. The round includes primary capital for business expansion along with a secondary component that gives partial liquidity to early shareholders. Inc42 reported that the funding amounts to about $13.7 million and that the round also included a secondary stake sale to undisclosed early investors. The company's board includes backers such as Sony Innovation Fund, SOSV and Duane Park. Live2.ai is operated through Woovly India Private Limited, and it was previously part of Woovly, a business included in Xelpmoc Design and Tech's portfolio.

The company says it will use the new capital to build out its AI agent platform, grow its enterprise business and strengthen its cloud infrastructure across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific. It also plans to expand its engineering, data science and customer success teams in North America, Europe, Singapore and India. Live2.ai offers a shoppable video product through the Shopify App Store, which lets businesses add interactive videos to online stores with features for product discovery, customer engagement and analytics. Its wider platform monitors brand conversations on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X and review websites. According to the company, the platform uses eight AI agents for tasks such as crisis detection, trend identification, campaign auditing and automated responses, with governance controls and human review.

The company's chief executive and cofounder, J Venkat, said in a statement that brands are overwhelmed with signals but short on action, and that the funding will help close that gap for enterprise customers in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific. The startup was founded by Venkat, Neha Suyal and Yash Arora. Live2.ai said it serves more than 200 brands across the United States, Europe and Southeast Asia, with reported customers including Henkel's Schwarzkopf, Salonory, Titan Brands and Shiseido. It reported that its revenue grew fourfold over the past 12 months, with most of it generated outside India, though the two articles differ on the exact share, with one putting it at 90% and the other at 10% from India.

The company has not disclosed its absolute revenue or valuation. The reports place the funding within a broader trend of enterprises adopting AI to automate marketing and other business workflows. Inc42 pointed to recent deals in which Adobe acquired the agentic AI martech startup Rilo and MoEngage acquired Aampe to strengthen their agentic marketing offerings. The articles do not state a timeline for the planned hiring or expansion, or any further funding plans beyond the current round.

stories.Headline: Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer Used AI to Describe Her Daughter for School, Sparking a Parenting Debate
stories.Summary:
Former Yahoo chief executive Marissa Mayer said she used her own AI assistant to come up with a description of her daughter for a school task. Ahead of her daughter Marielle's tenth birthday, a teacher asked parents for three bullet points on what made each child special. Mayer, who felt overwhelmed by the range of possible answers, asked Dazzle, a personal assistant built by her startup, which replied that her daughter was empathetic, creative and an animal lover. She shared the story in an interview with The New York Times, published on October 25, 2026, and called the answer perfect.

Dazzle has been available since late September and analyzes images in a user's camera roll to answer questions, perform tasks and make suggestions. Mayer has said it recognized Marielle's interest in magic and suggested a magic shop in San Francisco for an outing, and that it helped her choose skis for her mother. She has said it blends AI models with personal context and, for complicated requests, human help. The New York Post reported that the app shares camera roll data with third-party platforms for shopping and assistance features. Mayer is 51, runs a team of about 10 engineers, and led Yahoo from 2012 to 2017 after becoming Google's first female engineer.

Mayer is the one at the center of the reaction, and she has defended the broader idea behind her product rather than this particular use. She has pitched Dazzle as an "AI wife" aimed at women, meant to ease the mental load of domestic planning for busy parents, and she said she hopes it will help draw more women into AI. In the Times interview she said that as a woman she wants to see more people like her at the table where decisions are made. Critics, including commentators on X and Reddit, argued that the three descriptors were generic enough to fit millions of children and questioned why a parent needed software for such a personal question. The Post said it had reached out to Mayer for comment, and neither report included a response from her to the criticism.

Supporters of AI tools countered that organizing observations can save time for parents juggling work and childcare. It remains unclear whether the school knew AI had been involved, and there is no evidence of a complaint from the school. Mayer has not said that Dazzle replaced her own knowledge of her daughter. The episode adds to a history of criticism of Mayer, including her time at Yahoo, when she resigned after the company's core operations were sold to Verizon and lawmakers subpoenaed her over security breaches. The articles do not say what Mayer or Dazzle will do next in response to the debate.

stories.Headline: Why F1’s rule-makers are turning to AI to keep up with the teams and close loopholes
stories.Summary:
The Formula 1 governing body, the FIA, has chosen Amazon Web Services as its new partner for artificial intelligence, cloud computing, machine learning, and cloud infrastructure, an announcement made on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. The move follows the F1 organization's own work with AWS, which began in 2018, and comes as all 11 teams have already announced partnerships with AI firms. The FIA writes the final rulebook and polices how cars must look and perform aerodynamically, so the new deal is aimed at its own technical work. AWS already helped shape car design rules for the 2022 and 2026 regulation cycles.

The partnership gives the FIA more access to AWS capabilities, including newer and better hardware, while reducing costs. AWS's head of motorsport, Michael Aghataher, said the approach lets the FIA run thousands of simulations in parallel, turning a process that once took months into one that can finish in hours. The FIA is also looking at AI for policing track limits, with a road map to expand its use over the next couple of years. Under that plan, a human would still make each call, while AI pulls the needed data points and camera footage. Each F1 car carries 300 sensors that produce 1.1 million data points per second, or 24 million data points per race, which the FIA also hopes to process faster with AI.

The FIA's single-seater deputy technical director, Dominic Harlow, said AI is among the top interests for engineers right now and framed the effort as a way to keep pace with the teams. He said the teams are working hard to find loopholes in the rules, and that the FIA's technical department faces larger staff groups at each team. Aghataher described AWS as a supporting tool that optimizes human performance rather than a replacement for people. Harlow also said generative AI in car design regulation was something the FIA could imagine in the future, but that the work remains human-driven for now.

AI is now a regular agenda item at F1 Commission meetings, which set the rules and include the teams, the FIA and the F1 organization. Harlow said the sport is still in an exploration phase and has not yet made a large deployment or a real shift in how people work. The FIA plans to keep discussing the technology and monitor how it affects the areas that matter most to the sport. Given F1's long positioning at the leading edge of technology, all parties are watching closely how AI will be put into practice.

stories.Headline: Biometric information on tourists necessary
stories.Summary:
Home Affairs Director General Mkhuseli Apleni has said it is necessary to take fingerprints from all tourists and travellers visiting South Africa, a position he set out at a Pretoria meeting attended by key tourism and immigration stakeholders. He argued that fingerprints help identify a person, particularly when a crime has been committed. The meeting, which the article dates to 7 December 2016, was held to discuss developments in the immigration regulations. Apleni stressed that taking fingerprints of everyone entering the country was important.

The Department of Home Affairs had introduced a biometric system the previous April that captures travellers' fingerprints at South Africa's international airports. The department said the system would be rolled out to six of the country's busiest land ports of entry. The system is currently used at OR Tambo International Airport and is expected to reach other major airports. Apleni said the department was working on ways to avoid delays there, particularly at OR Tambo, and that people do not have to wait long to have their fingerprints taken. He also expressed hope that other countries would adopt the same biometric system to reduce delays at ports of entry.

Aneme Malan, Deputy Director-General at the Department of Tourism, said her department was working closely with Home Affairs on visa regulations. She noted that the number of tourists arriving in the country had increased, but said the sector had not yet reached its potential and that some areas needed further engagement. The article also covers rules on children, which Apleni and the stakeholders emphasised. Since June 2015, stricter requirements have applied to anyone under 18 travelling to or from South Africa, whether a citizen or a foreigner. A Parental Consent Affidavit must accompany an unabridged birth certificate or equivalent document when a parent is not travelling with the child.

Parents travelling with their children can apply at any Home Affairs office for a fee of R75, bringing their identity documents and the child's abridged birth certificate, while South Africans abroad can apply at their nearest embassy. The article says the law is aimed at curbing child trafficking. According to Home Affairs, 132 353 children were processed in June 2015 across arrivals and departures, of whom 1 878 did not meet the requirements, leaving compliance at 98%. Foreign children numbered about 57 436 on arrival and 74 917 on departure that month.

stories.Headline: Asia stocks rally as SK Hynix earnings boost AI trade; Fed decision ahead
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets rallied on Wednesday, led by South Korea after chipmaker SK Hynix reported a sharp jump in quarterly profit that fed optimism about demand for artificial intelligence. South Korea's KOSPI ended 6.6% higher, reaching its highest level in two weeks. SK Hynix shares closed nearly 11% higher after the company reported a 631% rise in third-quarter operating profit, supported by strong demand for memory chips used in AI applications. The company also announced an additional 60 trillion won in shareholder returns, which added to investor enthusiasm. Samsung Electronics, another major memory chip supplier, rose 9%.

The gains followed an advance on Wall Street overnight, where technology shares led the market higher. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.5%, with chipmakers leading, as Kioxia Holdings jumped 13.8% and Taiyo Yuden gained more than 7%. China's Shanghai Composite and CSI 300 each rose 0.9%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up 0.2%. Elsewhere, moves were subdued as investors waited for the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy announcement later in the day, with interest rates widely expected to stay unchanged. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 finished largely flat, and India's Nifty 50 fell 0.4%.

Investors were also focused on quarterly results from Alphabet and Microsoft, due after the U.S. market close, for evidence that heavy spending on AI infrastructure is producing lasting revenue growth. The rally in AI-related shares has been reinforced by a series of funding announcements and by Anthropic's filing for an initial public offering. Earlier concerns about the cost of building data centres and the long-term sustainability of AI investment had weighed on sentiment. Markets will also look for guidance from Fed policymakers on the outlook for borrowing costs, since persistent inflation and elevated oil prices complicate the picture.

Oil prices also rose, with Brent crude trading above $115 a barrel, which adds to concerns that energy costs could keep inflation under pressure and limit central banks' room to cut rates. Australian data showed underlying inflation accelerating more than expected in the third quarter, strengthening the case for a Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike next week. New Zealand's central bank unexpectedly kept rates unchanged, and New Zealand's NZX 50 edged 0.1% higher. In India, Jio Platforms shares surged more than 20% in their Mumbai market debut after the country's largest-ever initial public offering.

stories.Headline: Hanwha Asset Management's HBM Semiconductor ETF Tops South Korean-Listed Overseas Chip Funds With approximately $445.5 Million in Retail Net Buying
stories.Summary:
Hanwha Asset Management's "PLUS Global HBM Semiconductor" exchange-traded fund has drawn the largest retail net buying among overseas semiconductor ETFs listed in South Korea this year. According to the company, individual investors had net bought 593.3 billion won, roughly $445.5 million, as of October 26. The company announced the figures on October 28, and the fund ranked first in that category. Year-to-date inflows are close to 600 billion won, or about $450.6 million.

The fund's returns are cited as the main reason for the inflows, even amid volatile markets. Its year-to-date return is 88.30%, which ranks 10th among all South Korea-listed ETFs, including leveraged and inverse products. Cumulative returns were 135.01% over one year, 368.22% over two years and 526.75% over three years, as of the same date. The fund's makeup also sets it apart from other domestic chip ETFs, which mostly concentrate on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. It holds Micron alongside those two, and in its May rebalancing it added SanDisk, Teradyne and Techwing.

Hanwha Asset Management credits its differentiated portfolio strategy for the performance, describing the holdings as spanning high-bandwidth memory, DRAM, NAND and equipment. Kim Jung-seop, head of the company's ETF business division, said the top ranking shows investors see memory chips as a structural beneficiary of AI infrastructure growth rather than a short-term theme. He added that the company would act as a reliable partner for long-term investment. The company also pointed to Anthropic, whose IPO registration statement filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission flagged semiconductor supply shortages as a key risk.

Market expectations for continued memory industry growth are tied to the spread of artificial intelligence, and analysts see the upturn continuing. Investors are also looking ahead to the third-quarter earnings reports from SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. The inflows suggest individual investors are spreading money across the global memory value chain rather than a single theme. Analysts say the fund's mix of HBM and back-end equipment names has helped it capture demand tied to AI infrastructure investment.

stories.Headline: New AI tool could end weeks of waiting for inflation data – Study
stories.Summary:
Ghana may soon shorten the wait for inflation figures, after researchers at the Bank of Ghana developed an artificial intelligence tool that produces near real-time estimates of consumer price movements. The system, called e-Inflation, uses big data and AI methods to track prices across online platforms and generate inflation estimates before official numbers are released. The study was reported by GNA and carried by BusinessGhana on October 29, 2026, and by The Ghanaian Chronicle two days earlier. Its authors say the model could give policymakers, businesses and investors timelier information for their decisions.

Official inflation data are currently gathered through conventional price collection and published only after each reference month ends. The study says this delay, though needed for validation and compilation, can limit how quickly policymakers and market players respond to changing conditions. To close that gap, the researchers built an AI framework that gathers and analyses large volumes of price data from websites and other digital sources. It uses web-scraping tools and machine learning algorithms to follow prices of goods and services that consumers buy often. The study indicates the system mirrored official inflation trends well, and that the e-Inflation measure closely tracked Ghana's official inflation rate over the study period.

The researchers said such indicators could be especially useful to the Bank of Ghana's Monetary Policy Committee, whose interest rate decisions depend on current and expected inflation. The study also pointed to the growing role of digital technology in economic management, noting that online platforms offer cheaper and more frequent ways to collect price information. It stressed, however, that the tool is not meant to replace official statistics compiled by the Ghana Statistical Service. Instead, it is intended to complement existing methods by giving faster insight into emerging price trends. The authors argue that wider use of big data and AI could improve the timeliness of economic statistics and support efforts to maintain price stability as Ghana's digital economy grows.
