stories.Headline: Crusoe Spark supports NVIDIA DSX POD
stories.Summary:
Crusoe announced on October 21, 2026 that its Crusoe Spark modular AI data center platform will support NVIDIA's newly unveiled DSX POD reference design, a blueprint for modular infrastructure built around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform. The reference design, unveiled at GTC Berlin, packages computing, networking, rack-level power and liquid cooling into standardized containers that manufacturers would fully integrate, cable and test before shipping them to a site. NVIDIA says this could cut deployment time at a prepared site from six months to as few as 14 days, with partner deployments targeted for early 2027. Crusoe also unveiled Crusoe Spark Liquid, its sixth-generation modular AI factory built for ultra-high-density systems such as the Vera Rubin NVL72. Crusoe says it has built and operated modular AI factories since 2020, and it produces Spark units at its 352,000-square-foot Crusoe Spark Factory in Brighton, Colorado.

The announcement shows how Crusoe is positioning itself within NVIDIA's expanding modular ecosystem. Crusoe describes itself as the first provider to combine in-house modular data center manufacturing with its own cloud platform, Crusoe Cloud, from end to end. Customers can access Vera Rubin capacity through Crusoe Cloud, deploy dedicated units through Crusoe Edge Zones, or add standardized modular capacity to existing sites. Crusoe says it can deliver productive AI capacity in as little as three months. It also reports that it recently reached NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud performance inside a modular AI factory, which it presents as evidence that Spark delivers consistent performance per total cost of ownership.

Crusoe's head of Spark, Bryan Schramm, said modular design has been part of the company's approach since its founding and that Crusoe brings nearly a decade of operational field experience to the DSX POD effort. NVIDIA's vice president of DGX Systems, Charlie Boyle, said modular AI factories are essential to meeting global demand for accelerated computing and credited Crusoe with helping customers bring production inference online faster. NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang has argued that an AI factory creates value once it starts producing tokens, not when construction ends. The broader trend reflects operators' pressure to bring power-dense AI infrastructure online while facing labor shortages, long construction schedules and changing hardware requirements. Industry coverage notes that power availability and supply chain constraints remain the main tests, since NVIDIA's two-week timeline depends on prepared sites, reliable components and energy infrastructure that can take years to build.

stories.Headline: KT Cloud Ties Up With Vertiv on AI Data Center Technology
stories.Summary:
KT Cloud, the cloud and data center arm of KT Corporation, announced on October 28, 2026 that it has signed a strategic technology partnership with Vertiv, a global artificial intelligence infrastructure specialist. The agreement expands cooperation on power, cooling and modular solutions for next-generation AI data centers. The move follows rapid growth in demand for power and cooling, driven by heavier AI workloads and denser clusters of graphics processing units. Both companies said the partnership was formed to meet those rising requirements.

Under the agreement, the two companies will take part jointly from the design stage of the AI data centers KT Cloud is building, reviewing in advance how power infrastructure, liquid cooling and modular systems fit together. KT Cloud plans to use Vertiv's modular infrastructure at its AI data center in Gunsan to speed up construction. One main product, SmartRun, is a prefabricated offering that combines power, cooling and network infrastructure in a single pre-built structure. According to the reports, it can cut installation time by up to 85 percent compared with conventional on-site construction.

Paul Churchill, vice president and general manager for Asia at Vertiv, said that integrated infrastructure able to flexibly support rapidly changing AI workloads is becoming more important. He said the company will combine its global technology with KT Cloud's data center expertise to accelerate construction of AI-optimized facilities. Kim Bong-kyun, chief executive of KT Cloud, said the company will pair Vertiv's technology with its own construction and operating capabilities to strengthen its competitiveness in next-generation AI infrastructure. He added that this will provide stable support for the KT Group's plan to expand its AI data center capacity to 1 gigawatt.

The partnership reflects a broader push by data center operators to build AI-ready facilities faster and with fewer vendors on site. The articles do not say when the Gunsan facility is scheduled to open or how the partnership's results will be measured. They also do not describe any financial terms of the agreement. Further progress would be shown by construction milestones at the Gunsan site and by the pace at which KT Group advances toward its 1 gigawatt target.

stories.Headline: Behind-the-Meter Power Draws $700 Million Bet as AI Demand Surges
stories.Summary:
Neuberger Specialty Finance, the financing arm of the private investment firm Neuberger, announced earlier this month a $700 million financing facility for Crusoe, an AI infrastructure developer. The money is meant to buy power infrastructure that will directly energize AI factories that Crusoe builds and owns. The article describes this as a potentially risky bet that behind-the-meter power projects, and possibly microgrids, will spread as demand for energy-hungry AI facilities grows. Rod Walton, the managing editor of Microgrid Knowledge, wrote the piece, which was published on October 28, 2026.

The deal fits a wider pattern in which private equity firms are funding dedicated power for data centers because the public grid is constrained. Blackstone, KKR, Brookfield and ArcLight Capital Partners have each announced larger commitments to dedicated energy infrastructure. Crusoe is planning more than six gigawatts of AI infrastructure and wants off-grid power to avoid long waits in grid interconnection queues. The companies say that producing its own power lets it move faster than the grid allows.

Nick Sammut, the senior vice president of strategic finance and corporate development at Crusoe, said in a statement that the company is building AI factories at a pace and scale the market has never seen and needs financing partners who can move with the same urgency. He said the structure lets Crusoe secure long-lead power generation assets that match its development timelines. Sean Hinze, a managing director at Neuberger Specialty Finance, said the firm sees significant value in the power generation assets that support Crusoe's growth. He added that behind-the-meter power is becoming increasingly important to the AI buildout.

The article places the deal within a larger market. Crusoe closed a $3.9 billion Series F round in September at a valuation reported near $31 billion, and it has built data centers for OpenAI, Microsoft and Google in Texas. It is also planning facilities in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Colorado and Norway. Goldman Sachs forecast last year that global electricity demand from AI and cloud computing could reach 84 gigawatts by 2027, and it said demand could add more than 100 gigawatts by the mid-2030s. The article does not say what will happen next with the Neuberger facility or with Crusoe's planned sites.

stories.Headline: For AI, Your Selfie Is a Medical Scan; But It's Not All Rosy
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston built an artificial intelligence model that can estimate a person's biological age and predict cancer survival from a single facial photograph. The findings were published in October 2026 in The Lancet Digital Health. The system, called FAHR-Face, was trained on more than 40 million facial images and then fine-tuned for two tasks. One version estimates biological age from the skin around the temples, forehead and mouth, while the other focuses on the bridge of the nose and the area beneath the eyes to assess mortality risk. The study reports that people in cancer treatment whose faces appeared at least five years older than their actual age had a 21 per cent higher risk of dying over an average four-year follow-up.

Those who looked five years younger had a 17 per cent lower risk. Among a group of 122 patients identified as high risk, 52.5 per cent died within 90 days of the photograph being taken. The researchers say this is the first AI algorithm able to predict cancer patient survival directly from a simple face photo. The lead researcher, Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General, said the team was surprised that mortality signals could be picked up from a face alone. He noted that the same facial regions were described by Hippocrates in ancient medical texts, though the algorithms were trained only on photographs and had no knowledge of those writings.

The developers present the tool as a way to make the clinical judgment doctors already form about frailty more consistent and scalable, not as a replacement for physicians. The article also raises concerns about how such tools could be misused. A face scan could be used by insurers to decide on policies or claims, or by employers to screen candidates, and models trained on large datasets may carry demographic biases. A risk score is also a statistical probability rather than a diagnosis, so it could be misread by clinicians, patients or families. The authors warn that the technology is likely to grow more powerful, and that governance may struggle to keep pace with it.

stories.Headline: Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Army has selected Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to support Project Griffin, a pilot effort to build an AI-enabled cybersecurity capability, the service announced in late October 2026. The pilot has a combined value of $2.6 million and falls under the Army Rapid Development of Cyber Defense Systems program, which is driven by the project manager for cyber warfare under the portfolio management executive for intelligence and spectrum warfare. Army Cyber Command is also involved in the initiative. The selections followed a solicitation released in August for agentic AI solutions for an Intelligent Response and Orchestration Node capability, and the Army received more than 100 industry submissions before choosing two vendors.

The Army is seeking an agentic, autonomous AI platform that can help cyber defenders neutralize threats faster than human operators can. The goal is to reduce vulnerabilities that arise when network protection depends on manual data review and human action. The system is meant to draw on information from the Army's network sensors and take defensive measures against potential threats. Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which uses rapid industry sprints to speed the adoption of AI-enabled cyber defense tools. The pilot is one of three fast-tracked efforts under that initiative.

Brandon Pugh, the secretary of the Army's principal cyber advisor, leads the ARDS work and said the selections let the service move at the speed of business needed to deliver the capability. He said the Army will quickly deploy tools that detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and adopt agentic AI to scale network defense securely. Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare, said partnering with commercial industry is a national security imperative because private firms drive rapid innovation in AI, cloud architecture and cyber operations. Officials at AWS and WWT did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though a WWT executive publicly highlighted the selection on LinkedIn.

The pilot comes after other recent Army cybersecurity moves, including the naming of eight companies in May to compete for work under a potential $49 million contract backing the Next-Gen Commercial Operations in Defended Enclaves pilot for small defense suppliers. The Army also enlisted Keysight to test zero trust security on its unified network. Defense officials are increasingly focused on the threat of AI-enabled digital attacks against their systems, and Project Griffin is intended to answer that threat with commercial tools. The articles do not say when the pilot will conclude or when its capabilities will be fielded across the Army's networks.

stories.Headline: Ad Empires in the AI Crosshairs: Meta’s Massive Infra Spending vs. Google’s Search Defense
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms and Alphabet both missed earnings-per-share estimates this month, and in both cases the shortfall came from items outside their advertising businesses. Meta recorded a $9.89 billion legal charge, while Alphabet took an $8.70 billion loss on equity securities. Beneath those charges, both companies grew their ad operations quickly even as spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure climbed and free cash flow turned negative. The analysis compares how each company is pursuing its AI strategy and how investors are valuing them.

Meta's revenue rose 26.1% to $64.60 billion, with the average price per ad up 14%. Nearly 10 million advertisers used a generative AI creative tool. Without the legal charge, Meta's operating income would have risen 11%. Alphabet's standout was Google Cloud, where revenue grew 103% to $30.71 billion. Sundar Pichai said the year-over-year growth rate in search queries is the highest it has been in five years, which the article presents as an answer to fears that AI chatbots would erode Search.

Meta's AI agent, Muse, drew more than 10 million users in the United States and Canada within about six weeks, and over 25% of weekly users already shop through it. Mark Zuckerberg acknowledged that running Muse is very compute-intensive and said Meta is aiming for a more than tenfold efficiency gain within a year. To help fund the expansion, Meta plans a new nonvoting share class, which the article describes as an effective two-for-one stock split. Alphabet, by contrast, sells its infrastructure to outside customers, and Pichai cited strong demand for its TPU systems across a range of customers.

The article notes Meta's 2026 capital expenditure plan of $135 billion to $145 billion and says the company must show Muse can generate commerce fees and subscriptions. Alphabet held its 2026 capex outlook steady but expects a significant increase in 2027, and it has raised cash through $28.7 billion in notes and at-the-market stock sales. Meta shares fell 12.19% in the week after earnings, and Alphabet trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 14 compared with Meta's 22. The writer leans toward Alphabet because its spending is supported by paying Cloud customers today, though that view could change if Muse revenue becomes clear in 2027 and the legal uncertainty passes.

stories.Headline: Cadence Introduces Maestro, a Domain-Specialized AI Model Portfolio to Revolutionize Agentic Chip and System Design
stories.Summary:
Cadence has announced the Maestro AI Model Portfolio, a set of domain-specialized models built to power its AI Super Agents for semiconductor and system design. The announcement, dated October 28, 2026 by design-reuse.com and October 26, 2026 by EMSNow, says the models are combined with reinforcement learning loops and Cadence's established electronic design automation and system design automation tools. Cadence describes the result as an integrated agentic engineering platform meant to improve engineering results and shorten time to market. The company says the portfolio spans several model sizes and architectures, mixing post-trained large language models, trained decision models and self-improving agent skills. The portfolio is designed to run alongside frontier and open-weight models, with deployment possible on Cadence's secure cloud, on public clouds, or in a customer-controlled on-premises environment.

Initial results cited by Cadence show up to 30 percent improvement in quality of results and up to 5X greater token efficiency compared with a general-purpose foundation model. Those gains are attributed to a learning environment that pairs Cadence domain knowledge, curated engineering datasets, AI Super Agents, EDA and SDA tools, and evaluation harnesses. Cadence says its deterministic solvers check outputs against engineering objectives, constraints and ground truth to close the feedback loop. Customers can further post-train the models on their own proprietary data, designs and workflows. The first Maestro models will be offered to select early access customers in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Cadence's chief executive, Anirudh Devgan, said that complex engineering work needs deep domain-specialized intelligence and that pairing Maestro with leading frontier and open-weight models lets the AI Super Agents drive Cadence tools more skillfully. NVIDIA's Tim Costa said agentic chip design requires AI that can generate design content, weigh tradeoffs and learn from verified results, and noted that NVIDIA Nemotron and OpenShell are part of the collaboration. Socionext's COO, Hisato Yoshida, said his company is deploying the InnoStack AI Super Agent in production and expects up to 5X overall productivity gains while keeping design quality. Silicon Labs' Garima Sharda reported faster root-cause analysis and debug during pre-silicon low power verification using ChipStack. Cadence and NVIDIA also describe joint work on agent security through the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture.

The announcement arrives in a busy stretch for the company, with related Cadence items in the same reports covering a European sovereign AI platform developed with NVIDIA and AI Super Agent work with Nokia and Socionext. The articles frame Maestro as a way for chip and system designers to use AI that is tuned to engineering tasks rather than general language use. Neither article reports independent testing of the performance figures, and both rely on Cadence's own initial results. The articles do not describe pricing or broad commercial release beyond the early access group, so the timing of wider availability remains unstated.

stories.Summary:
The Rotary Club World Affairs Conference took place in Fort Wayne, Indiana, on a Tuesday in late October 2026, bringing hundreds of high school students to Purdue Fort Wayne to learn about artificial intelligence. The event featured an interactive two-part activity in which students practiced designing, testing, branding, and marketing with the technology. Speakers also addressed how AI is changing education and the workforce. Organizers described the conference as a way for students to raise awareness of global issues while building skills in critical thinking, communication, collaboration, problem-solving, conflict and sustainability resolution, and leadership.

Separately, a Georgia report published on October 26, 2026, examined how students at Arabia Mountain High School in Stonecrest are adjusting to classroom limits on AI. Under DeKalb County School District guidelines, individual teachers decide when students may use AI on assignments, and students may not submit AI-generated work as their own without permission. Students interviewed said the limits have made schoolwork take longer but have pushed them to think more independently. Some said they now pay closer attention in class, while others turn to resources such as Khan Academy and YouTube for step-by-step explanations.

The district's guidelines also cover inappropriate AI uses, including creating deepfakes, impersonating others, harassment, and unauthorized help on tests, which can be treated as academic integrity violations under the Student Code of Conduct. The district's Instructional Technology website promotes its Gemini AI Certification Program, which teaches students about AI safety, digital citizenship, writing prompts, and real-world applications. The report was written by Sofia Robertson, a student reporter in Robert Calloway's A/V and Film class, and Calloway, a teacher at the school, is quoted describing the challenge of balancing technology use with real learning. The students' views differed, with some suggesting AI could be useful for group projects or for explaining hard topics, while others worried about dependence and about teachers relying on AI to create classroom materials. The article presents these views as part of an ongoing conversation about how schools can ensure the technology supports learning rather than replacing it.

stories.Headline: Trusting and verifying agentic AI for investigations
stories.Summary:
The Thomson Reuters article, published on October 28, 2026, argues that corporate investigators are adopting agentic AI tools to keep pace with criminals, who are using the same technology to earn profits four times higher than earlier digital methods, according to the 2026 INTERPOL Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment. It cites a Thomson Reuters Institute report finding that 40% of organizations already use or plan to use agentic AI tools. Speaking at a Thomson Reuters webinar, Amy Fardella, Senior Vice President of BSA Operations at First National Bank of Texas, said speed is now essential because people may create false evidence as well as destroy it. Investigators face fraud methods such as impersonation schemes, romance and investment scams, and business email compromise, each made more frequent and more deceptive by AI.

The article says the most effective approaches keep a human in the loop, so that AI speeds up data gathering and analysis while experienced staff interpret the results. Susan Woods, Senior Ethics and Compliance Investigator at Balfour Beatty Investments, said that data gains meaning only once context is added, and that investigators must ask whether a risk is isolated, individual or systemic. The authors treat AI as something that extends expertise rather than replacing it. Tools can now map relationships, spot unusual patterns across large datasets and produce sourced reports, and Fardella described turning an interview recording into a transcript, an interview report and an executive summary almost immediately. She also said the tools can keep track of an investigative line of questioning across follow-up queries.

The article says trustworthy use requires enterprise-grade security, including role-based access controls, audit logging and strong data privacy protections, along with a clear method that lets investigators trace each finding to its original source. Woods raised questions about who can access the information entered into these systems, how reliable that information is, and how human interaction central to many interviews should be handled. Fardella said quick action helps confirm whether an allegation is credible while also reassuring the people involved that the company is responding. The article closes by saying that corporate risk teams must adapt their investigative methods to keep up with AI-enhanced threats, and that properly supervised agentic tools can strengthen investigations without lowering standards.

stories.Headline: Nvidia backs Simplismart in $14 million funding for AI efficiency
stories.Summary:
On October 27 and 28, 2026, reports described how Bengaluru-based AI infrastructure startup Simplismart raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with Nvidia investing alongside Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The four-year-old company, founded in 2022 by Amritanshu Jain and Devansh Ghatak, is now valued at about $100 million including the new money. Its software sits between AI models and computing hardware, automating how models are deployed and managed so that customers can tune response speed, request handling and computing consumption. Simplismart employs 58 people.

The funding is aimed at reducing dependence on GPUs, the specialized chips used to run AI models, by helping companies get more out of the hardware they already have. The company plans to use the money to expand its presence in the United States and North America, grow its team, and further develop its inference platform. It also intends to build partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI players. Simplismart has also been developing a dynamic GPU scheduling layer intended to match workloads with available capacity across regions and time zones, which would help cloud providers improve utilization. The company does not own computing infrastructure itself, instead supplying the software layer that lets providers offer AI services on their own hardware.

Jain and Ghatak said the advantage in AI now lies in how models are run rather than simply having access to them, pointing to cost per interaction, response speed and reliability as demand grows. Dayakar Puskoor, managing partner at Dallas Venture Capital, said inferencing is becoming one of the biggest factors in AI economics. Jain also said Nvidia has collaborated with Simplismart on technical integrations, including its Dynamo inference software, and has introduced the startup to potential customers and partners. The company has said its software helped video-generation platform InVideo cut GPU serving costs by 56 per cent.

The context is a shift among enterprises toward controlling what it costs to run AI applications in production, as open-weight models offer alternatives to proprietary models accessed through paid interfaces. Simplismart's annualised revenue run rate grew 14-fold over six months to an eight-figure sum, and more than half of its revenue comes from the U.S., even though it has more customers in India. Its clients include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema, and Indian cloud provider Yotta uses its technology to power the serverless inference layer of Shakti Studio. Simplismart competes with Nvidia itself, major cloud providers and numerous other startups building tools for faster and cheaper AI operations. Jain said the company wins where clients have strict service-level agreements and total cost of ownership requirements.

stories.Headline: AI is changing our world. First, let's understand what it is.
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has been around for decades, but generative AI has made it feel suddenly everywhere. A Pew Research Center survey from June found nearly half of U.S. adults use AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, and one in four of them use one every day. About a third of American homes have devices with AI built in, such as doorbells, thermostats or smart speakers. Use is growing even as many people remain skeptical, with more adults expecting a negative rather than positive impact on them and on society.

Generative AI differs from older tools such as the iPhone's Siri, which worked with limited data inside preexisting code. Newer systems learn from enormous quantities of data and produce original text, images, audio, video and computer code in response to user prompts. The field changed quickly after a 2017 Google paper on the "Transformer" framework, and by late 2022 OpenAI had released GPT-3 to the public. Companies including Google, OpenAI and Anthropic have since raced to build more advanced models, and many are now described as agents that can act on their own without a human prompt. Gerol C. Petruzella, an academic technology consultant at Williams College, argues that this shift means society must figure out new rules for a world where humans are no longer the only entities able to act independently.

The article was written by Ben Niewoehner and introduces a three-part series by Petruzella in The Berkshire Eagle, which will examine AI's effects on local businesses and systems, daily life, and what separates the technology from profit-driven hype. Petruzella defines AI broadly as any technology that does things that would traditionally have required human cognition. He says AI is already part of the digital tools and apps people use, and it is becoming part of the environment in which people work and live. The series is meant to explore how the technology will affect Berkshire County in the coming months and years.

stories.Headline: Prosecutors say Rhode Island agency used AI to create backdated Medicaid records in alleged $2 million fraud scheme
stories.Summary:
Seven people tied to a Providence community health worker agency were indicted by a Rhode Island grand jury over an alleged $2 million Medicaid fraud scheme. Prosecutors say the agency's owner and an employee used artificial intelligence to produce patient notes and treatment records months after the services supposedly occurred. Attorney General Peter Neronha announced a 51-count indictment on Oct. 22. The allegations have not been proven in court, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

The defendants are linked to U'Nique Diversity Innovations LLC, a provider on Branch Avenue in Providence that the state approved as a Medicaid community health worker provider in November 2024. Prosecutors allege that from then until June 2025, the owner billed for services never provided, services greatly overstated, services billed for family members, and services supposedly given to people who were incarcerated. They further allege that backdated training certificates were created and signed to make it appear staff had completed required training, and that none of the seven were certified as community health workers during that period. The indictment also describes cash bonuses for recruiting Medicaid members and alleged personal spending of Medicaid money. Charges vary by defendant and include Medicaid fraud, conspiracy, identity theft and racketeering.

Attorney General Neronha said that people who commit Medicaid fraud, as alleged here, are stealing public funds. The owner, Shanee Vega, 44, faces 48 of the counts and was released on $50,000 bail with surety after her arrest at home. The other six defendants turned themselves in over the following days. The investigation began in May 2025, when the state's Medicaid program integrity office referred the case to the attorney general's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, and investigators searched the agency's offices in July 2025.

The case lands against a backdrop of concern about the community health worker program, which helps Medicaid members connect with doctors, food and housing support. Advocates have said these workers can prevent more costly care, while state officials said in 2025 that a crackdown with tighter billing rules was saving Medicaid nearly $2 million a month. The company has since closed. The records question matters beyond this case, since AI-generated notes can look complete on paper, so auditors may need to check records against appointment logs, phone records or member confirmations. Medicaid members who spot unfamiliar charges can call their health plan, and suspected fraud can be reported to the attorney general's unit or the HHS Office of Inspector General at 1-800-HHS-TIPS.

stories.Headline: Google AI Privacy: How Personal Data Fuels Ads
stories.Summary:
Google's privacy policy, which took effect on October 16, 2026, now allows personal content from Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive to help shape personalized ads when users connect those apps to other Google services. The change sits alongside a new feature called Personal Intelligence, which lets AI Mode in Search and Gemini draw on a user's messages, inbox, and photos to answer questions. Android Authority first noticed the exception, and other outlets followed. Google's earlier policy had said it did not show personalized ads based on content from those services, and that statement remains, but it now carries an exception for users who opt in to share the data with other services.

The policy exception matters because Google's help documentation says that summaries, excerpts, generated media, and inferences drawn from connected emails and files may be used, and that the same inferences and summaries may be used to show advertisements. Google says the raw messages stay where they are, and that Gemini Apps chats are not currently used for ads, with users to be told if that changes. Turning off personalized ads in My Ad Center may not stop connected-app data from being processed for AI personalization, and disconnecting an app does not delete data already retained. Some connected data may also be read by human reviewers and used for product improvement, including AI training. Google's advertising business produced $82.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, about 72 per cent of Alphabet's revenue for that period.

Google's public statements say the company does not sell users' information, and that advertisers do not get access to Gmail or Photos. The company's advertising policy also says it does not personalize ads around health, race, religion, or sexual orientation. Google has described the Personal Intelligence feature as opt-in, and its help pages present the connected-content features as separate from other Google AI services. Critics of the arrangement argue that a single consent click covers two different uses, and that the explanation sits in a policy most people never read. In 2017, Google stopped scanning consumer Gmail to personalize ads after years of criticism.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires consent to be free, specific, informed, and unconditional, and limited to the purpose stated. Parts of the Act are already in force, but the main obligations are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027, and the consent manager provisions on November 13, 2026. The Act places on the company the burden of proving valid consent for a new use of data, and it is for the Data Protection Board to decide whether one click can cover advertising. Ads in AI Mode for users with Personal Intelligence turned on are now being tested, and Google has said it expected ads to work this way for connected users later.

Waters says this keeps data integrity, traceability and compliance intact, and that the models are version-controlled and stay fixed until a laboratory chooses to retrain and approve a new one. Customers can enroll now for early access beginning in December 2026, and validated, compliant deployment is expected to follow in mid-2027. The company describes it as the second step after AI/ML Anomaly Detection, which launched in February 2025.

Waters, which is listed on the NYSE under the ticker WAT, is responsible for the announcement. She said the company has a full pipeline of further capabilities planned. The company also says it is working with several large pharmaceutical customers and academic institutions on AI-enabled research and quality capabilities that move from discovery to release, and that the Empower installed base is about 500,000 users.

Separately, on October 22, 2026, South Korea's K-water signed a contract with Song Duong JSC to introduce its AI water treatment plant operation technology at the Song Duong Water Treatment Plant in Hanoi, Vietnam, which produces 300,000 cubic meters of tap water per day. The three-phase project is worth about 1.94 billion won, or $1.41 million, and it is the second such export after a project at the Kenh Dong plant in Ho Chi Minh City in April. K-water said the system will analyze water quality and flow data in real time to optimize coagulant and chlorine dosing. The company also said the technology was named a Global Lighthouse by the World Economic Forum and advanced in an ISO vote ahead of a 2027 international standard. K-water's Han Seong-yong, head of its Green Infrastructure Division, called the deal meaningful for showing that its water technology can keep expanding overseas, and the company also signed memoranda of understanding with VIWASEEN and the Vietnam Water Supply and Sewerage Association on October 21.

stories.Headline: Oracle Cloud to Offer Google TPUs and New AI Chips
stories.Summary:
Oracle said on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at its Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas, that it will become the first hyperscaler to offer Google's Tensor Processing Units outside Google Cloud. The company is broadening the AI chips available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, to include inference chips from OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova and Positron AI as well. The announcement came alongside an expanded partnership with Nvidia, and Oracle said Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. It also plans to grow OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt scale using the Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. Google described the TPU move as part of a wider expansion of its partnership with Oracle across AI infrastructure, enterprise data and agentic AI.

Oracle said Google TPUs for training and inference will arrive on OCI in 2027, with adoption ramping over several years. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for fast inference is also due in 2027, while Positron AI's Positron Atlas inference chip is already generally available. Oracle will deploy OpenAI's Jalapeño inference accelerators, built with Broadcom, but did not say when they will be available on OCI. OpenAI and Broadcom have previously said they expect initial deployment of Jalapeño by the end of 2026. SambaNova is also working with Oracle to deploy its SN50 inference chips, though no date was given; the company claims up to five times the speed of rival chips at one third the total cost of ownership, and an average draw of 20 kW per rack.

Industry analysts offered their views on the shift. Brendan Burke, research director at Futurum Group, said Oracle is aligning with the industry's move toward heterogeneous computing, and that offering several accelerators gives customers choice. Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, called the plan an aggressive expansion in which Oracle is trying to be the open silicon cloud, with something for everybody. Burke added that Oracle must prove the new accelerators are competitive with Nvidia-based offerings and show a long-term commitment rather than treating them as limited experiments. Kimball said putting TPUs on OCI lets customers use them without moving their data to Google Cloud, since Oracle already holds a lot of customer data and AI workloads.

Oracle's cloud has relied mainly on Nvidia GPUs, with some AMD GPU deployments, according to analysts. Google's eighth-generation TPU family includes the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference, and Google says both offer up to twice the performance per watt. It also says the 8t delivers up to 2.7 times better performance per dollar and the 8i up to 80% better than the prior generation. Burke said Google appears to have decided that making its compute capacity available externally is worth more than keeping it all for internal teams, partly because the AI compute market remains tight. AWS has reportedly considered selling its Trainium chip for use in third-party data centers, which suggests hyperscalers see a wider market for their custom silicon.

stories.Headline: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services engineers have described how their team handles Linux kernel vulnerabilities for the kernel used in its EC2 infrastructure. Dylan Johnson and Justinien Bouron presented the method at the Linux Plumbers Conference in Prague, and it combines an automated filter, an AI agent, and human review. The team maintains this kernel separately from Amazon Linux and from the kernels customers run in their own virtual machines. Since the Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, the volume has risen sharply, with about two kernel CVEs a week before then and roughly 16 a day afterwards. The first stage uses a script rather than AI, discarding any CVE whose affected version range excludes the running kernel or whose listed source files are not built into the image.

In AWS's environment this removes about 70 percent of CVEs, though Bouron said the figure depends heavily on kernel configuration. The remaining CVEs go to an AI agent, which receives AWS's kernel source tree, per-platform configurations, a description of the environment and threat model, and a severity rubric. The agent produces a table covering the affected subsystem, vulnerability type, and attack vector, and it takes about 3.4 seconds per CVE. Bouron said the team ignores CVSS scores because they are not specific to its environment, calling the agent "a very fancy classifier." Two engineers usually review the table, and Bouron said that step is now the slowest and will not be removed.

Bouron informally estimated that between 5 and 10 percent of the agent's decisions were problematic, and the talk did not describe a formal evaluation. The team also disables unneeded kernel features to reduce the number of applicable CVEs, a task he called "deceptively difficult" given more than 32,000 configuration options. The team's data also shows that older long-term-support branches receive fixes later and accumulate more unfixed CVEs. For six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 and 18.1 days for 6.18, and on 16 September 1,709 known CVEs were unfixed in 5.10 compared with 229 in 6.18. AWS has also shortened its own upgrades, moving from 4.19 to 5.10 over about two years and then to 6.18 in about six months.

Microsoft's Azure Linux team described a similar pipeline at the same conference, using a rule table for triage verdicts with AI suggesting inputs, and agents for backporting. Google DeepMind's CodeMender focuses on writing fixes, with human researchers reviewing every patch before submission. AWS has not released its tools, but Johnson said the team would like to explore sharing the filtering tool. The approach is presented as a way for an operator running its own kernel to keep pace with a rising flow of vulnerability records.

stories.Headline: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than news, so the breaking-story format does not apply, and I have written it as a four-paragraph piece in my own words. Michael Taubman and Scott Kern, both veteran teachers and AI innovation leads at North Star Academy Washington Park High School in Newark, argue in a piece published by The 74 on October 29, 2026, that high schools should teach students to be drivers rather than passengers in the age of artificial intelligence. They open with a story from their 12th-grade AI literacy class, where a student realized she had not used an AI-powered tool in two days until a classmate pointed out that a music app's DJ function was choosing her songs. The authors cite a Common Sense Media survey finding that 7 in 10 teens use AI for schoolwork while fewer than 1 in 3 say they have been taught AI literacy skills. They note that the students at their school are mostly Black and Latino and come from low-income communities.

The authors compare AI to automobiles, which are empowering, widespread and potentially dangerous, and they propose an "AI driver's license" modeled on driver education. Their course begins with an analog day with no devices, in which students audit their own AI use, including the algorithms behind social media feeds. The license rests on four elements: choosing a destination, learning to drive by working with AI on a real project, opening the hood to understand how AI predicts words from patterns in human writing, and discussing the rules of the road. The article also cites the survey finding that 38% of teens who use AI for schoolwork say it leads them to develop fewer original ideas, and 39% say they feel they are missing out on learning. Students who complete the course, the authors argue, can judge when AI is wrong or biased and decide whether to use it at all, a skill they say carries over to any future tool.

Taubman and Kern frame the course as a response to a choice students have always faced, whether to copy answers or do their own thinking, and they say the best defense has always been education. Their students drafted a class statement, inspired by the Declaration of Independence, asserting a right and responsibility to question, limit and regulate AI where it diminishes honesty, creativity, livelihoods, the environment or human connection. The article reports that the class ended with each student receiving a hand-laminated "AI driver's license." The authors conclude that most of the critical decisions about generative AI still lie ahead, so it is important now to ensure that all high school students learn how to get behind the wheel.

stories.Headline: Bond investors have gotten picky about AI
stories.Summary:
Bond investors have grown more selective about which AI-linked borrowers they will finance, even as AI borrowing keeps rising. The shift follows a sell-off in early October, when yields on bonds issued by CoreWeave, a heavily indebted AI company, climbed sharply, meaning its bond prices fell. Since then the broader corporate bond market has calmed, and enthusiasm around Anthropic and Meta has helped restore confidence in the AI trade that supports stock prices. Axios reporter Matt Phillips, writing on October 28, 2026, says that calm hides lingering caution toward the more leveraged players.

The price moves have spread beyond CoreWeave itself. Bonds that finance data centers leased to CoreWeave, including those issued by Edged Compute, Core Scientific and Applied Digital, saw their yields creep higher after CoreWeave's bonds fell, with CoreWeave's own unsecured bonds reaching yields of around 16 percent. Data center debt tied to Oracle has moved in step with Oracle's own bonds. Roughly $14 billion of bonds maturing in 2045, issued to build a large data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, wobbled along with Oracle's over the past couple of weeks. Ratings agencies say Oracle's signed 17-year lease for that campus is a major support for those bonds.

Citigroup's high-yield debt analysts said in a note last week that tenant-specific risk was exposed during the October pullback, with CoreWeave and similar neocloud and data center companies bearing most of the selloff. They warned that data center bonds are not immune to tenant default and can reprice quickly as that risk rises. Axios reports that the same pattern is visible among safer investment-grade bonds, where investors now distinguish sharply between borrowers rather than treating AI-related debt as largely interchangeable. The articles do not say how these conditions will evolve.

stories.Headline: Autonomous machine learning
stories.Summary:
Two sources cover very different things, so I will treat them separately. The first is a research article titled "Autonomous machine learning," published in Science China Information Sciences on 28 October 2026 by Wenwu Zhu, Xin Wang and Zhiqiang Xu. The article itself is only partly visible here: it lists a set of references on self-supervised learning, active learning, AutoML, meta-learning and self-directed learning, and notes funding from the Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology under Grant No. BNR2026TD03005. The authors are affiliated with Tsinghua University in Beijing and Xi'an Jiaotong University. The visible text does not state the paper's findings, so no claims about its results can be drawn from it.

The second source, published on 27 October 2026, describes geoscientists in China who used high-resolution 3D seismic imaging together with machine learning to map fault networks in the deep Tarim Basin. Earlier surveys relied on seismic data gathered from widely spaced grids, which could not detect smaller fracture lines. The researchers instead ran 3D reflection surveys in the Shunbei central region and applied machine learning classifiers to millions of seismic data points, which found many low-order branch connections between major fault fragments automatically. The article says this speeded up fault mapping and reduced human bias, though it reports no specific figures for the speedup. Physical sandbox experiments using sand and silicone were also used to model deep basement faulting, and they suggested that large regional faults absorb tectonic strain early on, leaving secondary faults inactive.

The article attributes the work to geoscientists focusing on China and does not name individual researchers. It presents the findings as relevant to understanding continental deformation, planning oil and geothermal extraction in desert environments, and avoiding dangerous drilling problems. It also says that revised fault maps at different scales could help connect plate tectonic theory with reservoir engineering and guide future drilling projects. The articles do not describe any further steps or timelines beyond these general aims.

stories.Headline: Opera launches local browser AI, testing enterprise privacy and AI PC strategies
stories.Summary:
Opera has begun rolling out AI models that run locally in its browser, and it introduced WebAI, a proposed web standard, as an opt-in early preview in its Opera One browser on October 27, 2026. The technology lets websites and browser extensions reach AI models running on the user's own device for tasks such as generating text and classifying content. The preview works on 64-bit Windows PCs with Intel or AMD processors and on Macs with Apple silicon, but not yet on Windows on Arm. Opera says the feature is optional, that models download only after users enable it, and that site-specific permissions control which websites can access them. Opera also says its implementation supports models including Google's Gemma and, on compatible Macs, Apple's on-device foundation model.

The company says the approach lets developers add AI features without running their own AI infrastructure or paying for every request, and it argues that users keep their data on their own device without needing an AI subscription. Opera has said Opera GX and Opera Neon will get the same capability soon, and it plans to add models optimized for different hardware over time. Local processing puts more demand on the computer, so performance depends on the device's hardware, and Opera does not specify a need for a dedicated neural processing unit. Analysts quoted by Computerworld see the change as a possible way to reduce enterprise privacy risk, although the benefit depends on how organizations control access to locally running models.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said that processing sensitive information locally could reduce the need to send data to outside AI providers. He warned, however, that it can be harder for IT departments to monitor activity on individual laptops than network traffic. Jain also said malicious websites could try to manipulate local models through hidden prompts, and that rogue browser extensions could reach sensitive information shown on screen. Tulika Sheel, senior vice president at Kadence International, said enterprises would still need controls over which websites and extensions can use local models and how those models and permissions are managed. She also said lower usage costs do not automatically mean lower total costs, since model updates and system integration still carry expenses.

Jain said smaller models could handle tasks such as summarization and rewriting on existing PCs, which could delay some hardware upgrades, while complex workloads will still need dedicated hardware or cloud services. He expects a hybrid future in which browser AI handles simpler tasks and cloud AI supports advanced ones. Opera's move comes as privacy concerns grow about the personal data users hand to AI chatbots, and Opera has made digital privacy a central selling point for years. The articles do not say when WebAI might become a broader standard or how widely enterprises will adopt it.

stories.Headline: Chinese investment in Vietnam expands into AI, other high-tech sectors, as businesses eye deeper cooperation
stories.Summary:
Chinese investment in Vietnam is expanding beyond traditional manufacturing into artificial intelligence, the digital economy and semiconductors, according to attendees at an investment forum in Beijing on Tuesday. The growing interest was highlighted at the China-Vietnam Economic, Trade and Investment Cooperation Exchange Meeting, jointly hosted by the Vietnamese Embassy in China and the China Overseas Development Association. Businesses there explored investment opportunities and possible partnerships in emerging industries. Vietnamese companies are also seeking closer cooperation with Chinese firms in advanced technologies.

Do Quang Tung, counselor at the Vietnamese Embassy in Beijing, described bilateral economic ties as marked by expanding trade, diversified investment and a clear move toward high-quality, technology-intensive sectors. He said China remains Vietnam's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching about $256.5 billion in 2025 and exceeding $253 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Chinese investors registered $2.27 billion in newly licensed capital in the first nine months of 2026. China also ranked first by number of new projects, with about 850 in the first seven months of the year. Do said this investment is shifting from traditional processing toward railway links, clean energy, the digital economy, AI and semiconductors.

The presence of Chinese investors is already visible in Vietnam's industrial parks, where manufacturers are bringing businesses that sit along their supply chains. Bui The Long, general manager of Green i-Park Corp, said his park hosts 36 Chinese investors, mainly in electronics and electrical appliances, agricultural equipment and lighting products. He said upstream and downstream suppliers have followed these companies into the park. Earlier, Chinese investors were generally smaller in scale, while South Korean and Japanese firms made up a larger share of foreign investment, but Bui said large Chinese companies are now arriving. He also said Vietnam's AI sector is still at an early stage, and he hopes Chinese companies will develop AI projects there.

He Zhenwei, president of the China Overseas Development Association, argued that the next phase of cooperation should improve quality as well as trade volume, particularly in AI and the digital economy. He suggested AI cooperation could focus on localizing large-language models and big data applications in Vietnam. He said the aim should be local application of Chinese technologies rather than simple introduction, helping Vietnam advance industrialization and modernization. Do said the forum helped both sides better understand each other's policies and needs, which he called a crucial foundation for long-term partnerships. He called for more frequent exchanges and welcomed Chinese enterprises investing in high-quality, technology-intensive and environmentally sustainable projects in Vietnam.

stories.Headline: Arctic Wolf Named a Leader in 2026 QKS SPARK Matrix for AI SOC Automation
stories.Summary:
Arctic Wolf, a cybersecurity and AI company based in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, announced on October 29, 2026 that QKS Group had named it a Leader in the Q4 2026 QKS SPARK Matrix for AI SOC Automation. QKS Group also rated the company the highest vendor overall for customer service excellence, ease of deployment and use, and proven record. The recognition centers on the Aurora Agentic SOC, which conducts more than 200,000 investigations weekly. According to the announcement, the platform lets organizations scale security operations without building agentic capabilities in-house.

QKS Group defined AI SOC Automation as a security platform or set of solutions that uses artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative AI and agentic AI to automate tasks across alert enrichment, triage, investigation, decision-making and response. The report praised Arctic Wolf's governed, agent-led approach, delivered as a turnkey managed service. Its AI Trust Engine includes asset-sensitive approval gates, adjustable confidence thresholds and tiered handling that ranges from autonomous resolution to human-led decisions. According to the company, its Swarm of Experts resolves more than 60% of investigations autonomously, and investigations can finish in as little as 12 seconds. The Aurora Agentic SOC can deploy in as little as 10 days and is described as roughly 12 times more cost-effective than building an agentic SOC internally.

Andrew Aken, associate vice president and principal advisor at QKS Group, said Arctic Wolf has built a strong position in the AI SOC market and shows a strong mix of technology innovation and operational impact. He added that continued investment in agent governance, integration speed and customer self-service would strengthen that position further. Dan Schiappa, President of Technology and Services at Arctic Wolf, said organizations need security operations that move at machine speed, produce outcomes they can trust and avoid added complexity. The company's own description frames its work as ending cyber risk by turning it into business resilience.

The announcement comes as the broader AI risk landscape is shifting quickly. A separate Aon report from May 2026 notes that 88% of organizations reported using AI in at least one business function in 2025, and it describes AI-enabled phishing and deepfake fraud as growing concerns for security teams. The same report says cyber risk remains the top enterprise threat through 2028. The articles do not say whether the Arctic Wolf recognition will change how customers buy or use these services, and they offer no independent testing of the performance claims.

The announcement appeared in TechGig on October 28, 2026, and was also covered by The New Stack on October 26, 2026. The guide is aimed at teams that run Kubernetes platforms and need to prepare them for workloads that are expected to arrive in the coming year. It was framed as a set of checks rather than a single product or standard, so its recommendations are meant to be applied across different environments. The publication positions itself as a starting point for planning.

On the technical side, the ebook recommends stress-testing model-serving systems under realistic loads and rehearsing failure scenarios. It advises teams to measure platform health beyond GPU utilization alone. For agents that access clusters, it calls for every agent to have an identifiable owner and narrow permissions, along with approval gates and audit trails that link tool calls to the tasks that prompted them. Teams are also asked to evaluate the quality of AI output, since a fast answer that is wrong offers little value. The guide additionally covers policy enforcement across multiple clusters, visibility into services that run outside Kubernetes, upgrade and restoration drills, and developer self-service with clear ownership, review dates, and cost visibility.

The ebook itself is credited to The New Stack in partnership with HPE, and the articles do not name individual authors. The material is presented as guidance meant to prompt discussion among platform, application, security, and business teams, rather than as a set of mandatory requirements. The articles do not say how many organizations have adopted these checks or whether any regulator or industry body has endorsed them. Neither source describes follow-up plans beyond the release of the ebook itself, so the next steps for the guidance remain unstated.

stories.Headline: How to make the most of AI tools without feeling overwhelmed
stories.Summary:
Small business owners are being urged to stop chasing every new AI release and instead focus on the tasks that actually slow them down. The guidance comes from a Wix-produced article, distributed by Stacker and published on October 29, 2026, which cites experts including Avery Chi of Made4Vital, Kristin Ginn of trnsfrmAItn, behavioral psychologist Bob Hutchins, and newsletter writer Jeremy Caplan. The piece argues that keeping up with weekly AI launches can become a second job of its own, and it points to a study of 15 young professionals that found generative AI can ease workloads while also adding stress from staying informed and adopting changing technology. Experts describe this as technostress and say the answer is to be selective rather than adding more tools.

The experts offer a set of practical steps. Hutchins recommends an "annoyance audit," in which a person logs every irritating task over one work week, such as copying data between systems or repeatedly searching for the same document, then looks for recurring patterns that point to real problems worth solving. Before buying anything new, owners are advised to check whether tools they already pay for can cover the need, since many AI uses such as drafting emails or reviewing invoices do not require a separate subscription. When testing a new tool, Hutchins suggests trying only one at a time, scheduling the review during a calm stretch of the week, and abandoning any tool that has been opened several times without accomplishing the intended task. He also warns against deciding to try a tool right after a sales pitch or during a stressful period.

Automation is also discussed as something that should be limited to suitable work. Ginn describes an approach in which an agent drafts an email and then waits for the owner's approval before sending it, so the person keeps control of final decisions. Hutchins advises sorting tasks by how much a customer would notice or care whether a machine handled them, keeping human contact for moments such as complaints, thank-you notes, and sensitive interactions. He notes that an AI agent can still be useful for simple questions at odd hours, provided customers can easily reach a person and know whether they are talking to a machine. The article concludes that making the most of AI means identifying where a business is stuck and what work would truly benefit from automation, rather than following every trend.

stories.Headline: As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
stories.Summary:
Experts warn that AI-made political content is spreading faster and looking more realistic as the election season moves forward. The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that social media videos believed to be made with AI and linked to Russia are using real people's names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in close races, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and James Talarico in Texas. Ari Lightman, a digital media and marketing professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said foreign adversaries are using increasingly advanced tools to push polarization and favor certain political outcomes. The use is not limited to foreign actors, since political groups in the United States are also using AI in campaign ads.

The Wesleyan Media Project has tracked 220 midterm election ads generated at least in part with AI tools, a count it called almost certainly an undercount. Most of those ads came from Republican candidates and organizations, though stakeholders in both parties used them. Spending on AI-generated ads had exceeded $137 million as of earlier this month, compared with less than $50,000 in the 2024 cycle, according to the project's co-director, Erika Franklin Fowler. She said much of the AI use goes undisclosed through any kind of disclaimer. Thirty-one states have enacted laws regulating deepfakes in political messaging, though some have been challenged in court on free speech grounds, and there are still no federal disclosure requirements.

Experts say voters cannot rely on visual clues alone, such as misshapen hands, unnaturally smooth skin, or misaligned shadows, because the technology has grown too sophisticated for most people to spot these flaws. Lightman advised voters to check the credentials and context behind potential AI content and to verify information through independent sources. He also said voters should be wary of content designed to provoke an immediate emotional response and should think twice before sharing it on social media. OpenAI confirmed on Wednesday that it is launching an Election Operations Center this week to track misinformation and address potential misuse of tools like ChatGPT, running until all votes are counted, according to Politico. A new Brennan Center report found OpenAI was the only company that significantly improved protections against generating fake election content since the center tested six popular models earlier this year.

stories.Headline: China's new export curbs draw a line around its AI crown jewels
stories.Summary:
China has proposed new rules on artificial intelligence exports that would keep its most valuable AI technology at home while still letting foreign customers use its services. The draft rules were released on October 16, 2026, and China is expected to adopt them by the end of 2026, with implementation guidelines to follow later. They would add 23 AI-related technologies to the list of items banned or restricted from export, including advanced models, autonomous agents and chip-design tools. A temporary requirement to register certain transfers has already taken effect.

Under the proposals, overseas users could broadly access Chinese AI through websites and cloud platforms, but some transfers of underlying technology or overseas deployments would need government approval. The draft sets three tests for which models would be covered: training computation above 10 to the power of 26 calculations, a size of at least 2 trillion parameters, or a place among the world's top 10 in certain performance, use or efficiency assessments. The rules also cover methods for coordinating more than 10,000 AI chips and offer simplified approvals for Chinese firms running their own computing facilities abroad. The proposals are open for public comment until November 15.

The rules were drafted by Chinese authorities, and the China commerce ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Alfredo Montufar-Helu, a managing director at consultancy Ankura in Beijing, said the leadership prefers keeping research and intellectual property onshore while selling operations and access abroad. He also said security concerns, including keeping powerful cyberattack capabilities and sensitive data in China, accompany the commercial goal of protecting technological advantages. Yang Jingru, a partner at law firm Jincheng Tongda & Neal, described the approach as a counterpart to US restrictions on China's access to advanced chips and investment. Liu Jing of Beijing Dacheng Law Offices said companies want more clarity on which models would be covered.

The approach is set against intensifying rivalry with the United States, where Nvidia's most advanced processors cannot be exported to China. Some Chinese AI developers have used overseas computing facilities to reach such chips, and researchers at major labs are seeking clarity on whether they can train or run their most advanced models on foreign-owned servers. In a worst case, developers might have to maintain separate domestic and overseas versions of the same downloadable model. The rules could also reach corporate deals, with registration requirements covering transfers that put Chinese technology under foreign ownership or control, including transactions already underway. Beijing earlier this year ordered Meta to unwind its more than $2 billion acquisition of the Chinese-founded startup Manus, which shows the risks for foreign buyers.

stories.Headline: Cash is king as investors draw new battle lines in AI spending boom
stories.Summary:
Investors on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, sharply separated companies they see as profiting from artificial intelligence from those struggling to control its costs. Microsoft and Oracle were rewarded for showing they could fund their large AI plans without repeatedly turning to investors for money. Alphabet, Google's parent, was punished for burning through cash, and slower growth in Google Search raised worries that rivals were hurting the business that pays for its AI push. By Thursday's premarket trading, Microsoft shares had risen more than 2 per cent while Alphabet had fallen nearly 11 per cent.

The split reflects a shift in what investors want to see after years of rewarding firms for spending heavily on computing capacity, often with borrowed money. Now they are asking for proof that the growth from those investments can pay for the next round of spending. Meta gave an early signal the week before, when better-than-expected revenue and an upbeat outlook were overshadowed by its cash burn. Oracle, by contrast, closed nearly 11 per cent higher on Wednesday after saying it would cap external financing and expected its cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028.

Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha, said the two companies looked like night and day, describing Microsoft's growth as disciplined while Google was burning cash and its core business fell short of expectations. She suggested investors might now ask whether AI was taking some share from Google Search. The figures behind the concern are stark: Alphabet put 121.4 per cent of its operating cash flow into capital spending in the September quarter, against 68 per cent at Microsoft, excluding finance leases. Google Search revenue grew 12 per cent in that quarter, below the 14.7 per cent analysts had expected, even though CEO Sundar Pichai said queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years. Alphabet's capital spending could reach as much as $205 billion this year and rise significantly in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.

Alphabet's cloud business offered a counterpoint, as Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, though spending overwhelmed that gain and cash burn reached $9.07 billion. Jeremy Saltzberg of Check Capital, which owns Alphabet shares, defended the spending as necessary to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly $10 billion above Wall Street's expectations, while investing $45.2 billion in computing infrastructure. Its Azure revenue rose 48 per cent, and CEO Satya Nadella said businesses were moving past experiments toward long-term AI contracts.

stories.Headline: What Argentina Needs to Fulfill its AI Ambitions
stories.Summary:
Argentina's President Javier Milei proposed at the UN General Assembly last month that the world develop artificial intelligence in Argentina, offering tax breaks, limited liability for companies operating AI agents, and a pledge not to regulate the technology preemptively. The author, Soledad Guilera, writes that the appeal is understandable because good ideas in Argentina often stall in paperwork. She notes that the European Union has had to delay parts of its own AI law because the technical standards needed to comply were not ready. Milei's ambition is admirable, she says, and the country has real strengths, including engineers who have founded global companies and a knowledge services industry that earned a record $9.6 billion in exports last year.

Guilera argues that Argentina's AI sector hinges less on deregulation than on steps that build certainty for everyone involved. She points out that Chile, Brazil and Uruguay lead the 2026 Latin American AI Index, while Argentina ranks sixth out of 20, even though all of them score the same on the index's regulation indicator. The country holds just 2.3% of the region's GPUs and 1.1% of its processing power, and it has seven certified data centers compared with Chile's 37. Federal science spending is on track to fall to about 0.16% of GDP this year, from 0.30% in 2023, and staff at the main federal science agencies fell 13% between December 2023 and August 2026.

Argentina's data protection law dates from 2000 and caps fines at 100,000 pesos, about $65. The author also describes an announced data center in Patagonia, worth up to $25 billion and based on a letter of intent between OpenAI and a local energy company, which does not appear among the projects approved under the incentive regime a year later. A new incentive law for AI and data centers passed the lower house in June and still awaits a Senate vote, and a bill allowing companies to operate through AI agents has sat in a Senate committee since June without a formal report. Guilera says consumers, from doctors to loan officers to retirees, need answers about responsibility, data use and human review before they trust these systems.

She proposes four steps: funded transmission lines and computing power tied to every incentive, joint programs to train AI talent and protect core research teams, a modernized data protection law such as the one the national authority drafted in 2023, and public-sector transparency about the algorithms the state uses. Guilera concludes that these measures would not follow the European rulebook but would give both capital and people the certainty they need to commit to Argentina. She argues that the president's idea of companies run by AI agents would be far easier to accept if everyone knows who answers for them. In her view, investors will not come on a promise alone, and Argentines will not trust a technology that no one answers for.

stories.Headline: Meta launches two new AI apps, including one aimed at kids
stories.Summary:
Meta launched two new AI-powered apps in the week covered by this report, as the company uses its own AI models to generate app code faster. One of them, Waddle World, is aimed at kids and gives users a virtual pet that can remember things they say and create content based on their interests. The other, Style Sketch, uses AI to suggest outfit combinations from clothes users already own. Meta describes Waddle World as a cozy, 16-bit pet care game with no streaks or scores to chase. The article notes that Waddle World is currently only available to users in the Philippines.

Style Sketch builds a virtual wardrobe by integrating with Instagram and pulling clothing items from images users have shared there. Users can also add items by hand, and the app then builds looks from those pieces. According to analyst Matt Navarra, Style Sketch is only available in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. The article says Waddle World collects personal data including location, contact information and user ID, according to the app's iOS page. Both launches come amid ongoing concerns about AI tools making potentially dangerous recommendations to users.

The article describes Meta as experimenting in this way because AI tools make it much easier to build and release new apps and see which ones gain traction. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on the company's July earnings call that AI is speeding up product development, pointing to recent launches including Instagram Instants, Forum and Seller. The article lists other test apps Meta has released or is working on, including Pocket, Vibes, StoryKit and a prediction markets app called Arena. It says whether Arena reaches a full launch remains to be seen.

The writer argues that most of these experimental apps are unlikely to last long, though a few may help Meta keep people engaged on its platforms. The article also points to Meta adding parental oversight to its Meta AI app as related coverage. Against that backdrop, the writer calls Waddle World's cute design somewhat disingenuous given how the company uses such tools to gather data. The article does not describe any formal regulatory response or announced changes to either app's data practices.

stories.Headline: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
stories.Summary:
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, a Ukrainian tech entrepreneur, turned to drone warfare after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. His companies, The Fourth Law and Odd Systems, are among the leading producers of AI-powered drones in Ukraine, and dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, the Lupynis-10-TFL-1. The reporting describes a broader shift in which artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable. Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine.

The Lupynis-10-TFL-1 is a small, affordable first-person-view drone paired with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. For the last 500 meters, or 0.3 miles, of a flight, an onboard computer and AI technology take control from the human operator. The system relies on relatively simple image recognition tools rather than the large AI systems used in data centers or self-driving cars. Azhnyuk says this lets a drone navigate without a person, select a target, or fly toward one on its own. The company's testers say the drone's microcomputer runs a deep-learning network trained on hours of combat footage to recognize vehicles, armored vehicles, tanks and flying objects.

Azhnyuk argues that AI gives a smaller military an asymmetric advantage, claiming it can make a drone "10,000 times more effective." He acknowledges concern about destructive weapons but says the worry is not specific to AI, comparing it to earlier tools like fire or steel that can be used for good or bad. The company's test and integration lead, who uses the call sign Stab, says safeguards are in place so the drones will not go rogue and that humans select the targets. Azhnyuk rejects comparisons to killer robots, calling the systems "just sort of calculators," though he concedes that future drones might one day make their own targeting decisions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.

Azhnyuk's main argument is that Ukraine cannot afford to refuse AI in defense when adversaries are already using it for offensive decisions. He says Russian systems can decide in microseconds while human control takes minutes, hours or sometimes days, and he warns that if Ukraine loses, there would be no room to debate the ethics of AI. The company names its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians, with the Lupynis drone honoring a poet who endured Soviet imprisonment. The articles do not describe any specific outcome beyond these claims or set out formal rules governing the use of such drones.
