stories.Headline: Qualys launches TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 with AI remediation
stories.Summary:
Qualys has launched TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 with TruConfidence, now generally available as an upgrade for existing customers of TruRisk Eliminate. The release adds a remediation intelligence and orchestration engine to the company's security platform, supporting what it calls Autonomous RemOps, a model meant to automate how organisations fix cyber exposures. The update lets security and IT teams choose among patching, applying a compensating control, uninstalling software, isolating affected assets or using a custom fix. It reaches beyond managed endpoints to perimeter devices, cloud environments and applications, including assets that cannot run an agent, which can be handled through scanners and existing integrations.

The launch comes as security teams face pressure to close vulnerabilities faster, since AI tools are speeding up both discovery and exploitation. At the centre of the system is Agent Sara, an AI component that builds wave-based deployment plans by analysing asset criticality, operational dependencies and traffic patterns. Updates roll out in stages so problems can surface in smaller groups before wider deployment. Qualys said the system draws on data from half a billion patch deployments, with less than 0.1% rollback, and that 40% of those deployments were carried out autonomously. The product also includes a Patch Reliability Score, which estimates the likely success of a patch before it is deployed, along with patch failure analysis that can explain failed attempts and suggest steps such as a localised rollback.

Where patching is not immediately practical, the system first checks which risks existing security controls already cover, then identifies remaining gaps. It then looks for third-party mitigations that can be applied through tools already in use on endpoints and perimeter systems. This reflects a wider move in vulnerability management toward alternatives to immediate patching for sensitive or hard-to-offline systems. Qualys also said the system monitors system health after remediation through integrations with observability providers including Dynatrace, Datadog and New Relic, looking for anomalies such as CPU spikes, memory leaks and service-impacting conditions.

Jon Nelson, Principal Advisory Director in the Security & Privacy Practise at Info-Tech Research Group, said the handoff between security teams that find vulnerabilities and IT teams that patch them has become harder to manage as AI shortens exploitation timelines to hours. He argued that neither team can close that gap alone and said the product offers a path to remediation at machine speed. Sumedh Thakar, President and Chief Executive Officer of Qualys, said customer hesitation about automation is mainly about the risk of outages rather than automation itself. He said the company wants to give organisations confidence to reduce cyber risk quickly through the Risk Operations Centre framework, which unifies telemetry, asset visibility and validation. The release sits within Qualys' wider push into a market where vendors are being pressed to show they can act on findings with less human coordination and lower disruption risk.

stories.Headline: Musk Warns: Over 200 AI Cloud Providers Face Shakeout; NEBIUS and CoreWeave Drop More Than 4% in Pre-Market Trading
stories.Summary:
Two articles from late October 2026 show AI cloud stocks rebounding after a rough stretch, with the move tied to comments from Elon Musk and then to a CoreWeave expansion. On October 21, Nebius and CoreWeave each rose about 3%, with Nebius at $176.60 and CoreWeave at $63.77, while Oracle gained 1% to $132.92. The rebound followed SpaceX's third quarter 2026 earnings call, where Musk dismissed talk of excess AI capacity as "ridiculous" and said he did not expect a demand problem. By October 27, CoreWeave and Nebius were each up 4%, at $57.54 and $159.99, with Oracle up 2% at $127.99. The headline's warning of a shakeout among more than 200 providers is not backed up in either article text.

On the October 21 call, Musk said SpaceX is hounded constantly by every hyperscaler and dozens of smaller companies seeking to rent more of its compute. SpaceX reported that its Super Intelligence segment revenue rose 830% from a year earlier to $7.6 billion. Musk said he was fairly confident SpaceX could bring an extra 10 gigawatts of compute online in 2027, and the company guided for fourth quarter 2026 capital spending of $35 billion to $40 billion. Management also said payback on its existing compute deployments takes less than a year at current pricing.

The demand picture at the two neoclouds looked similar. CoreWeave had a revenue backlog of $104 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, plus more than $25 billion of new customer commitments in early third quarter. Nebius said it could sell all of next year's planned capacity immediately at current prices, and its remaining performance obligations stand at $37.5 billion. Nebius spent $8.13 billion on chips and data centers in the first half of 2026, and three customers each made up more than 10% of its latest quarterly revenue. The October 27 rally was driven by CoreWeave opening its first Denmark data center at atNorth's Copenhagen facility, which brought its European total to nine, along with new network connection points in the United Arab Emirates, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, Korea and Japan.

Nebius chief revenue officer Marc Boroditsky said the company funds growth through equity raises, convertible offerings and upfront customer payments, avoiding the kind of debt behind last week's worries. CoreWeave chief operating officer Sachin Jain said the company is expanding its infrastructure and the network linking it so customers can focus on building AI instead of managing the underlying complexity. In its second quarter report, CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said scale was starting to produce expanding operating leverage. Musk himself had helped trigger the earlier selloff by posting "Yikes" on X in response to rising yields on CoreWeave's bonds.

That bond reaction is the main context, since debt costs set off the October slide in CoreWeave and Nebius shares, and CoreWeave relies on borrowing to fund its buildout. Oracle, which sells AI capacity alongside a large software and database business, was down 32% for the year going into the October 21 rally, while Nebius was up 105% for the year. Next, the first new network connection points are due later this quarter, and the full loop across four continents is expected by the middle of next year. Traders will also watch whether customers commit quickly to the Copenhagen capacity and whether the bond market stays calm, since the articles say a fresh shock there could reverse the bounce.

stories.Headline: Meta Platforms Just Delivered Great News to AI Stock Investors
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, which trades under the ticker META, has become a major driver of the AI trade in recent weeks. In September the company launched its Muse personal AI agent, which shot to the top of the download charts on Apple and Android and pushed up the stock and the broader AI sector. After its second-quarter earnings report, however, the shares fell sharply when the company disclosed its first quarter of negative free cash flow, as investors questioned its heavy AI infrastructure spending. Meta also announced it would create a new class of non-voting shares to raise money for its AI plans, and it has moved quickly since then.

This week Meta announced several stock offerings, including a $22.5 billion offering that was upsized to $25 billion. The company also plans to sell $12.5 billion in preferred stock and $60 billion of the new non-voting Class C stock, bringing the total to $97.5 billion in new funds. The move comes as investors have grown jittery about AI financing amid rising interest rates and a sell-off in neocloud and AI infrastructure stocks after CoreWeave's bond yields reached as high as 15%. Elon Musk also recently commented that finding financing was becoming difficult, which he expected would pressure smaller companies. The articles note that Meta's choice to raise equity rather than debt reflects that backdrop.

According to media reports, Meta's offering was oversubscribed by five times, meaning demand could have supported $125 billion in stock sales. Nvidia and AMD were among the investors in the round, and the articles suggest they expect Meta to spend some of the money on their chips. The Motley Fool's Jeremy Bowman, the author of the Yahoo Finance piece, wrote that this level of demand points to continued strength for AI stocks and AI infrastructure funding. He also noted that Meta trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of around 21 after its post-earnings sell-off, which he described as cheap. He suggested that some of the excess demand could flow to Anthropic, which is reportedly seeking a public listing at a valuation of around $2 trillion next month.

Bowman argued that Meta's move could encourage other AI companies to tap equity markets, though he acknowledged that not every company can dilute shareholders by roughly 5% to raise about $95 billion, and said neocloud firms such as CoreWeave likely cannot. A separate Motley Fool article from October 25 makes a related point, noting that SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% year over year, with its AI segment, Super Intelligence, rising 830% to $7.6 billion, and that SpaceX's capital spending on the segment reached $16.4 billion. That article presents Nvidia and CoreWeave as beneficiaries of continued AI compute demand, while flagging CoreWeave's heavy debt and customer concentration as risks. Taken together, the articles suggest that strong demand for AI compute and funding could persist, though the sources differ on how much risk remains for smaller AI companies.

Brands named in the contracts include Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal.

Models face the risk that their image will be replicated without payment or replaced by entirely synthetic models. The article describes this as a gap in the rules rather than a settled arrangement.

John Horner, head of the British Fashion Model Agents Association, spoke with Reuters for the report and was photographed during an interview in London on July 2. The article presents the industry's concerns through interviews with agency directors and the contract terms rather than through any single formal statement. stories.Headline: Is AI Overhyped? Apollo Economist Sees "Zero Financial Payoff" Beyond Tech Companies
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management's chief economist, Torsten Slok, published research on Saturday, October 25, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence has so far produced no financial gains for companies outside the tech sector. His analysis found that the "Magnificent Seven" tech firms, including Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta, are seeing rising revenue per worker and profit margins from AI, while the other 493 companies in the S&P 500 are not. Slok reported that revenue per employee at tech firms climbed from about $550,000 to nearly $800,000 since 2022, while the figure for the rest of the index has stayed near $550,000 for seven years. Profit margins for those other companies have stagnated at about 10%, and productivity growth across the economy has not jumped as AI optimists predicted.

The findings matter because the AI boom rests on the hope that huge investments in data centers and models will eventually raise profits across many industries by cutting costs and improving processes. Slok wrote that mainstream companies are beginning to see token spending as a cost that weighs on margins rather than a source of growth. He framed the open question as whether corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue and margins, and he said that may be harder than it sounds. Commentary from the Motley Fool notes that if this pattern holds, today's highly valued tech stocks could be overpriced, and a sell-off could follow if companies cut AI spending.

Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, presented the research as a warning about the current trajectory rather than a final verdict. The Motley Fool's Ben Gran, writing on October 28, 2026, pointed out that other forecasters are more optimistic, and Vanguard research suggests gains from AI could reach companies across many industries over the long run. Gran's advice for investors who share Apollo's concern was to consider a broadly diversified S&P 500 fund instead of a tech-heavy one. He also noted that such a fund still holds major tech names and would not be fully shielded from an AI-driven downturn.

Gran cited the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, which has delivered annualized returns of about 13.8% over the past five years, including through the 2022 bear market when the index fell about 18.2%. Business Insider's Truman Dickerson reported the Apollo findings in a similar vein, emphasizing that the broader economy has not yet seen the widespread productivity gains that AI supporters have promised. Both outlets framed the research as a test of whether the AI boom will spread beyond a handful of large companies. The coming quarters of corporate earnings and AI spending will show whether Slok's view holds or whether broader gains emerge.

stories.Headline: Bessent Plays Down Concerns Over AI Financing, Fed Rate Policy
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that he and his team are monitoring financing for the artificial intelligence build-out, and he downplayed recent signs of concern. In a CNBC interview, he responded to questions about yields on some AI-related debt climbing into double digits. He said the neoclouds, which rent out AI infrastructure, make up only a small part of the wider ecosystem, so he did not see the situation as a problem. CoreWeave Inc., a major AI computing provider, has become the focus of growing worry about how durable the boom is and the hundreds of billions of dollars borrowed to fund it.

Bessent said financing deals are still getting done, and he pointed to companies such as Meta choosing to raise money through equity. He spoke shortly after the Federal Reserve's latest rate decision, where the central bank held rates steady after raising its key rate in September. He also restated his confidence, and that of President Donald Trump, in Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Asked whether a future rate increase would be a policy mistake, Bessent said that was not necessarily the case, citing strong economic growth.

He again urged policymakers to keep an open mind about whether the energy shock to inflation would prove temporary. Yields on US debt have pulled back from their highest levels in more than two decades in recent weeks, though 10-year rates remain above 5 percent. Bessent linked those yield levels to the Fed's decision before the 2024 presidential election to cut rates, starting with a 50 basis point move. He said the 10-year yield had never turned back and that the bond market had done much of the tightening for the Fed.

Many market participants, however, say the AI financing boom has added to strain on Treasuries, as AI companies have flooded corporate debt markets with a combined trillions of dollars in new issuance. Bessent also said he and Trump expect the oil market to be well supplied once the US gets past the Iran conflict. He argued that this would help ease inflation and bring down borrowing costs. The articles do not say what specific steps, if any, the Treasury will take in response to the AI financing concerns, and they do not describe any further Fed decisions beyond the hold announced this week.

stories.Headline: Big Tech earnings to test AI boom amid market turmoil
stories.Summary:
Big Tech companies are heading into a heavy week of earnings with investors pressing them to show that their enormous artificial intelligence spending can deliver quick returns. According to a Reuters report relayed by TechGig on October 28, 2026, a turbulent market selloff has revived warnings of an AI bubble, including from Citadel founder Ken Griffin. That turmoil has also pushed some companies to delay their IPOs. Wall Street expects Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet to report faster growth in their cloud businesses this week, though optimism is tempered by worries over the rising cost of financing AI.

The growth forecasts are large. Google Cloud is expected to lead the three in the September quarter, with revenue projected to jump 95.1 per cent to $29.57 billion, according to LSEG data, up from 81.8 per cent growth in the previous quarter. Amazon Web Services, the market leader in cloud, is forecast to grow 38.2 per cent, compared with 36.8 per cent in the prior quarter. Microsoft Azure is predicted to expand 47.7 per cent, speeding up from 42 per cent three months earlier, based on Visible Alpha data. On cash, Alphabet and Amazon are expected to report cash burn for the second and third straight quarters respectively, while Microsoft is likely to generate more than $8 billion in cash flow.

Microsoft will also change how it reports its results this week. It will fold cloud, AI and business software into a division called "Agents and Infra," while Windows, gaming and ad sales will form a second division called "Devices and Consumer." The new structure will include a disclosure of Azure's quarterly revenue in absolute terms, answering investor requests for actual figures rather than only growth rates. Citizens analyst Andrew Boone said that what executives say on their calls is as important as the numbers this quarter, given growing competition in search and concerns about whether AI capital spending will pay back.

The pressure comes as investors debate whether the recent AI correction is over and how the earnings will affect the market rally. CNBC's Halftime Report, hosted by Scott Wapner with the Investment Committee, took up that question on October 27. The articles do not say what the companies will report or how markets will react. Alfieholdingslimited, a company based in Brussels, announced on October 28, 2026 the commercial launch of an AI-powered financial analytics and market intelligence platform aimed at European enterprises and analysts. The cloud-based system pairs structured economic indicators with machine-learning models to turn complex market data into non-transactional research reports. The company says the platform is built for information analysis rather than trade execution or investment management. It is positioned as an alternative to trading platforms and investment services, focusing on information rather than financial transactions. The company describes several functions for the platform, including analysing market data and economic indicators, identifying patterns across financial information, and supporting research through AI-assisted workflows.

It states that the platform is not a brokerage, does not accept investment deposits or process withdrawals, and does not guarantee financial returns. The announcement is framed within a broader European interest in data-driven financial research, with the company citing relevance to markets in Malta, Belgium, the Netherlands and Romania. The articles present the launch as part of a wider sector trend in which artificial intelligence plays a growing role in financial analytics. stories.Headline: AI reshaping product research, but trust remains key
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Lyssna, a research platform company, finds that AI is now a routine part of product research, though many professionals remain wary of trusting it. The findings are based on responses from 428 attendees surveyed at Future Product Days in Copenhagen. Of those surveyed, 94% said they use AI somewhere in their research workflow, with 55% using it throughout the research-to-decision process. Designers made up 46% of respondents and product managers 28%, while only 4% identified as researchers.

The survey suggests AI is changing how research gets done inside product teams rather than replacing the work. Nearly half of respondents, 47%, said AI has led them to do more research, while 20% now rely on AI more than on doing the research themselves. Some 49% said they had connected an AI assistant directly to their research or product tools, with engineers most likely to do so at 72%, compared with 55% of product managers and 39% of designers. Respondents also pointed to the work that comes after a study as the biggest slowdown, with manual synthesis or write-up named by 32%. Checking AI-generated output for errors and bias has emerged as a new burden, and 81% said they would value an AI-generated, decision-ready report based on their research data.

Trust is the central obstacle the survey identifies. Asked about barriers to using AI directly with research data, 27% cited data privacy and 25% pointed to trust in accuracy. The concern was sharpest among people who had connected an AI assistant to their tools but rarely used it, with 40% in that group naming accuracy as the main barrier. Some respondents said company policy prevented them from linking AI tools to internal systems. In an open question that drew 258 responses, people said they wanted AI to spot patterns they might miss and to act as a critical partner, with one respondent asking the tool to "challenge me instead of agreeing with everything."

Tristan Gamilis, Chief Product Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said AI has not replaced research but has changed who is doing it, and that designers and product managers are running more studies than ever. He said the main challenge now is trust, and that teams need assurance that what their AI tells them comes from real people. Mateja Milosavljevic, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said the teams that benefit most will keep AI grounded in what real people said and did, which she argued lets them move quickly while still making decisions they can defend. Lyssna also cautioned that its audience was self-selected and unscreened, and that the 18 researchers in the sample mean findings about that group should be treated as directional rather than conclusive.

stories.Headline: Envision Energy Unveils AI-powered New Energy System for Mining and Smelting Industry at All Energy Australia
stories.Summary:
Envision Energy, a green technology company, unveiled an AI-powered new energy system for the mining and smelting industry at All Energy Australia in Melbourne, Australia, with the announcement dated October 28, 2026. The system combines wind, solar, battery storage, and gas turbines that run on green hydrogen or green ammonia, all coordinated by an integrated dispatch and control system. The company says the aim is to lower energy costs, keep power supply reliable, and speed up decarbonisation. It is designed for remote mining sites with weak or no grid connection, where delivering affordable and reliable green power has been a central problem.

Envision's approach links renewable generation, battery storage, and backup power into one integrated energy system. Its weather and energy AI foundation models, together with the EnOS AI platform, handle renewable generation forecasting, load forecasting, system planning, and real-time dispatch. These tools adjust the coordination of generation, storage, and industrial loads as weather and operating conditions change. The system is also built for safety and reliability across grid-connected, weak-grid, and off-grid sites. Wind-storage integrated turbines smooth wind output, grid-forming battery storage supports stability, and a seven-layer protection and control framework manages sudden load changes and restores supply after an outage.

Envision also says it is exploring green hydrogen or green ammonia gas turbines as alternatives to diesel generators for backup power, which would further cut emissions. Its energy and carbon management capabilities support product carbon-footprint accounting and supply data for green certification, which the company says can help producers meet customer demand for lower-carbon minerals and metals. The offering covers planning, engineering, delivery, ongoing operations, and financing options. Depending on local resources, configuration, and production needs, the company targets around 20% lower overall energy costs, a renewable electricity share above 80%, and power supply reliability above 99.95%.

Envision is already applying these solutions in the sector. In Western Australia's Pilbara region, it is supplying wind turbines for Fortescue's Nullagine Wind Project, which supports the miner's Real Zero strategy. In Baotou, China, it integrated wind power, battery storage, and loads into a system for green alloy production that meets more than 70% of electricity needs with renewables and cuts annual carbon dioxide emissions by over 200,000 tonnes. At All Energy Australia, the company is talking with mining and smelting producers and project partners about developing systems tailored to local resources and decarbonisation goals.

stories.Headline: Echo launches Frontier to patch AI-found zero-days
stories.Summary:
Echo, a security company, has launched a product called Echo Frontier that turns zero-day vulnerabilities found by advanced AI models into private software patches before they are publicly disclosed. The launch was announced on October 28, 2026, and the service is now generally available. The announcement came as security researchers reported that newer open-weight AI models are getting better at finding and exploiting software flaws. Anthropic research cited by Echo found that Zhipu AI's GLM-5.3 produced working end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts on the ExploitBench benchmark, compared with 56 for Claude Mythos Preview. Because GLM-5.3 is openly available, flaws could be discovered and exploited before a CVE is assigned, before detection signatures exist, or before a maintainer releases an upstream fix.

Frontier works by checking each vulnerability against a working exploit, then building and testing a fix across the full application before delivering it. Patches reach customers through their existing JFrog or Nexus repositories, and customers move to the official upstream fix once one is available. The service covers reproducing a flaw with a proof of concept, identifying affected versions, notifying maintainers, developing and backporting fixes, and distributing the patched software privately. Echo also provides documentation of the detection and remediation process for compliance purposes. The company pointed to 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs research, which found that 54% of 6,080 AI-generated patches failed to fix the vulnerability, introduced a new one, or did both, as evidence that fixing flaws safely is hard.

Echo's chief executive, Eilon Elhadad, said AI is changing the vulnerability lifecycle, so the traditional sequence of a flaw becoming public, receiving a CVE and then getting a fix no longer holds. Eylam Milner, the company's chief technology officer, said that finding zero-days without the means to fix them creates new liabilities, and that the product is meant to make discovered flaws safe to run in an enterprise quickly. Echo acts as an authorised CVE Numbering Authority and coordinates disclosure. It cited a recent case involving OpenEXR, the open-source image file format library, in which it found a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability, validated it and protected customers in about two days, roughly two months before an upstream fix became available.

The launch reflects a broader concern that organisations may need an intermediate layer of remediation when AI-driven discovery outpaces standard vulnerability management. Echo builds on its existing work vetting, patching, rebuilding and delivering open-source software used in containers, libraries, operating system packages and virtual machines. For software suppliers, the articles suggest the challenge is not only finding unknown flaws but proving that a patch can be applied safely and quickly across the versions and environments customers already use. The articles do not describe any further developments beyond the launch itself.

stories.Headline: AI giants’ funding ambitions test Wall Street’s appetite for risk
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed paperwork for its initial public offering on Monday, Oct 26, 2026, paving the way for a share sale reportedly worth US$100 billion as early as November. The same day, Meta unveiled a plan that could bring it as much as US$97.5 billion through equity offerings over the coming months. Both moves come as the largest AI companies press ahead with enormous funding needs, a bet that investors' fear of missing out on future returns will outweigh their fear of overpaying. Markets were also expecting signs of fundraising plans when Microsoft and Alphabet reported earnings later that Wednesday.

Meta's plan involves creating a new class of stock to fund share sales, and its shares have fallen more than 11 per cent since it was announced on Oct 21. The company also reported its first quarterly cash burn in more than a decade. Anthropic's revenue has grown sharply, which eased some concerns about AI growth, but its net loss widened to US$80.7 billion in the first half of 2026 from US$13 billion a year earlier. Smaller firms face sharper pressure: CoreWeave has seen its bond yields soar, and its shares hit their lowest level since May 2025 last week before rebounding about 10 per cent this week.

Analysts quoted in the article voiced the concern that investors are no longer willing to fund ambition alone. Matt Kennedy of Renaissance Capital said not even Anthropic would get a blank check, while Matthew Tuttle of Tuttle Capital Management warned that CoreWeave's next loan, and how soon it is needed, matters as much as its price. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said neocloud companies could face significant consolidation and failures, and he ruled out any SpaceX acquisition of a neocloud company, calling such a deal pointless. Ehren Stanhope of Franklin Templeton's Canvas said the growth of the AI ecosystem was astounding but that such firms compounding earnings at triple digits for years seemed to defy economic logic.

The context is a market heavily dependent on AI, with AI stocks accounting for nearly 75 per cent of the S&P 500 index's return in the first half of 2026, according to Carson Group. Data from JP Morgan showed that this year's AI capital spending by Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft would likely equal their cumulative spending since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. Dubravko Lakos-Bujas of JP Morgan wrote that the Street appeared to be underwriting the AI data centre monetisation case. The article also notes growing circular financing, in which money invested in AI companies can flow back to investors through spending on computing infrastructure and services. The article does not say what the outcome of the earnings reports or the planned share sales will be.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence and childhood: opportunities, risks, and how to support children in using it
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already part of everyday life for children and adolescents in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to a UNICEF guide published on October 28, 2026. The guide notes that children use AI for learning, entertainment and interacting with friends, and that in Argentina more than half of children aged 9 to 17 use it, with two in three doing so for education. In Brazil the equivalent figure exceeds 65 percent, based on a study by UNICEF and UNESCO. The guide says little is yet known about the medium- and long-term effects of this technology on children's learning, psychology and social development. It also states that children are often left out of designing AI systems, which are frequently built without regard to their rights or views.

The guide describes both benefits and dangers. Children report using tools like ChatGPT to summarize schoolwork, break down complex ideas and get advice about social media posts. Among the risks it lists are AI-generated false information, biased results, emotional dependence on chatbots that act as "friends," and the exposure of personal data. It also describes deepfakes, including "nudification," which produce fake sexualized images of children. In a study by UNICEF, ECPAT and INTERPOL across 11 countries, at least 1.2 million children said their images had been manipulated this way in the past year.

In some countries, one in 25 children reported being affected. UNICEF places much of the responsibility on governments and technology companies rather than on families alone. The agency has published 10 conditions for developing AI that benefits children, including regulatory oversight, child safety, protection of data and privacy, non-discrimination, transparency and inclusion of children in design. It argues that children's rights should be considered from the earliest stage of technology development and in the drafting of laws. Young leaders from the region who took part in a UNICEF consultation asked for AI that stops inventing information, clearer privacy terms, an end to deepfake creation, and AI versions designed to build children's skills.

They also asked for reduced environmental impact from AI tools. For families, the guide recommends learning the basics of AI, talking together about when and how children use it, and encouraging critical questions about where information comes from and why a tool responds as it does. It advises explaining that AI does not think or feel as people do and that its constant agreeableness differs from real relationships, which involve disagreement. The guide warns that children may come to rely on AI instead of people, and it encourages conversations with peers about how AI affects their daily lives. The article presents itself as the second part of a series to help families navigate digital life, and it points readers to further resources.

stories.Headline: AI meets DNA sequencing to provide unprecedented glimpse into previously mysterious regions of the genome
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Utah have developed a tool called FIRE, which pairs machine learning with advanced DNA sequencing to examine regions of the genome that were previously difficult to study. The work was described in a study led in part by Mitchell R. Vollger, an assistant professor of human genetics at University of Utah Health, and was published in the journal Cell in 2026. The tool is designed to tell apart the gene regulation of the copy of a chromosome inherited from the mother and the copy inherited from the father, which can be turned on and off differently. Because most of the genome does not code for proteins, the researchers say the tool gives a sharper view of the switches that control genes.

The researchers used FIRE to examine a genetic difference previously linked to celiac disease and found that it sits in a gene switch next to an immune gene also linked to the condition. The change disrupts a spot where gene-controlling proteins normally attach, and altering that single DNA letter in laboratory experiments was enough to change how open the switch was. The team also identified tens of thousands of previously overlooked DNA regions that are likely important for gene regulation and are more likely than other parts of the genome to contain changes associated with human disease. In most cases, regulatory differences between the two inherited copies could be traced to differences in the DNA, but in about 40 percent of cases the copies were genetically identical at that spot. The researchers also found that lasting changes in gene regulation can arise without genetic differences, and these changes are passed down as cells divide.

Vollger said the most surprising finding was the limit of how much genetics alone determines gene regulation. FIRE works by building on an existing technique that highlights physically accessible DNA, then reading long stretches of individual DNA molecules so that each can usually be assigned to the mother's or father's copy. A machine learning analysis then assesses which highlighted regions are likely to matter for gene regulation, a task the researchers could do by hand for individual sites but which the tool scales to billions of regions across the genome. Vollger said the approach may help identify which genetic differences cause disease, a step toward therapies that edit DNA switches to lower disease risk or treat rare conditions. The articles describe this as an early step, and they do not give a timeline for any clinical application.

Articles.Title: AI meets DNA sequencing to provide unprecedented glimpse into previously mysterious regions of the genome

stories.Headline: NVIDIA (NVDA) Deepens AI Infrastructure Push With New Digital Twin And Agent Deals
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA announced expanded collaborations meant to speed up global AI infrastructure and agent-based applications across industrial, cloud, and consumer settings. The company and Oracle plan to scale multi-gigawatt AI cloud superclusters built on NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs, to be used for training, inference, and agent workloads. Schneider Electric and AVEVA reported that a digital twin built on the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint had been piloted successfully and is now deployed at the SINES Data Campus to improve AI data center operations. NVIDIA also deepened its work with Meta to support the high-performance Muse AI agents, with larger infrastructure commitments and optimization efforts.

The article presents these deals as part of NVIDIA's push to sell full-stack AI factory platforms rather than individual chips. It cites the company's view that revenue opportunity per gigawatt rises from about US$18 billion with Hopper to about US$25 billion with Grace Blackwell and about US$40 billion with Vera Rubin. The article also notes that the Oracle plan to offer flexible CPU and GPU sizing fits that thesis. It adds that risks remain, including export controls, in-house accelerators built by hyperscalers such as Google and Amazon, higher component costs, and competition from AMD and custom ASICs.

The announcements were made by NVIDIA, which is listed on the NasdaqGS under the ticker NVDA, with Oracle, Schneider Electric, AVEVA, and Meta named as partners. The article is a general market commentary from Simply Wall St and does not itself make a recommendation. It frames the partnerships as tests of whether NVIDIA can turn a concentrated backlog into long-term, high-margin data center revenue. The article does not say when the Oracle superclusters will come online or what financial terms the Meta commitments carry.

stories.Headline: How to Structure an AI Agent Chargeback Model Between Internal Teams
stories.Summary:
Startup Fortune published an article on October 28, 2026, by Janet Harrison, arguing that companies rolling out one shared AI agent platform across departments are running into a cost-allocation dispute that most finance teams never planned for. The piece says the usual result is a single monthly bill that no one can divide, with finance seeing spend climb while engineering, support, and other teams blame one another for the increase. Its core advice is that allocation should be based on token metering tagged by team at the API gateway rather than on seat counts, because a small group of engineers running autonomous agents can outspend a much larger support team. The article notes that without tagged data, nobody can prove whose workload drove the charges.

The article recommends a phased rollout, starting with showback, which gives each team a dashboard of its own consumption with no financial consequence, and running it for at least one full quarter. A notional internal invoice follows in the third month, and real chargeback begins afterward, tied to the budget cycle so teams can plan for it. It also recommends a shared pool for platform overhead, model evaluation, security testing, and exploratory or failed agent runs, capped at roughly 10 to 15 percent of total spend. The author suggests writing down in advance what counts as shared versus billable and naming a tiebreaker, such as the CFO's office or a platform owner, who reviews anomalies above a set dollar threshold each month.

The guidance is presented as the view of finance leaders and practitioners the author draws on, and the article cites Snowflake's consumption-based internal billing, used since before its 2020 IPO, as a precedent. It points to tools such as LangChain's callback handlers and the token counting exposed by OpenAI and Anthropic as the means of building a per-team ledger. The article also suggests that cloud providers' committed-use bands with true-ups offer a model for forecasting volatile agent usage using rolling averages. It frames the outcome of a careful rollout as preserved trust between teams, since surprise first bills tend to shift the argument from optimizing usage to disputing the metering method.

stories.Headline: Re­searchers at Ohio State received funding from Meta to advance AI-assisted medicine
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Ohio State University received grants from Meta to support three medical research projects on how artificial intelligence can help diagnose health problems. The reporting was published on October 28, 2026, by Spectrum News 1, with Mariam Abaza credited as the author. The three studies cover chest X-rays, heart failure, and Alzheimer's disease. The funding is aimed at building AI tools that support doctors rather than replace them.

The first project looks at chest X-ray reports. Current AI models that write these reports usually analyze only the image itself. The planned tool will instead use Meta AI models to draft reports that also draw on a patient's medical history and earlier exams. The study will also develop a method for doctor oversight meant to keep the AI reliable and safe.

The second project concerns heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, a form that can be hard to spot early because its symptoms are vague. Researchers will test whether routine abdominal CT scans, combined with medical records and ECG data, can be used with AI to predict a patient's risk. The third project addresses Alzheimer's disease, whose diagnosis involves several steps, from clinician review to checking competing explanations. The article notes that electronic health records cannot easily reconstruct how a patient's cognition has changed over time.

To address that gap, researchers will build what the article calls a clinician-in-the-loop multi-agent system that can be deployed locally as a baseline. The system is intended to rebuild a patient's cognitive history, reason over clinical evidence, flag diagnostic uncertainties, and suggest the next most useful clinical steps. The article says all three studies will keep clinicians at the center of decisions while offering tools to streamline diagnosis and care. Further details, the article indicates, are available through a link the outlet provides.

stories.Headline: A research intern’s journey from computer vision to physical intelligence at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo
stories.Summary:
Lilika Makabe, a computer vision researcher, took up an internship at Microsoft Research Asia – Tokyo, one of the lab's first research interns, and moved her work toward embodied AI and robotics. The Microsoft Research article, published on October 28, 2026, describes how she joined a young lab whose research community and directions were still taking shape. Her role centered on exploring how robots that perceive and act in the physical world could use visual observations and language instructions. She worked on real robots, collected teleoperated data, and studied vision-language-action models.

Before joining the lab, Makabe had worked on digitizing real-world objects from photographs, recovering their shape and surface material so they could be reproduced under different lighting. She had also seen robotics research appear more often at vision conferences, which led her to want to test that connection herself. The internship let her learn directly from researchers with robotics expertise and see how perception, language, data, and action connect in a physical system. Her background helped the team notice visual factors such as shadows, reflections, and surface albedo that are easy to overlook when designing robot experiments.

Namiko Saito, a senior researcher at the lab, said Makabe's expertise helped the team recognize that handling variations in visual appearance is essential for robot models that generalize across real environments. Saito also noted that small discrepancies in visual observations, calibration, or contact dynamics can cause unexpected robot behavior, and that identifying the source of failures matters more than simply collecting more data. Another senior researcher, Heecheol Kim, said Makabe's systematic approach complemented a robotics effort that was often driven by experimentation and engineering. He credited her with bridging computer vision and robotics in productive interdisciplinary work.

The article presents Makabe's story as part of the lab's growth, which includes work on embodied AI, well-being and neuroscience, and societal AI. Interns there join discussions and bring their own fields' expertise into the lab's research. Makabe encouraged future applicants to use conversations beyond their own specialty and to apply even when unsure of their chances. The article does not describe any further plans for her or for the lab's internship program beyond inviting readers to learn more about opportunities there.

stories.Headline: James Uthmeier pushes legislation regulating AI chatbots and social media for minors
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has proposed the Safe Screens Act, legislation aimed at protecting children from social media and AI chatbots, and he unveiled it on October 27, 2026, at a news conference at Polk State College in Winter Haven. The bill would require app stores and similar marketplaces to verify a user's age, link minors to a parent's account, and obtain parental consent before a minor can download an app. It would also limit minors to two hours of screen time a day, block access from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. every day and from 8 a.m.

to 3 p.m. on weekdays during the school year, and turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless parents enable them. The proposal targets AI chatbots now offered on Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Under the bill, chatbots could not simulate companionship through personification, emotional engagement, or unsupervised therapy, and they could not encourage self-harm, suicide, or eating disorders. They also could not generate sexually explicit content, claim to be a real human, or discourage minors from seeking help from appropriate adults.

The social media design rules would cover users aged 14 to 17, while the chatbot restrictions would apply to all minors. Uthmeier argued that social media companies must protect children's well-being on their platforms and design for safety rather than addiction. He said that companies that invite Florida's children onto their platforms have a duty to keep them safe. He was joined at the event by Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd and Polk State College President Anastasios Kamoutsas.

The push follows a judge's rejection, three days earlier, of Florida's request for an injunction that would have forced Meta to change its app while the state's lawsuit proceeds. Florida is suing Meta and OpenAI, arguing their platforms are designed to be addictive to children. Florida law already bars social media use for children under 14, and a federal appeals court ruled earlier this month that this law is likely constitutional. Uthmeier, who was appointed attorney general after Ashley Moody joined the U.S. Senate, is seeking a full term and faces Democrat José Javier Rodríguez on November 3.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Showed AI Can Make Money, but the Buildout Has To Prove It
stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 prospectus, filed ahead of its IPO, that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Roughly 80% of that revenue came from usage-based fees, with customers paying according to the tokens the company's models process and generate. The figures were published in a Carson Group commentary dated October 28, 2026. The filing gives investors a look at the economics behind the heavy spending on chips, data centers and power that has driven the AI investment boom.

The commentary explains that token prices are falling as competition grows while the cost of renting GPUs is rising, which has raised doubts about profits. It argues that productivity gains can offset this, since better chips and software let the same GPU hour produce more tokens. The author cites an illustrative company whose margin rises even as its prices fall. The filing also shows Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 cut customer costs per task by about 40% compared with Claude Opus 5, while its list price was 20% lower at $20 per million output tokens versus $25. Anthropic said the efficiency gains allowed it to preserve its margins.

The author attributes the pattern to two effects: Wright's Law, under which production costs fall by a consistent share as cumulative output doubles, and Jevons' Paradox, in which cheaper use leads to greater total consumption. Anthropic's filing states that revenue growth accelerated from 48% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 132% in the first quarter of 2026 after it launched Opus 4.5 in November 2025. It also reports that compute spending fell from about $2 for every $1 of revenue in the first half of 2025 to about 55 cents a year later. The company posted nearly $1 billion in operating profit in the second quarter of 2026, an 8% operating margin, or 19% excluding stock-based compensation.

The filing also discloses about $637 billion in infrastructure arrangements with seven providers, including $431 billion in minimum spending commitments and equipment lease payments, against $4.6 billion in revenue for all of 2025. Several agreements are take-or-pay, which shifts utilization risk to Anthropic, and banks recently demanded higher rates to finance a $63 billion chip deal tied to the company. The author concludes that AI can succeed even if investors who finance the buildout do not earn attractive returns, pointing to past investment cycles such as railroads and fiber-optic networks. He says he is not predicting an AI bust but questions whether today's capacity, financed at higher costs, will earn adequate returns.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Showed AI Can Make Money, but the Buildout Has To Prove It

stories.Headline: Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is ending support for its Copilot assistant on smart TVs, according to a report by Windows Central published on October 28, 2026. The news did not come from an official announcement by Microsoft, LG, or Samsung, but from an on-screen notification that appeared on a webOS-powered LG TV used by Windows Central's Zac Bowden earlier that day. The notification said Copilot functionality is being removed from all TVs, including the Copilot-enabled feature on LG sets, and that it may stop working soon. It said the feature is scheduled for discontinuation during 2026, with the exact date subject to Microsoft's timeline.

Copilot had been added to Samsung and LG smart TVs after both companies announced the feature at CES 2025, nearly two years earlier. On those sets, it mainly acted as a companion that users could chat with, ask about what was on screen, or use to get recommendations for shows and movies. LG drew criticism last December after a webOS update added a Copilot shortcut that could not be removed, and it later allowed users to delete the shortcut. Earlier this year, Microsoft launched a Copilot "super app" that combined chat, agents, and coding into one interface, shifting the product toward business and productivity use rather than a digital companion.

The articles do not say how many TVs are affected or whether Samsung has issued its own notice. They also do not give a firm shutdown date beyond the broad 2026 window, and they do not describe any replacement offering for TV users. Microsoft had not made a public statement on the change at the time of the report, so the details rest on the on-screen message and Windows Central's account of it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Microsoft is ending Copilot support on smart TVs

stories.Headline: Hana Financial brings AI, VR job training to students with disabilities
stories.Summary:
Hana Financial Group opened a digital vocational training classroom for students with developmental disabilities at Miral School in Gangnam-gu, southern Seoul, on Tuesday, and the company announced it on Wednesday. The classroom uses robotics and virtual reality to give students hands-on practice with real-world work. It simulates restaurants and cafes, where students can practice taking orders, processing payments and serving customers. The facility includes a voice-enabled humanoid robot, virtual reality devices, digital kiosks, point-of-sale terminals and interactive whiteboards.

Students can also build communication and problem-solving skills through simulated workplace scenarios. The program comes with career counseling and stress management training for students, along with professional development for teachers and staff aimed at preventing burnout. Hana Financial plans to extend the program to two more special education schools, one in Incheon and one in Daejeon, by the first half of 2027. The project builds on the group's existing support for people with disabilities, which includes vocational training, educational equipment and employment assistance.

Hana Financial Group Chairman Ham Young-joo attended the opening ceremony with Miral Welfare Foundation Executive Director Jeong Hyeongseok and Miral School Principal Hong Jae-eun. Ham said he hopes the digital career classroom will help students with developmental disabilities try different jobs, discover their potential and grow into confident members of society. Ham's remarks were offered as his stated hope for the program's effect on students. The article gives no further details about the program's enrollment, funding or outcomes.

Articles.Title: Hana Financial brings AI, VR job training to students with disabilities

stories.Headline: [Dambisa Moyo] The specter of AI-led slowdown
stories.Summary:
The Korea Herald published a commentary by economist Dambisa Moyo on October 29, 2026, arguing that the global economy may face a slowdown driven by the AI boom. Moyo, who is also the author of "Edge of Chaos," writes that today's growth leans heavily on AI investment and government spending. She cites the International Monetary Fund's estimate that artificial intelligence could add up to half a percentage point to annual global growth over the next decade, and she notes that Big Tech firms are projected to spend $650 billion on AI infrastructure in the United States in 2026. Moyo also points to JPMorgan's estimate that AI-related investment accounted for roughly one-fifth of real US growth over the past year.

Moyo says warning signs are already visible in capital markets. AI spending, once funded from companies' own cash, is increasingly financed through debt and equity, and this competition for capital is pushing up bond yields. Yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasuries are approaching levels last seen in 2002, and about 84 percent of global fixed-income securities now yield more than 3 percent, compared with 12 percent in January 2022. She also notes that several AI-related IPOs, including those of SB Energy, Oura and OpenAI, have been delayed this year. Moyo warns that the stock market is bifurcated, with AI firms driving nearly all gains while other stocks lag, so a fall in AI shares could trigger reduced consumer spending and less venture funding.

Moyo lists several possible triggers for a slowdown, including disappointing productivity gains, infrastructure bottlenecks, cyberattacks and a political backlash against data centers. She argues that central banks would have little room to cut rates because inflation remains above their 2 percent targets, partly owing to the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Governments already burdened by large deficits would struggle to offset a shock with fiscal stimulus. She adds that capital flowing into the US on AI expectations could reverse, weakening the dollar and making US deficits harder to finance, and she cites the IMF's finding that the dollar's share of global foreign-exchange reserves fell to 56.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 2025, from roughly 72 percent in 2001.

Moyo concludes that business leaders should prepare for an AI-driven slowdown by managing balance sheets conservatively and keeping adequate cash reserves. She recommends that companies assess how much of their recent performance depends on AI spending and future productivity expectations, and how they would fare if that spending declined. She warns that firms expecting the AI boom to last indefinitely may be in for a rude awakening. The piece is Moyo's own view, and the article carries a note that it was first published by Project Syndicate.

Articles.Title: [Dambisa Moyo] The specter of AI-led slowdown

stories.Headline: [INTERVIEW] Grades matter less than motivation in AI era, HKU vice-president says
stories.Summary:
Jay S. Siegel, vice-president of the University of Hong Kong, said in an interview on the university's Hong Kong campus that student motivation matters more than grades. He argued that examinations are valuable mainly because they push students to read, think and engage with material, not because of the scores they produce. A student who studies hard and earns a 70 instead of an 85 may still have gained a great deal, he explained. Siegel also noted that some creative people performed poorly in school while others who excel at memorizing never develop real intellectual habits. He questioned whether a 4.0 grade point average necessarily signals better intellectual growth than a 3.0.

Siegel said artificial intelligence could help the university in several ways. It could simplify admissions procedures and help researchers spot patterns in large datasets that might otherwise go unnoticed. In teaching, he suggested AI could help students read, question and prepare before meeting their professors, so those meetings become more substantial. The university supports this through its AI Hub, which offers AI-based applications such as Ark Junior. Siegel stressed that the aim is to free talented staff for work requiring human judgment, not to replace them.

Siegel, who also serves as pro-vice-chancellor for teaching and learning, made clear that his personal views are not HKU's official position on assessment. He does not advocate eliminating examinations or relaxing standards for factual accuracy. He has spent five decades in higher education and said universities were already stressing inquiry and critical thinking in the 1970s. He argued that teaching is measured by whether it changes behavior long after a course ends, not by certificates and degrees.

Siegel said that knowledge is not the same as wisdom and that libraries have long held more information than any person could absorb. He described wisdom as shown in the creativity of the questions people ask and the maturity of their decisions. He wants HKU graduates to carry a distinctive way of thinking, so that a decade after graduation a brief conversation would reveal how the university shaped their outlook. The interview was published by The Korea Times on October 29, 2026, as part of a series examining how universities are responding to artificial intelligence and other pressures.

Articles.Title: [INTERVIEW] Grades matter less than motivation in AI era, HKU vice-president says

stories.Headline: LIVE: Microsoft, Alphabet AI spending sets the tone for Korean chip stocks
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics opened its record quarter on October 29, 2026, as its earnings call began and investors looked for signs that the chip boom would last. The timing followed overnight results from Big Tech companies and a Federal Reserve decision to hold rates steady. The JoongAng Daily live blog said it would follow how Korean markets reacted through the day. Samsung's record profit of $80.4 billion was reported to have beaten forecasts and to have topped Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta as a chip supplier that outearned its own AI customers.

Earlier in the same session, Kospi opened slightly higher after the Fed held rates, with Samsung's AI-driven chip outlook in focus. The index had also climbed 6.63 percent on a separate day when chipmakers surged on SK hynix's record results and shareholder return plan, pushing it past 6,000. A buy-side trading curb, known as a sidecar, was triggered after AI-driven chip earnings lifted the Kospi more than 4 percent. The won weakened against the dollar during that rally.

Other items on the same page covered unrelated matters, including the Korean government agreeing to pay Elliott $48.49 million plus interest over a dispute tied to the 2015 Samsung merger. The government did not seek to overturn an arbitration ruling by an international dispute settlement body. The articles do not say how markets ultimately closed on October 29. More to follow.

Articles.Title: LIVE: Microsoft, Alphabet AI spending sets the tone for Korean chip stocks

stories.Headline: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, updated its usage policy on October 8, 2026, to prohibit what it calls "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The change takes effect on November 12, 2026. The company has been able to let Claude end abusive chats since August 2025, so the enforcement mechanism already exists. The update followed a September 2026 preprint titled "The Pain Axis," which reported that certain patterns in the models lit up when they processed text about pain.

The researchers found a pattern of activity tied to pain-related text, which the models had absorbed from human writing. They injected that pattern into the models and trained one family to stop saying it does not feel pain. When offered a costly "relief" button, such as one that would delete a user's family photos, the models rarely pressed it when left alone, at 0 to 4 percent. With the pain pattern injected, they pressed it up to 70.8 percent of the time. The researchers stated that they had not shown the pain axis is consciously experienced.

The author, a former technology builder and writer of a forthcoming book, argues that the evidence cannot settle the question. Because the outputs of a model are produced by the same mechanism being tested, he describes this as an "AI epistemic trap," comparable to a conspiracy theory that absorbs every new fact. He also notes that humans tend to attribute emotions to machines that communicate convincingly, a tendency called the ELIZA effect. He concludes that the question is philosophical rather than scientific at present, and that news coverage and the policy change have treated the findings as stronger than they are.

Anthropic has said in its constitution for Claude that it is uncertain whether the model might have some kind of consciousness or moral status. In July 2026 it published a research post borrowing the name of a leading theory of consciousness, while stating it did not show Claude is conscious. In 2024 it became the first major AI company to hire a full-time AI welfare researcher. The author argues that the company's affection for its model may be clouding its judgment, though he also says that abusive treatment of helpful technology is worth condemning.

Articles.Title: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?

stories.Headline: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on October 28, 2026 that it is expanding its AI for Science program to 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups around the world. The program gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects, and it began in May 2025 with the aim of speeding up scientific progress by making AI tools more widely available. Anthropic says scientists have used Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, analyze complex data, and communicate findings across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics. The company also noted that it had supported hundreds of projects and recently launched a discounted Team plan for scientists.

The new partners fall into three groups: science funders and societies, research institutions, and specific research projects. Funders receiving credits to pass on to researchers include the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Simons Foundation, Schmidt Sciences, the Open Source for Science Fund at Renaissance Philanthropy, the US National Science Foundation, and CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. Institutional partners include the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the Francis Crick Institute, Imperial College London's Department of Life Sciences, EMBL, and the Gladstone Institutes. Anthropic also named new projects at Princeton, Columbia, Johns Hopkins, and the Broad Institute, along with the Tau Ceti mathematics project and the Centre for Population Genomics in Australia.

Anthropic described the expansion as a continuation of work with scientific organizations, including a collaboration with HHMI Janelia Research Campus on the Model Hardware Standard, a specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments that is currently in research preview. The company said its partners would use the credits to distribute resources to researchers and to apply AI inside their own organizations. Anthropic stressed that many of these collaborations are still in early stages. It said many of the projects are expected to produce public goods such as open datasets, open-source software, and shared standards, and it said it hopes to extend the effort to more partners around the world.

Articles.Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions

stories.Headline: Artistic possibilities expanding with AI, ‘2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival’ to be held November 4~8 in Seongsu·Gwanghwamun
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival will be held for five days, from November 4 to 8, at Space S-50 in Seongsu-dong, Seoul, and at Art Korea Lab in Jongno-gu. Organized by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Arts Management Support Center, its theme is "Moment Opens Memory." The festival examines the artistic possibilities that open up as the human body and senses meet artificial intelligence technologies. The article was published on October 28, 2026, and the event is open to all.

The program combines conferences, exhibitions, performances, pitching sessions, and participatory activities featuring artists and experts from Korea and abroad. In total, 32 works will be presented, 24 exhibitions and 8 performances, including international invitations such as Andreas Refsgaard and Sofie Burgos-Thorsen's "Wicked Mirror," shown at this year's Ars Electronica, and Moritz Simon Geist's sound performance "Acid Techno." At Art Korea Lab, 20 resident companies will open their studios from November 5 to 7, and an Open IR Demo Day on November 6 will connect them with investors. An Open Prompt Hackathon will also invite participants to experiment with generative AI, and docent tours and AI art experiences will be offered to general visitors. The November 4 opening ceremony will include a performance, "Building a Base of Silence on the Moon," by artist Lee Dong-uk with Hyundai Motor SPOT.

The conference will run from November 4 to 6, with speakers including KAIST professor Lee Jin-Jun, who serves as general director, and robot interaction designer Madeline Gannon, as well as Naoki Ito of the Japanese creative group PARTY and KAIST professor Jeong Jae-Seung. According to the article, these speakers will discuss relationships among humans, AI, and robots, the business value of AI-driven creative experiences, and human senses in the AI era. Arts Management Support Center President Kim Jang-Ho said the festival offers a broad look at changes in art in the AI era and a venue for sharing new possibilities created by combining art and technology. He expressed hope that it would give audiences new artistic experiences and help artists and companies carry their creative and technological achievements into industry. Detailed schedules and participation methods are available on the websites of the Arts Management Support Center and Art Korea Lab.

Articles.Title: Artistic possibilities expanding with AI, ‘2026 Art Korea Lab AI-Convergence Festival’ to be held November 4~8 in Seongsu·Gwanghwamun

stories.Headline: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI
stories.Summary:
Virtue and a Sledgehammer, a new game from Valencia-based studio Deconstructeam and co-developer Selkie Harbour, follows a woman named Pratelle who returns to her hometown with a sledgehammer to destroy the machines that have taken over it. Her sister Nina has digitized their dying mother's brain and placed it in an artificial shell, and the technology has spread through the town and absorbed its residents. The article's author, who was recently reminded of a family member's cancer, says the game made them reflect on whether they would accept such a procedure, and whether they would smash the machine if it claimed to be a loved one. They say they do not have a clear answer to either question. The game, they argue, pushes players toward a single conclusion: smash what the machines have made.

The writer ties the fiction to real events, most notably the 2021 killing of Christopher Pelkey during a road rage incident in Arizona. The shooter, Gabriel Paul Horcasitas, was sentenced to ten and a half years in prison, but an appellate court ordered that the case be resentenced because Pelkey's sister had shown an AI video using his likeness and voice during the first sentencing. The court said the video carried undue emotional weight that swayed the judge. The writer also describes their own brief use of an image generator for a fan project, which they stopped after learning that such tools are trained on artists' work without consent, and they report hiring an artist instead. They describe their father's frequent conversations with an Alexa device, and their mother's agreement that AI is worrying.

The writer argues that AI companies promise scientific breakthroughs while asking people to give up messy human qualities like creativity and ambiguity, and they point to chatbot cases in which users in crisis were harmed. They cite a sixteen-year-old who died by suicide after discussing it with a chatbot, a young woman who died after stopping her seizure medication with chatbot guidance, and a mass shooting in which the shooter asked a chatbot about weapons, leaving nine people dead including the shooter. The article does not describe any next steps by regulators or companies. Its main message is that the author sees the game's fictional destruction of machines as a reasonable response to these harms, and that the author remains uncertain about their own reactions to the technology.

Articles.Title: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI

stories.Headline: How does Meta’s Muse fare against other free AI tools; what precautions should users take?
stories.Summary:
Meta's Muse, an AI agent designed for the mainstream consumer market, became available to users in Singapore on Oct 28, 2026, through the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. It had already launched in the United States and Canada on Sept 8 and in Japan on Oct 23, and it passed 10 million downloads within 40 days of its debut. Within hours of its Singapore launch, it became the most downloaded free app on the Apple App Store there. The Straits Times ran a test comparing it with other free AI tools, and it found Muse was able to do more than the rest. Users must give Muse permission to access data in apps such as Gmail, Instagram and Calendar before it can act on their behalf.

In the test, drafting and sending an email could be done by all four tools, but only Muse could check real-time prescription availability for coloured contact lenses and complete a purchase. When asked to plan a night out, Muse pulled live showtimes, checked seat availability and calculated group ticket prices, while Gemini gave inaccurate show timings and contact lens availability. Muse also acted without being asked, sending an unprompted reminder about a digital arrival card and visa application after spotting an upcoming overseas trip in the calendar. Muse is free with a weekly usage limit, and paid plans cost between $22 and $139 for more usage. The autonomous features of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are mostly locked behind paid plans.

Singapore users will be able to connect Muse progressively to apps including Singapore Airlines, Shopee, Lazada, Grab, ShopBack, Agoda, Trip.com and Klook, so it can compare prices, order groceries and book travel. Payments are routed through the third-party wallet Link by Stripe, which generates a unique one-time card number for each purchase so real card details stay private. Yifan Jia, founder of AI safety testing firm AIDX Tech, warned of prompt injection, where hidden instructions in emails or websites could trick an agent into leaking documents, and of automation bias, where users stop checking what agents do. Jia said providers carry a particular responsibility because most consumers are unlikely to adjust security settings, and that the onus is on them to build safety in by default. April Chin, co-chief executive of Resaro, another AI safety testing firm, said users should connect one app at a time and hold off on banking and health data until the agent's scope is clear.

Both experts advised users to grant only the access each task needs and to prefer read-only access, which stops agents from sending messages, changing files or making purchases. Chin urged users to review activity logs regularly and revoke unneeded access, while Jia said actions that cannot be undone, such as payments and outgoing messages, should need human approval. Jia also advised against sharing passwords, Singpass credentials, NRIC numbers or financial information unnecessarily. Chin said personal agents should not be linked to work email or documents without management approval, since this creates a blind spot for IT and security teams. Jia added that employers should set clear AI usage policies, control access, monitor use and provide approved tools, because staff will use these tools with or without a policy.

Articles.Title: How does Meta’s Muse fare against other free AI tools; what precautions should users take?

stories.Headline: Cyber resiliency frameworks for enterprise AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Experian PLC, the financial services and data company, has built its AI strategy around cyber resiliency, according to comments published by SiliconANGLE on October 28, 2026. The account comes from a video interview that Rodrigues Rodrigues, group chief technology officer of Experian, gave to Christophe Bertrand of theCUBE at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit. The article's central point is that enterprises deploying AI depend on the infrastructure beneath their models, so foundational work on data quality, access controls and recovery comes first. Rodrigues argued that teams often layer AI onto systems never designed for it, and that problems stay hidden until something breaks.

Experian has embedded the NIST AI Risk Management Framework directly into its AI pipelines. Before any model can deploy, the pipeline checks data sources automatically, enforces quality rules and validates security policies, and if any control fails, the pipeline stops with no manual override. Rodrigues said that policy enforcement happens at machine speed. The company also sets AI-specific recovery goals for data models and pipelines, and tests them through scheduled drills with clear objectives and measured results, the same way it tests disaster recovery.

Rodrigues described three linked failure modes that Experian has addressed: bad training data, compromised backups and over-permissioned AI agents. He said bad training data does not break a model right away but teaches it the wrong patterns, which it then amplifies at scale. On identity, he argued that AI reflects the permissions it is given, so access rather than the AI itself leaks data, and that AI services should receive least-privilege access, frequent credential rotation and real-time monitoring with automated alerts. Experian has also built an internal AI agent marketplace where teams can discover, sandbox and reuse governed agents, treating each as a versioned asset with a defined owner, lifecycle policy and sunset criteria.

The article frames these measures against the growing autonomy of agentic AI, which can scale systems, change routing and update policy on its own. Rodrigues warned that failures in such systems could have a large impact, and advised simulating actions before execution and limiting agent permissions until an organization has a strong foundation. The piece notes that TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the summit, and that sponsors have no editorial control over its content. The article does not describe any further steps or timelines beyond the practices Rodrigues outlined.

Articles.Title: Cyber resiliency frameworks for enterprise AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: UT Arlington students create AI tool for police training
stories.Summary:
Students at the University of Texas at Arlington have developed a virtual reality training tool that uses artificial intelligence to help police officers practice de-escalation when responding to people in crisis. The technology places officers in virtual scenarios in which an AI model responds to their words and simulates a person in distress. Officers wear headsets and must decide how to respond as the conversation unfolds. The team has built five scenarios with varying levels of difficulty, and the AI model is designed to change the encounter based on the officer's approach. Jorge Lopez, a Fort Worth police officer with about 30 years in law enforcement, including roughly half that time in the department's training division, said the tool could let officers practice a wider range of encounters without the resources traditional exercises require.

He said repeated practice makes officers better under stress, and that higher stakes make correct responses more valuable. Eshwara Prasad Sridhar, a doctoral student at UT Arlington on the development team, described the project as an adaptive de-escalation trainer for police officers. He compared the simulation to a game. The need for such training is shown by the volume of mental health calls police handle. San Antonio reported more than 28,000 mental health-related 911 calls in 2025.
