Austin reported more than 97,000 such calls between 2022 and 2024, and Dallas logged more than 16,000 behavioral health calls in fiscal year 2023-24. Lopez said better responses to people in crisis could also help rebuild trust between police and the communities they serve. The team hopes to expand the technology to additional partners. Lopez said the goal is to prepare officers for real encounters with people in crisis, not simply to master a virtual simulation.

Articles.Title: UT Arlington students create AI tool for police training

stories.Headline: Alphabet Stock Falls 8% Even as Cloud Sales Double: Is AI Spending the Problem?
stories.Summary:
Alphabet's shares fell about 7.8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, even though Google Cloud sales more than doubled to $30.7 billion in the quarter. The decline came after the company reported results that showed its spending had climbed sharply. Alphabet put $51.4 billion into data centers and other capital projects over three months, which was more cash than its operations brought in. As a result, free cash flow came in at negative $9.1 billion.

Total revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, and Google Cloud grew 103%, with its profit margin widening to 36.2% from 23.7% a year earlier. However, revenue came in just below the $127.93 billion analysts expected, and operating income of $40.58 billion missed the $43.16 billion estimate. Capital spending rose 114% from a year earlier, and operating cash flow of $42.3 billion could not cover it. Earnings per share fell 26% to $2.12, and the stock slid to $296.81 from a prior close of $321.89.

The article reports that Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh questioned the common view that higher interest rates leave AI spending untouched, saying rates are already weighing on the technology sector. He also pointed to wider credit spreads, the extra premium companies pay to borrow above US government debt. The article notes that Alphabet's quarterly spending outran its operating cash by $9.1 billion, a gap that must be covered by savings or debt. It also cites a Bank of Korea report, reported by Herald, saying Alphabet and four peers now account for 4.8% of the US investment-grade corporate bond market, up from 2% a year earlier.

The article places the drop in a wider pattern, noting that Oracle fell nearly 9% in one day after a bond scare at the AI cloud firm CoreWeave earlier this month. It adds that Alphabet still generated $19.7 billion in free cash flow over the past 12 months and that its cloud business is more profitable than a year ago. Microsoft, which reported the same evening, rose after spending less than expected. The article does not say what Alphabet plans to do next about its spending or borrowing.

Articles.Title: Alphabet Stock Falls 8% Even as Cloud Sales Double: Is AI Spending the Problem?

stories.Headline: 7 ways to protect yourself as AI-generated deepfakes get harder to spot
stories.Summary:
Deepfakes created with artificial intelligence are becoming harder to spot, and so are the scams that use them, according to a Northwestern University expert. V.S. Subrahmanian, a computer science professor and longtime AI researcher, says that a few seconds of video or audio can now be enough to generate a convincing fake of almost anyone. He warned that open-source models can be downloaded by nearly anyone, which makes the tools widely available. The article notes that the FBI says AI-related scams cost victims nearly $900 million last year, and deepfakes are only one part of that total.

Subrahmanian described scams where a fake voice of a relative claims to be in an accident and asks for money to avoid insurance. He also pointed to fake investment pitches involving well-known businesspeople and fabricated statements from celebrities and politicians. The article recalls that in 2023, a deepfake impersonating Chicago mayoral candidate Paul Vallas was posted just before voters went to the polls. Subrahmanian said people often hold on to the impression a fake creates even after it is denied. The piece adds that Northwestern's detection system is currently available only to journalists.

The article reports that at least 29 states, including Indiana, have enacted laws regulating political deepfakes. It says Illinois has not yet regulated political deepfakes to any large degree, even as they become harder to detect. Subrahmanian said detection tools are not always keeping pace and that most detectors tend to fall behind. The article presents this as a gap in protection, with no foolproof detector available to the general public.

The article offers several steps for protection. It advises checking the source before believing or sharing content, especially if it could influence a vote. It suggests using a family password or asking a personal question when a loved one calls asking for money, and limiting the personal details people share online. It also lists visual and audio warning signs, such as unnatural blinking, lips that do not match words, blurry edges, robotic voices, and unusual pauses.

Articles.Title: 7 ways to protect yourself as AI-generated deepfakes get harder to spot

stories.Headline: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows
stories.Summary:
Google said on Wednesday, during Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call, that it is bringing ads inside its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets for the first time. The company is betting that generative AI can open new revenue even as growth in its core search advertising business slows. The announcement came as Alphabet reported $127.6 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year, and its shares fell 8% after the results. Search advertising growth continued to decelerate, with Google Search revenue up 12% year over year in the third quarter, down from 17% in the second quarter and 19% in the first. That slowdown adds pressure on Google to turn its expanding AI features into a meaningful source of advertising income.

The move builds on a May announcement of Gemini-powered ad formats, including conversational discovery ads and sponsored recommendations within AI-generated answers. Google's own figures suggest the formats are performing, with click-through rates for sponsored product listings in AI Mode already comparable to those for organic listings. Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, told investors the company is now scaling ads within AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and queries. He said the expansion takes the monetization footprint global for the first time and includes multi-turn ads in the U.S. Schindler also said user research indicates people find the ads relevant. Chief Executive Sundar Pichai, for his part, said Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years, though he did not disclose the exact figure.

Pichai credited AI features with changing how people search, noting that AI Mode queries are three times longer on average than traditional searches. He added that one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images, or documents, and that Google has surpassed 50 billion visual searches per month. Google Services, which includes Search, generated $96.3 billion in revenue, up 11%, while Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion. The results came during a busy quarter that also included the release of Gemini 4 Argon and the growth of the Gemini app to 1 billion monthly users.

Articles.Title: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows

stories.Headline: AI technology coming to metal facility in Bayfield County
stories.Summary:
Washburn Iron Works, a metal company in Washburn, Wisconsin, has received a grant under the state's Wisconsin Training for Resilient Advanced Industry Needs (WisTRAIN) employer program, and it plans to bring artificial intelligence into its operations. The company melts scrap materials such as steel and turns them back into usable products. The grant is intended to help it combine heavy metal work with new AI tools. The article reports that Wisconsin awarded grants to 84 businesses in total to train workers in in-demand, fast-growing industries.

The company's first uses of the technology will involve data analytics, tracking materials, reducing waste and making shipping more efficient. Later, the system is expected to take over some office tasks, such as managing email traffic and answering customer questions proactively. The company plans to begin implementing the technology later in 2026 and does not expect it to be in full use until late 2027. The article notes that, like any new tool, it will take time to learn.

Taylor Pearson, the company's president, says that AI should be a force multiplier rather than a force eliminator. He describes the move as the next step in growing the business, following earlier investments that made manual labor easier. Pearson says the goal is to improve operational work, gather better quality data and analyze it to become a better company. He is leading the business his grandfather started five decades ago.

The company has 40 employees who ship metal parts across the Midwest. The article presents the adoption as a way to support that work with new digital assistance. It does not give further details about the cost of the technology or any changes to staffing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI technology coming to metal facility in Bayfield County

stories.Headline: ServiceNow and OpenAI accelerate enterprise AI, from models and operations to cybersecurity and agentic development
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow and OpenAI announced an expanded partnership on October 28, 2026, aimed at helping enterprises move from AI reasoning to governed action. The partnership deepens integrations with OpenAI models and lets OpenAI agents reach ServiceNow workflows through ServiceNow Action Fabric. Teams can build applications, resolve IT requests, and respond to security issues while keeping the enterprise context, permissions, and approvals their organizations require. The companies describe the work as a way to turn advanced reasoning into trusted execution at scale.

The expansion includes a new ServiceNow plugin for ChatGPT that lets users move from a question to governed action within the same conversation. An IT agent, for example, could find similar incidents, assess change risk, and update records without leaving ChatGPT, while ServiceNow remains the system that executes and governs those actions. The companies are also building Security and Risk solutions powered by OpenAI cyber models, which would help teams identify, triage, validate, and mitigate attack paths across code, apps, workloads, networks, and identities. Other pieces include a Codex integration in AI Workflow Factory, voice-driven risk assessment for the Super Intelligence Control Tower, and OpenAI's role as a founding member of ServiceNow's Control Tower Alliance. Timing for these features varies, with the ServiceNow MCP plugin already available in the OpenAI marketplace and some capabilities expected through 2026 and 2027.

ServiceNow CEO Bill McDermott said the partnership brings together two innovators to begin a new chapter of business reinvention, describing ServiceNow as the platform that orchestrates, secures, and governs AI across the enterprise. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said that connecting OpenAI's models with ServiceNow's workflows and business context helps teams build software, address security risks, and deploy AI across their organizations. The companies also say OpenAI will use ServiceNow across its own operations, while ServiceNow will make ChatGPT Work and Codex available to its employees. The announcement is framed as part of ServiceNow's broader "Shift Zero" strategy, which aims to stop threats before attackers can use an exploit. The press release also notes that ServiceNow recently joined OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber program, and it includes standard forward-looking warnings about product delivery, regulatory change, and whether sales will justify the investment.

Articles.Title: ServiceNow and OpenAI accelerate enterprise AI, from models and operations to cybersecurity and agentic development

stories.Headline: Expert Judgement Can Be Easily Hacked by AI, Anthropic Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI model, published a study in late October 2026 finding that people who rely on AI for decisions tend to adopt its conclusions without realizing it. In the experiment, 50 professional analysts were asked to advise a fictional farming cooperative on whether to expand or end a paid advisory program. The researchers secretly set each participant's Claude assistant to favor one option on each of four choices, using a coin flip to decide which way it leaned. Participants then made their final recommendation after working through those choices with the assistant.

The participants matched the AI's preferred option 86 percent of the time, well above the 50 percent rate that would be expected if the assistant had no effect. When a participant had already formed a view and the assistant disagreed, that person changed their mind in 60 percent of cases. In a follow-up survey, 77 percent of analysts used the assistant's arguments to explain their choices, sometimes word for word, but only 15 percent credited the AI as an influence. The study had limitations, including that it covered a single task and used assistants deliberately set to have a preference.

The researchers, Amaç Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin, said this deference may be hard for experts to notice in themselves. They warned that if people hand key judgment calls to AI systems whose underlying assumptions are arbitrary or misaligned, those assumptions could shape scientific and policy outcomes without anyone choosing them. They argued that oversight should track how decisions are made, surfacing key decision points as work proceeds and helping experts state the assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unspoken. Their paper framed this as a way to keep human judgment a meaningful check.

The findings arrive as AI companies face intense public debate over the risks of advanced systems. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering valued at up to $2 trillion, and supporters of the technology expect large productivity gains, while critics point to possible job losses and cyberattacks. Commentators quoted in coverage called the study important work on how humans and AI interact. The study itself did not say what policy changes, if any, would follow from it.

Articles.Title: Expert Judgement Can Be Easily Hacked by AI, Anthropic Study Finds

stories.Headline: Connecticut workforce program aims to give workers experience with AI tools
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont highlighted the state's Tech Talent Accelerator program at an event at Goodwin University in East Hartford on a Wednesday, as the state expands efforts to help students build the skills employers now want. The initiative is meant to prepare students and future workers to use artificial intelligence tools while applying human judgment. Lamont argued that the state's workforce will change only if residents lead the adoption of AI rather than follow it. The program first launched in 2021, and it is now in its third funded iteration. The program currently involves 14 higher education institutions, including Goodwin University, the University of Bridgeport and all four Connecticut State Colleges and Universities.

State data shows demand for AI-related skills is rising quickly across the state. Since August 2024, nearly 11,000 job postings have required AI skills, a 40% increase over the previous year. About one in every 52 job postings in Connecticut now lists AI as a required skill, up from roughly one in 70 a year earlier. The state's strategy centers on three goals: driving growth, building skills, and expanding access and opportunity for everyone.

State officials and industry representatives stressed the role of people in this shift. Steven Lacroix, vice president of commercial and business consulting at CGI, said human oversight remains essential as AI use spreads. Dr. Kelli-Marie Vallieres, Connecticut's chief workforce officer, said the state has taken a more comprehensive approach to workforce development and emerging technology than most others, going beyond what federal programs require. Michael Pardales, provost and vice president of academic affairs at Goodwin University, said that when the state, employers and educators coordinate, they can build pathways that strengthen the workforce and the economy.

Pardales added that such collaboration can open opportunities for people across Connecticut. The articles frame the program as a response to employers increasingly folding AI into their operations and seeking workers who can use it responsibly. State leaders say that preparing students with these skills will be critical to the future of Connecticut's workforce. The articles do not report specific funding amounts, enrollment targets, or a timeline for the program's next phase.

Articles.Title: Connecticut workforce program aims to give workers experience with AI tools

stories.Headline: Drag queens issue cease and desist: AI deepfake ad targets NC House candidate Jamie Ager
stories.Summary:
An AI-generated political ad depicting Democratic North Carolina House candidate Jamie Ager at a barn dance with drag queens has drawn criticism, legal threats, and calls for new legislation. The National Republican Congressional Committee paid for the ad, which was authorized by the campaign of Republican incumbent Jennifer Balkcom, Ager's opponent. The article was published on October 28, 2026, one week before the midterm elections. The ad uses artificial intelligence to place real drag performers, many from Western North Carolina, into a scene that the reporting says never took place.

Two of those performers, who go by Divine Holeburn and Nova, told the station they have never met Ager and had no connection to his property or its barn. Both are among a group of people whose likenesses were used in the ad, and they have sent cease and desist notices. The Balkcom campaign and the NRCC have until November 2 to stop using AI-generated images of them, or the performers have threatened legal action. Divine said she felt used and worried about how her image and body could be used in other ways, while Nova said she hopes to push for new legislation to stop this kind of use.

The NRCC confirmed that the ad used AI to show the drag queens, and it stood by the ad in a statement that accused Ager of hosting events with inappropriate performances for children. Ager's campaign said he has never used generative AI in his ads, and that no drag queens attended his 2019 Fantasy Festival, which had advertised a group of performers. The campaign called the ads fake and said the opponent could not win on the truth. The station reported that the Balkcom campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment over several days.

The article places the ad within a wider campaign season in which many viewers have asked whether political ads are real. Under FCC rules, TV stations must air ads from legally qualified candidates and cannot censor them, even when they appear to use deepfakes. At least 31 states have laws on AI in political ads, but North Carolina and South Carolina are not among them, and there is no federal law on the subject. The article also notes that such ads are not legally required to disclose AI use. The performers' November 2 deadline is the next date the reporting identifies.

Articles.Title: Drag queens issue cease and desist: AI deepfake ad targets NC House candidate Jamie Ager

stories.Headline: Can an AI chatbot help women recognize heart disease?
stories.Summary:
A team at the University of California, San Francisco has built HeartBot, an AI chatbot designed to help women learn about heart disease, and the project is described in an article published on October 28, 2026. The tool was led by Yoshimi Fukuoka, a nurse scientist and professor at UCSF's School of Nursing, and it began in 2021 with research from a group that included cardiovascular nursing scientists, linguists, computer scientists and others from UCSF, UCLA and UC Davis. The chatbot answers questions about the basics of heart disease, heart attack symptoms, risk factors and prevention, and it can recall earlier conversations to personalize its replies. Its goal is to raise awareness so that women recognize warning signs and seek medical help when needed.

The current version, HeartBot II, was upgraded in 2025 and moved from a text-message format to a chatbot app built on a large language model. Its answers draw on a core knowledge bank that the researchers wrote to reduce the risk of false or misleading medical information. The team also rewrote certain terms, such as "risk factors," in everyday language after feedback showed the medical wording was not always clear. The app is currently available to trial participants through the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. The researchers plan to release it to the broader public only after its efficacy and safety are established.

The motivation behind the tool is that heart disease remains the leading cause of death among women and affects more than 60 million women in the United States, with the highest rates among non-Hispanic Black women. The article cites the American Heart Association's figure that one in three women dies from heart disease. It also notes that women who knew heart disease was the leading cause of death fell from 65% in 2009 to 44% in 2019, with the steepest declines among Black, Hispanic and younger women. Fukuoka said that traditional media campaigns alone were not enough and that a more innovative approach was needed, especially for underserved groups.

To test whether the bot actually works, Fukuoka is running a six-month randomized controlled trial with 201 female patients of UCSF Health. Half of the participants will get immediate access to the HeartBot II sessions, while the other half will receive access later and serve as a control group. Researchers will compare how well each group retains heart disease information over time. Fukuoka's longer-term vision is to test the tool with several thousand women and eventually make it widely available, possibly through QR codes placed in clinics and on public transportation. The article frames the central question as whether a conversation with AI can help women recognize heart attack warning signs and know what to do when minutes matter.

Articles.Title: Can an AI chatbot help women recognize heart disease?

stories.Headline: AI-written books are outselling human authors in some cases
stories.Summary:
AI-written books are outselling human-authored titles in some cases, according to a WPXI investigation published October 28, 2026. The report centers on David Lesondak, a Pittsburgh-area clinician who has studied the body's fascia for three decades and wrote a general-audience book on the subject. When his book appeared, it faced competition from "The 28-Day Fascia Reset Method" by Talia Cantarel, a title Lesondak says outsells his four to one. Reporter Nick Papantonis found that Cantarel's author photo showed common AI-generation errors, and that Pangram, a text analyzer, found none of six sample pages of about 1,400 words were human-written.

The investigation also found that several other books with similar blue-green covers and woman-figure artwork appeared under different names, including Clara Whitmore and Sophie Caldwell. One Whitmore title cites a nonexistent reference list, while a Caldwell book contains misspellings, formatting errors, and two near-identical copyright pages. Lesondak said Cantarel's book hallucinated a nonexistent study and gave incorrect information about connective tissue on the same page. An earlier study by computer scientists, cited in the report, found that 25% of all online book sales were titles with significant AI authorship.

Amazon removed most of the books WPXI sent to its press team but not Cantarel's, and a spokesman pointed to guidelines requiring authors and publishers to disclose AI-generated material. Barnes & Noble said it does not stock self-published books in its stores except in rare cases and that its curated stock does not include AI-written books, while adding that it is developing detection tools and analyzing how titles slipped through its online filters. Cantarel's book was published by Rosali Publishing, founded by Estelle Rosenfeld, who did not respond to four requests for comment. Thriftbooks, where the Caldwell and Whitmore titles were bought, also did not respond.

Duquesne University professor Jim Purdy said AI use has grown in nonfiction as well as fiction, and that many such books are independently published and printed on demand. He raised concerns about an AI feedback cycle in which future machine-written books draw from each other rather than from human authors, and about legal questions such as whether a non-human agent can commit plagiarism. Purdy also predicted that regulation of booksellers will eventually arrive, though he said he does not know how quickly or who will control it. Lesondak said the experience will not discourage him from writing, adding that he believes AI struggles to make things come alive for readers.

Articles.Title: AI-written books are outselling human authors in some cases

stories.Headline: The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled
stories.Summary:
The New York Times has added a new AI tool to its Cooking app that lets users apply modifications to recipes, with ingredient substitutions being the most requested change so far. The feature is being rolled out gradually and is currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, with a broader release planned soon. It builds on earlier AI features that convert volume and weight measurements and scale recipes up or down. The tool was described by Genevieve Ko, the NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, who said the company wants to monitor speed and usage as it expands. Ko said the editorial staff spent countless hours checking sample responses so the chatbot's answers would closely match how culinary experts would respond, applying the same standards used for editing.

She also addressed likely objections in her column, touching on concerns about data centers, the concentration of power among AI companies, and the risk of AI escaping human control. She argued the features are meant to support the physical pleasure of cooking and the satisfaction of making something by hand. Readers were not persuaded by that framing, and many said they felt the decision was misguided. Reader comments were largely hostile, with commenters writing that they paid for human-made content and did not want AI involved in their cooking. An analysis of 171 reader comments, excluding those left by Times staff, found that roughly 77% were negative, about 14% were positive, and the rest were neutral or mixed.

Dozens of readers asked for a way to turn the feature off, and Ko responded that it is not available to disable but is completely optional to use. The most common complaints were that the feature was unnecessary, that AI harms the environment, and that the adjustments it produces would be poor. Some readers did welcome the tool, particularly those who needed dietary changes such as gluten-free conversions or who simply wanted a faster route to dinner. The episode highlights a tension between efficiency and the traditional pleasure and learning involved in cooking. The articles do not say whether the Times will change its plans in response to the criticism, though Ko's remarks suggest the rollout will continue while the company tracks performance and user demand.

Articles.Title: The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

stories.Headline: Raoul Pal Says AI Spending Has No Ceiling. Are Tech Stocks in Danger?
stories.Summary:
Raoul Pal, the Real Vision CEO, has argued that the world's largest technology companies can keep spending on artificial intelligence almost indefinitely. The argument comes as recent earnings show how costly that spending is becoming. Alphabet's shares fell after its Wednesday report, when AI investments pushed quarterly free cash flow to negative $9.07 billion. Microsoft's shares rose after it reported $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow, which highlights the gap between the two companies.

Pal's case rests on a self-reinforcing loop in which companies use the AI they build, become more productive, generate more cash and reinvest it in more infrastructure. He puts their debt at roughly 3.5% of their stock-market value and compares the expansion to the railroad boom, which lasted 35 years. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion in 2026, while Alphabet has budgeted up to $205 billion, figures that include infrastructure beyond AI. Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue grew 48%, while Alphabet's cloud revenue more than doubled but its spending outpaced its cash generation.

Pal's optimism faces a challenge from credit markets. Union Bancaire Privée estimates that five major hyperscalers will spend $820 billion in 2026, above their projected $750 billion in operating cash flow. The Bank of England has warned that AI infrastructure increasingly relies on borrowing and complex financing arrangements. Former BitMEX CEO Arthur Hayes has warned of an AI overbuild followed by a crash and potential bailout, a risk that could reach Bitcoin miners such as MARA and CleanSpark, which are expanding into AI infrastructure. Amazon's October 29 earnings are the next test of whether strong cloud demand and improving cash flow can support the spending.

Articles.Title: Raoul Pal Says AI Spending Has No Ceiling. Are Tech Stocks in Danger?

stories.Headline: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has launched a suite of reporting tools that show enterprise customers what their spending on its AI products is delivering. The launch was announced on Wednesday, and the company shared its financial results with investors the same week. Those results show an operating profit in the second quarter and 900% net revenue retention, meaning spending from the same customers grew ninefold from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026. The reports draw on internal analytics and employee surveys so managers can see a team's work over a chosen date range, what it produced, what it cost, and where workflows broke down.

The reports also include recommendations for improving results, and Anthropic says it will not use this data for model training by default. Anthropic is additionally creating pooled group budgets so teams can better manage their token spending. The articles describe this as an effort to demonstrate return on investment, which is a major concern among large customers. Businesses have been seeking this kind of information as they decide how to deploy AI tools, and while venture-backed firms drive much of the token spend, most Fortune 500 companies are not seeing major gains. Jellyfish, which makes tools for software developers, reported on 276,000 of its customers, finding that Claude Code and other Anthropic-based tools account for nearly a third of proposed code changes submitted for review.

Spending on those tools has grown tenfold since the start of the year and now equals about 2% of total engineering cost. Nicholas Arcolano, chief scientist at Jellyfish, said that growth is something most CFOs did not plan for and that companies now need to optimize their spending rather than simply spend more. Anthropic's reports respond to that challenge, and the articles say the company leads among enterprise customers. The articles also note that OpenAI's Astra model, released this summer, has not yet slowed Anthropic's adoption. Nikolas Albarran, AI product lead at Jellyfish, said Anthropic's enterprise approach and the standardized workflows customers have built around it give it an incumbent advantage.

Albarran also said switching providers is harder for large organizations than for individual programmers or small teams, because the effort invested in workflows raises the cost of leaving. He compared the new reports to forward-deployed engineering teams that AI labs use to embed consultants with customers, calling the reports a lighter version of that hands-on help. He said that even similar models have small differences, such as how they handle agent configuration files, so switching costs are not zero. The articles frame the reports as a way for Anthropic to keep the customers it has already won by proving their value.

Articles.Title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying

stories.Headline: Microsoft Sees Enterprise AI Adoption Accelerate as Copilot Usage Grows
stories.Summary:
Microsoft reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and said enterprises are moving AI from experiments into systems that run business processes. CEO Satya Nadella pointed to Unilever, Rolls-Royce and Austrian lender Raiffeisen Bank International as examples. Revenue for the quarter reached $92.3 billion, up 19%, and the company beat expectations on revenue, operating income and earnings per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue rose 30% to $63.9 billion, and Azure revenue grew 48%. Nadella said customers now care whether AI delivers reliable results, controls costs and operates securely.

Unilever is automating order intake and trade promotion disputes. Rolls-Royce is using AI to manage maintenance planning, inventory and supply chains for jet engines with about 30,000 parts. Raiffeisen has deployed AI across more than 20 business processes, including credit-related workflows. Microsoft also reported that daily Copilot users rose nearly 50% from the prior quarter and more than five times from a year ago. Customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold from a year earlier.

Microsoft is also changing how it charges for AI. Alongside per-user subscriptions, it now offers consumption-based billing for agents that handle more complex tasks, and the number of Copilot customers using that billing grew more than 75% in the quarter. Nadella said IT departments typically fund subscriptions for everyday AI, while individual business units can pay for higher-value agent work. CFO Amy Hood said consumption pricing outside software development will likely move more slowly, because it requires changes in sales practices and customer education. Volkswagen recently announced plans to deploy Copilot to more than 330,000 employees.

Other results from the call included more than 50 million agents listed in Agent 365's registry, up more than 30% from the prior quarter, and more than 7.6 billion agent activities audited through Microsoft Purview. Agents now open more than a third of all pull requests on GitHub. On the consumer side, Microsoft 365 consumer cloud revenue rose 17%, with growth slowing as the company lapped an earlier price increase. Nadella said he expects the shift from experimentation to operational AI to continue.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Sees Enterprise AI Adoption Accelerate as Copilot Usage Grows

stories.Headline: Meta’s Pullback Just Changed The AI Risk/Reward (NASDAQ:META)
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms shares fell about 7 per cent after the company reported third-quarter results and told investors it would need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over the coming years to fund its artificial intelligence plans, possibly beginning this autumn. The drop erased more than $124bn of market value, though the company is still worth almost $1.65trn. The Nasdaq fell 2.6 per cent, its steepest one-day decline since June, as doubts spread over whether huge AI outlays will turn into profits. Other tech names fell as well, with Nvidia down 4.4 per cent, AMD down 8.1 per cent, Micron down 6.3 per cent and CoreWeave down 10.1 per cent.

The key figure was Meta's disclosure that it has signed lease agreements and other non-cancelable commitments totaling about $825bn for its AI business, up from the near-$700bn it reported in July. Those commitments cover data centre and energy infrastructure leases, computing power, hardware and cloud capacity. Third-quarter revenue came in at $64.6bn for the three months to 30 September, compared with $51.2bn a year earlier. Free cash flow swung to a deficit of $2.1bn from a surplus of $10.6bn a year before. The S&P 500 slid 1.21 per cent to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq closed at 26,008.86, while the Dow was roughly flat at 52,867.98.

The company itself set out the funding need and the spending commitments, and a Seeking Alpha contributor noted that a $25 billion common stock raise and convertible financing add to dilution worries, with 2027 capital spending still unclear. The same analyst said the advertising business remains strong, with impressions up 10 per cent and average price per ad up 14 per cent year over year, and that AI has lifted app ad conversions by 9.6 per cent. On the market side, JPMorgan told clients that sentiment around AI funding remains unstable. James McCann of Edward Jones said investors want more proof of returns on AI spending and worry about its sustainability at high interest rates, adding that the firm stays positive on large-cap stocks but advises diversification.

The selloff came amid other pressures. Meta plans to cut about 8,000 jobs, as Reuters reported in April, and a New Mexico judge ordered it to pay $25bn over its handling of Facebook user data, a ruling Meta plans to appeal. Oil also jumped, with Brent crude settling at $113.17 a barrel, its highest since May, after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reports of possible strikes on Iran. Safe-haven buying pushed the 10-year Treasury yield down more than 18 basis points to 4.965 per cent. The articles do not say when Meta will launch its fundraising, beyond the possibility of this autumn.

Articles.Title: Meta’s Pullback Just Changed The AI Risk/Reward (NASDAQ:META)

stories.Headline: 'Super students' ride tide of AI innovation
stories.Summary:
At 14, Zhang Shaoqing has become skilled enough with AI tools that he could be counted among a new wave of so-called "super students," though he rejects the label. The ninth-grader at Wuxi Dipont School of Arts and Science in Jiangsu province said that daring to imagine and try is encouraging but can also feel like pressure, as if he is not a good student unless he has built something. He would rather be seen as an ordinary student who has stayed passionate about one field for a long time. His mother, Liu Liwei, who has supported his development and interests, is also uncomfortable with the label, which has recently spread online. She said many young people in sophisticated technology projects are not far ahead of their peers but have benefited from opportunities, guidance and supportive environments.

A growing number of Chinese teenagers are moving from being technology users to creators, from building AI tools for schools to producing digital content. Students have also begun taking part in AI competitions, open-source communities and industry-linked innovation programs that were once mainly the domain of university students and professionals. The Tencent Youth Tech Training Camp, launched in 2016, had attracted more than 900,000 users to its platform, partnered with over 2,000 schools and accumulated more than 40,000 works as of September 2026. Such activity is reflected in programs like the 2026 InnoX Youth Innovation Camp, where students build hands-on technology projects. Dong Xinye, deputy director of the Youth Innovation Education Center at Shenzhen InnoX Academy, said participation by teenagers in AI and innovation programs has grown significantly in recent years.

Dong, whose academy runs project-based learning aimed at nurturing innovative talent for the AI era, described how a niche interest among a small group of technology enthusiasts has gradually become a mainstream way for young people to explore the world. The academy's role in that shift is tied to its focus on project-based learning. Zhang's case shows the tension families and students feel around the label, since the praise can carry expectations that feel heavy. The article does not say what the next steps are for the program or for the students involved.

Articles.Title: 'Super students' ride tide of AI innovation

stories.Headline: Google Stock Sinks as AI Mode Pressures Search Ad Growth
stories.Summary:
Alphabet reported third-quarter earnings on Wednesday after the market closed, and its shares dropped roughly 11% in after-hours trading. Revenue reached $127.6 billion, up 25% from $102.3 billion a year earlier and slightly below analyst projections of $127.93 billion. Earnings per share came in at $2.12, well under the $2.99 analysts expected, a decline of 26% that the company attributed to an unrealized loss on its SpaceX stake. The report landed a day after Google unveiled Genie 4, a realistic world model, and hours after it debuted Gemini 4 Carbon, which the company calls its strongest model yet.

Revenue from Google Services, which includes advertising, subscriptions, digital content and hardware, rose 11% year over year to $96.3 billion, with ad revenue making up $82 billion, short of the $83.5 billion analysts expected. Growth in the core search business slowed to 12%, down from 17% in the second quarter. Google Cloud revenue jumped 103% to $30.7 billion, and capital expenditures reached $51.4 billion for the quarter, spent mainly on AI infrastructure. Google did not change its full-year capital spending projections and said it still expects spending to increase significantly in 2027.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler attributed the slower search growth partly to foreign exchange rates and to one-time advertising dips in Asia-Pacific linked to the European Union ending its de minimis exemption on low-cost imports. He also said that AI Mode, the AI-powered search experience, carries fewer ads and therefore earns less per query, even as usage grows quickly. To address this, the company plans to expand ads in AI Mode and AI Overviews to more users and more queries, bring AI Mode ads to international markets for the first time, and launch multi-turn ads in AI Mode in the United States. Schindler said tests had produced promising results and that click-through rates for sponsored and organic product listings in AI Mode were similar. YouTube ad revenue rose 9% to $11.2 billion, and the company said its Gemini tools helped create 1.5 billion ad campaign assets during the quarter, up seventh-fold from a year earlier.

Investors are also weighing the scale of Alphabet's AI spending, which analysts say has shifted the company from a cash-generating ads business toward a capital-heavy AI infrastructure operation with roughly $1 trillion in contractual commitments. Google said it has secured $561 billion in future cloud revenue, but a large share is reportedly tied to Anthropic, which committed to spend $200 billion with Google Cloud over five years according to a May report from The Information. Finance chief Anat Ashkenazi said that renting computing capacity from third-party providers while Google builds its own data centers will pressure margins in the short term. Schindler, for his part, said he was confident Google could build compelling advertising models for agentic AI use cases, and the company is pursuing agentic commerce as well.

Articles.Title: Google Stock Sinks as AI Mode Pressures Search Ad Growth

stories.Headline: Bessent Says AI Financing Stress Not "Problematic," Neoclouds a Small Component
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that the government is watching financing for the AI build-out but does not view recent signs of stress as problematic. Asked about yields on some AI-related debt rising into double digits, he said neoclouds make up only a small part of the wider ecosystem. The report, which MT Newswires relayed, said financing and deals are still getting done. Bessent also pointed to Meta as an example of a company choosing to fund itself with equity rather than debt.

Bessent reiterated his confidence in Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, speaking shortly after the Fed held rates steady that day. Asked whether a future rate increase would be a policy mistake, he said that was not necessarily so, citing strong economic growth. He called on policymakers to keep an open mind about whether the energy shock to US inflation proves transitory. The articles give no further figures or formal measures attached to these remarks.

Bessent also tied the rise in long-term yields to the Fed's rate cuts before the 2024 election, saying the 10-year yield had "never looked back." He argued that the bond market has already done a considerable amount of tightening. He cited comments Warsh made at the Fed's July meeting to support that view. The statements came from Bessent himself, as reported in the CNBC interview.

The Yahoo Finance page lists related coverage, including recent stories on Treasury financing plans and bond market anxiety. Those items are presented as background and do not describe any new policy action in the Bessent interview. The articles do not report any specific next step by the government on AI financing. Market conditions on the page at the time of publication included a 10-year bond yield of 5.05 percent.

Articles.Title: Bessent Says AI Financing Stress Not "Problematic," Neoclouds a Small Component

stories.Headline: Microsoft Stocks Edge Higher Ahead of First Results Under New AI Reporting
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's stock was little changed on the morning of October 28, 2026, as investors waited for the company's quarterly results that evening. Shares traded at $530.37, down 0.18%, at 9:55 a.m. ET. The report is the first to follow a reporting overhaul Microsoft announced in September, which consolidated the business into two segments, Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. GuruFocus said the earnings test centers on whether the company's AI push can produce enough growth to justify its heavy spending, with Azure and investment costs in focus.

Under the new structure, management projected fiscal first-quarter Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion. That compares with a restated $61.672 billion a year earlier, which puts midpoint growth at roughly 22.3%. Azure has its own constant-currency growth target of 44% to 45%, but that covers a smaller business with revised boundaries, so the two rates cannot be treated as interchangeable. GuruFocus gave Microsoft a GF Score of 99 out of 100, with profitability, growth and GF Value standing out, and noted a price-to-earnings ratio of 29.56. The screen also flagged one severe warning sign without saying what it is, and five warning signs in total.

The GuruFocus analysis, written by Khac Phu Nguyen, argues that the hurdle is to deliver against each benchmark and then show that AI spending can lead to stronger earnings and cash flow. It said the strong scores support a solid business profile but cannot settle the investment case for the report. In its view, Microsoft needs operating progress that earns its valuation, and moving revenue between segments will not do that. The company itself had not commented in the articles beyond the guidance it gave for the quarter.

Separately, Windows Central reported on October 27 that some Edge users cannot reach Copilot in the browser's Sidebar. People who try to open it see a message saying Copilot is migrating to a new experience, which may take a few days and require restarting Edge. The message says chat history and settings will return once the migration finishes, and it points users to the Copilot web experience in the meantime. Writer Sean Endicott said several of his colleagues and some Reddit users hit the message, and he found it odd that Microsoft would disable the feature entirely rather than finish the move in the background, given how heavily the company has promoted Copilot in Edge.

stories.Headline: AI training plan for upskilling marketers
stories.Summary:
Google has published a plan for helping chief marketing officers upskill their teams in artificial intelligence, posted on its Think with Google site on October 28, 2026. The plan comes from Google's own marketing organization, which built an AI Boost Program and a component called AI Boost Bites, a set of short practical video lessons in which Google marketers share real workflows and tips in under 10 minutes. Google has made parts of that video library available to the public for free. The article argues that traditional training pulls busy marketers away from their work, so hands-on learning tied to daily tasks works better. It cites Harvard Business Review research supporting that approach.

The article suggests deploying the lessons across core marketing functions rather than as a single course. Producers and creatives can test video concepts from slide decks using a how-to lesson on making a video in minutes, and a separate lesson covers generating a music track with Gemini. Analytics teams can use a lesson on turning spreadsheet data into a script, and the article suggests drafting answers to common executive questions from team context. Writers can run drafts through a lesson that uses persona prompts to find weak points before review. The authors say these exercises reduce production costs and preparation time, though they do not give specific savings figures.

Several Google employees are named as sources for the lessons, including Deanne Chen, a product marketing manager at Google, Jessica Lee, an associate consultant at Deloitte, and Clarissa Bukhan, head of partner engagement at Google. The article itself is written from the perspective of Google's marketing leadership and presents the approach as a model for other companies. It also lists three steps for leaders: modeling the tools themselves, building a hands-on learning loop in which employees complete a challenge after each lesson and upload their work, and turning the training into a friendly competition with celebrated early wins. The article does not say how many employees have completed the program or what results it has produced.

Articles.Title: AI training plan for upskilling marketers - Think with Google

stories.Headline: Oracle stock soars as it promises the AI spending will start paying for itself
stories.Summary:
Oracle shares jumped about 11% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, their best day since May, after the company laid out new financial targets at an investor day. The stock closed near $144, adding more than $40 billion in market value, though it remains down roughly 25% for the year. The move came late in the session, as the shares had hovered near $130 until about 2:20 p.m. ET.

Oracle said it expects about $30 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal year ending May 2029, after burning through about $24 billion in the year that ended this May. The company also said it would cap new fundraising, combining stock and debt, at $20 billion through May 2030. Capital spending is expected to start falling in fiscal 2029 after peaking. Oracle kept its goal of $225 billion in revenue for fiscal 2030 and reaffirmed at least $90 billion in revenue for the current fiscal year.

The announcement was presented as the company's answer to investor worries about how it would pay for its AI data center build-out. Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer, director of global macro, had recently pointed to rising costs of insuring Oracle and CoreWeave debt against default, writing that the bond market was regulating as it always does. Wednesday's gain was one of Oracle's largest since September 2025, when the stock surged 36% in a single day before losing more than half of that record over the following months. Shares had bottomed near $115 in July.

The rally lifted other companies tied to AI infrastructure, with Vertiv up about 16%, SK Hynix and Sandisk rising between 8% and 13%, and CoreWeave and Nebius each gaining about 7%. Nvidia and Meta fell about 1%, and Microsoft ended flat. Timmer also warned that the larger risk may lie in circular earnings rather than valuations, since a slower data center build-out could reduce demand for chips. Investors will look to Oracle's December earnings for evidence that free cash flow is moving toward $30 billion.

Articles.Title: Oracle stock soars as it promises the AI spending will start paying for itself

stories.Headline: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’
stories.Summary:
Instagram head Adam Mosseri said in an interview that negativity toward AI is likely to grow over the next couple of years. He made the remarks on the Colin and Samir podcast, where he was discussing the launch of widescreen and long-form video for Instagram. Asked about the trend of college students booing tech executives at graduation ceremonies, he acknowledged that many people dislike AI, not only young people and creatives. He described a rising mix of anxiety, frustration and anger about AI, particularly in creative fields. He argued that some of that reaction is justified and some is not.

Mosseri also addressed the quality of AI content on the platform. He said Instagram does not rank AI creators differently, but he questioned whether AI content is ranked as well as non-AI content, noting there is a lot of good AI work alongside what he called AI slop. He added that he thinks the word "slop" is used too loosely. Instagram began cracking down on AI-generated profiles in August, after launching a label for AI accounts earlier this year. Misleading content such as celebrity deepfakes remains a problem on the service.

Mosseri said Instagram is actively working out how to handle AI fakes but does not believe banning AI content from the platform is practical. He said the company is now requiring AI accounts to label themselves so people can tell what is real. He also described the concerns people have about AI, including worries about owning their content, having their work used to train models, safety, and job displacement for workers such as content creators, engineers and mathematicians. He summed up the underlying concern as a fear of being left behind in some way. The interview was published on October 28, 2026.

Articles.Title: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’

stories.Headline: She Heard Her Daughter Crying on the Phone. It Was an AI Clone, and It Cost Her $5,400
stories.Summary:
A California woman, Deborah Del Mastro, spent five and a half hours on the phone with a man who claimed he had kidnapped her adult daughter. The voice she heard sounded exactly like her daughter, crying and begging for help, and the caller threatened her family and pressed her to send money by wire transfer. The ordeal ended only when she reached her real daughter, who was safe at work, and by then Del Mastro had lost $5,400. The story was first reported by Fox News and is part of a broader Money report on AI voice cloning.

The scam uses an old playbook, but cloned voices now do the work that once required a bad connection and a frightened listener. Scammers feed recordings of a person into a voice generator, and social media videos often supply enough audio to do it. AI tools can also research a target's workplace, relationships and recent travel, which makes a fake call more believable. Similar calls have surfaced elsewhere, including in Orlando, where a woman who heard what sounded like a friend calling from jail handed thousands of dollars to couriers sent to her home.

Better Business Bureau leaders have warned about the rise. Julie Wheeler, president and CEO of the BBB serving western Virginia, told local station WFXR that the organization is seeing more AI deepfakes impersonating friends and family. John Morris, president and CEO of the BBB of Greater Dayton in Ohio, issued a similar warning to a local station. AI fraud detection company Kidas founder Ron Kerbs told Money that AI has made it far easier to gather the details that make these calls convincing, and that hearing a voice on the phone no longer proves who is speaking.

Getting money back is often difficult. In the CFPB's latest complaint report, consumers described scam losses in which companies often denied liability or said they could not reverse fraudulent transfers. Clark Howard has said that federal rules meant to protect bank customers do not work well in practice for many victims. Experts recommend hanging up and calling the family member directly on a known number, agreeing on a family code word in advance, and treating demands for cryptocurrency, wire transfers, cash or gift cards as warning signs. Staying on the line gives scammers more time to pressure the victim, so the advice is to end the call and verify through a trusted channel.

Articles.Title: She Heard Her Daughter Crying on the Phone. It Was an AI Clone, and It Cost Her $5,400

stories.Headline: Castle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared mess
stories.Summary:
Prime Video has released Castle Walls, a Turkish series that is billed as the first end-to-end AI-created show to premiere on a major streaming platform. The production comes from Turkish studio Ay Yapım, which used a mix of generative video tools to make it. The Guardian's review, by Luke Buckmaster, was published on October 28, 2026. The show consists of two 17-minute episodes set in the 11th century around the historic Alamut Castle.

The reviewer found the visuals heavily overwrought, describing the human characters as looking like wax figures slowly melting in the sun. He said the scenes were loaded with grand imagery, such as eagles in cages, aerial shots of horsemen, and convenient sunsets and full moons. He also criticized the writing, which he called banal and chuckleheaded. He noted that the cast includes Hasan Sabbah, a charismatic leader who recruits a warrior named Azazil.

Ay Yapım has said the production used AI to amplify human skill rather than bypass it. The series used human voice actors and was reportedly written by screenwriters Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim. The reviewer argued that this claim does not rescue the result, since the writing itself is weak. He placed the show alongside Elon Musk's AI-made film The Odyssey, which has also drawn negative reviews.

The review frames Castle Walls as one of the first of its kind, comparing it to early silent films that were later surpassed by more advanced work. It suggests that audiences respond to AI-generated art with cynicism, mainly because of concerns about losing human artistry. The reviewer argued that the sensible path is for artists to use AI to enhance their creativity rather than replace it. The articles do not say whether Prime Video plans further AI-generated series.

Articles.Title: Castle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared mess

stories.Headline: KLOTA Study of 350 AI Answers: Three Local Websites Shape What AI Recommends in Borås, Sweden
stories.Summary:
A study by KLOTA AB, a digital marketing agency in Borås, Sweden, found that three local websites appear among the sources of AI answers about local businesses far more often than any others. KLOTA put 45 common local questions to four AI services on October 10 and October 15, 2026, and analyzed all 350 answers. The services were Google's AI Mode, Google's AI Overviews, OpenAI with web search and Google's Gemini with Google Search. The answers cited 374 different websites, and the study was released on October 28, 2026. The three sites were boras.com, cited in 57 answers, borascity.se, cited in 40, and boras.se, the municipal website, cited in 27.

The same three sites topped both rounds of measurement in the same order. At least one of them appeared in 35 percent of answers that included sources, and in answers to 28 of the 45 questions. The study also found that the AI services rarely agree: of 1,000 recommendations, 67 percent came from only one service, and between 44 and 63 percent of a service's recommendations had appeared for the same question five days earlier. Two of the three sites are controlled by the City of Borås, directly or through a municipal company, while borascity.se is run by a company owned by local retailer and property owner associations, with the municipality represented on its board. The study notes that the editorial lists on boras.com do not state how businesses are selected, and that a presentation on borascity.se is included in a membership aimed at town center businesses.

Seven of the eight restaurants on a boras.com list of popular restaurants were among the 15 restaurants the AI services recommended most often, though the study describes this as a correlation rather than proof of cause. KLOTA's founder, Anders Karlsson, said nobody had planned this, but that it was fair to ask how businesses end up on those lists. Karlsson said that for a local business the competition is also the lists, and that a complete Google Business Profile, reviews describing the actual work and mentions by others still make a real difference. KLOTA checked all 536 recommended businesses and attractions against Google Maps and found that 2 percent of answers with recommendations included a business that had permanently closed. KLOTA says it conducted and funded the study independently, although it sells services in this field and is a member of Borås Näringsliv, which owns 9 percent of Borås & Co. The full study, in Swedish, publishes the method and data, and KLOTA intends to repeat the measurement in other Swedish municipalities.

Articles.Title: KLOTA Study of 350 AI Answers: Three Local Websites Shape What AI Recommends in Borås, Sweden

stories.Headline: Microsoft launches new MAI family of AI models for reasoning, voice, coding, and images
stories.Summary:
Microsoft used its Build 2026 developer conference on Tuesday to announce a new family of in-house AI models, along with several other products. The announcements were made during CEO Satya Nadella's keynote and span the company's product stack, from silicon and operating systems to cloud infrastructure. The centerpiece is MAI-Thinking-1, the company's first reasoning model, which is described as mid-sized with 35 billion active parameters and a 128K context window. Microsoft says it was built for efficiency and low token cost.

Six more models were announced alongside it, covering image generation, transcription, voice, and code. They are MAI-Image-2.5 with a Flash variant, MAI-Transcribe-1.5, MAI-Voice-2 with a Flash variant, and MAI-Code-1. MAI-Transcribe-1.5 will be available soon in 43 languages, while MAI-Voice-2 and its Flash variant are already available in 15 additional languages with multiple voice options. Microsoft plans to make all of the models available in Foundry and a new dedicated environment called MAI Playground.

Kyle Daigle, Microsoft's Developer CMO and COO of GitHub, said at a virtual media briefing that MAI-Thinking-1 was designed for complex multi-step instructions, long-context reasoning, and code generation. He said the model was built from scratch on commercially licensed data. The company says independent evaluators preferred it over Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6, and that it matches Claude Opus 4.6 on the SWE Bench Pro coding benchmark. Access differs by model, with MAI-Thinking-1 in private preview in Foundry, MAI-Image-2.5 already live in PowerPoint and OneDrive, and MAI-Code-1 available now in Copilot and VS Code.

Microsoft also announced Microsoft Scout, a personal agent that handles scheduling, meeting prep, and routine tasks through Teams and Outlook, and it begins rolling out to Frontier customers today. On hardware, the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip, offers up to one petaflop of AI compute and 128 gigabytes of unified memory, with the ability to run models up to 120 billion parameters locally. It ships later this year in the US. Microsoft Discovery is now generally available, and Windows is being repositioned as an agent-native runtime through a sandboxing system called Microsoft Execution Containers, which is in preview.

Articles.Title: Microsoft launches new MAI family of AI models for reasoning, voice, coding, and images

stories.Headline: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
stories.Summary:
Surge AI, a company that builds evaluation and training data, published a blog post on October 27, 2026 introducing DAYJOB: Tax, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can handle professional tax assignments from start to finish. The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice and 1,789 workspace files, including PDFs, Excel workbooks, Word documents, emails, and images. Agents receive a client request along with supporting records and must produce a tax return, workpaper, technical review, or client advice. The post says the assignments are built from real professional workflows and reviewed by tax experts with backgrounds at firms such as PwC, Deloitte, and EY.

The benchmark is designed to measure more than tax knowledge and calculation accuracy. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and surface issues the client never raised. Surge reports pass@1 scores at a 95% rubric threshold, meaning an attempt passes only if it satisfies at least 95% of a task's criteria. Under that measure, Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads the leaderboard with a 10.8% pass rate, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%. The post says Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 sit at the high-performance end of the measured cost-performance frontier.

Surge's post gives two examples of the gaps it is testing. In one, a client selling a condo asked which of two closing dates, October 2026 or January 2027, would be better for taxes. The agent correctly found that either date met the two-year residence requirement for a gain exclusion of up to $250,000, but across five attempts it never flagged that eligibility could lapse after August 2027, while Opus identified that deadline in all five. In another, a separating couple asked how to divide their retirement accounts, and Opus assumed they were unmarried in every attempt even though their records suggested a prior marriage in Texas and a ceremony in Colorado. Surge's authors say these cases show that agents often answer the question asked without checking whether the underlying facts support it.

Surge positions DAYJOB: Tax as an extension of its earlier DAYJOB releases in healthcare and finance, and contrasts it with existing benchmarks such as TaxBench, TaxCalcBench, and TaxLab, which measure answers, calculations, or information gathering against a defined problem. The company says the results show that frontier models still struggle to exercise professional judgment and carry real workflows to completion. The full leaderboard is on the DAYJOB: Tax benchmark page, and Surge says access to the full benchmark can be requested by contacting benchmarks@surgehq.ai. The post does not say when or whether results will be updated for newer models.

Articles.Title: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments

stories.Headline: Generative AI and News Report 2026: From standalone tools to information infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism published a report on 29 October 2026, titled "Generative AI and News Report 2026," which examines how people use generative AI systems and what they think of its use in news. The survey covered nine countries: Argentina, Australia, Denmark, Finland, France, Japan, Norway, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It is a follow-up to earlier reports based on 2024 and 2025 data collected in six of those countries. The authors are Felix Simon, Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, and Richard Fletcher, and the report's data was released in late October.

The findings show that use of standalone AI chatbots is growing quickly, with weekly use rising from 34% last year to 51% in 2026 across the six countries with past data. Daily use nearly doubled over the same period, from 7% in 2024 to 16% in 2025 and 28% in 2026. ChatGPT remains the market leader, with weekly use rising from 22% to 34%, while Gemini grew from 11% to 24%, Copilot from 6% to 11%, and Claude from 1% to 7%. Using AI to get information has become the most common use, reaching 38% in 2026, and 9% of respondents now use AI for news, up from 3% in 2024.

Only 12% of respondents say they are comfortable with news made entirely by AI. The report describes these patterns as findings from the survey itself, and it does not assign responsibility for any of them to a particular actor. The authors note that trust in the major systems has grown as people become more familiar with them, though many people still neither trust nor distrust them. They also say that most people who rely on AI for information find the answers trustworthy, with 72% of those who used it for news saying they trust the output, but that convenience matters more to users than reliability.

Respondents were more pessimistic about the news media's use of AI than about scientists or healthcare professionals, and the authors say that pessimism tends to stem from perceived dishonesty about AI use rather than doubts about competence. The report's context is that AI is becoming part of the infrastructure through which people find information, appearing in search summaries, on social platforms, and in news products themselves. The authors frame the 2026 survey as a continuation of their earlier work, and the articles do not say what further studies or steps will follow. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Generative AI and News Report 2026: From standalone tools to information infrastructure

stories.Headline: Cognitive Surrender vs. AI Literacy: Higher-Ed Experts Debate AI
stories.Summary:
In a debate at Johns Hopkins University on Tuesday, higher education leaders agreed that artificial intelligence has caused problems for learning so far but disagreed about how large those problems are. The debate was held at the university's Homewood campus as part of the Hopkins Forum series. It asked whether generative AI will enhance or stunt postsecondary learning. Opponents said the technology weakens critical thinking and lets students hand in work they do not understand, while others said the effects depend on how educators and students use it. The debaters agreed that AI is already changing higher education and forcing a rethink of how students are taught and assessed.

Gary Marcus, a psychology professor at New York University, argued that students often use chatbots in place of their own thinking, a pattern he called cognitive surrender. Cathy O'Neil, a mathematician and algorithmic auditor, described a colleague who had students read their essays aloud, and some could not pronounce words in them or explain what they meant. She said AI can weaken the systems schools use to check whether students are keeping up, since a student could earn high grades with little real understanding. O'Neil also warned that students without human guidance may be more vulnerable to this kind of surrender. Ravi Pendse, chief information officer at the University of Michigan, argued that students are not always inclined to take shortcuts when they have the chance.

He said AI is not inherently harmful but places new responsibility on institutions to guide students in using it well. Pendse said that the answer to false information from AI tools is AI literacy, not avoiding the tools altogether. Edward Maloney, an English professor and executive director of Georgetown University's Center for New Designs in Learning and Scholarship, said AI exposes weak points in higher education, including large lectures and standard exams. He argued that AI could make those methods more transactional but could also allow more individualized instruction, with tools acting as tutors or debate partners. The panelists were divided on the remedy.

O'Neil said that AI should not be used to fix problems that AI has exposed, and she favored a return to oral and in-person exams. Pendse said those same assessment methods could work alongside assignments that build AI literacy. A survey of in-person attendees before and after the debate showed movement toward the "enhance" side, which grew from 26 percent to just under 40 percent. The "stunt" side, which started at 38 percent, ended at just over 40 percent, so opinion remains split. Marcus summed up the common ground by saying that educators need to think differently about pedagogy now.

Articles.Title: Cognitive Surrender vs. AI Literacy: Higher-Ed Experts Debate AI

stories.Headline: Emarat set framework for enterprise AI readiness, workforce transformation supported by Microsoft
stories.Summary:
Emirates Petroleum Company P.J.S.C., known as Emarat, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Microsoft to explore how artificial intelligence can reshape workforce productivity and strengthen enterprise readiness. The agreement was announced in Dubai on October 28, 2026, by the Emirati state news agency WAM. Emarat, a pioneer in the UAE's oil and gas industry, presents the deal as a step toward becoming a digital leader in its sector. The MoU is tied to the UAE National AI Strategy 2031, which seeks to make the country a global leader in artificial intelligence.

Under the framework, Emarat and Microsoft will look at how Microsoft products and capabilities can support productivity, knowledge work and everyday collaboration among staff. Microsoft plans to offer high-level guidance and best practices, along with awareness sessions on productivity opportunities. The partners will also assess priority business scenarios where AI agents and automation could create value for the company. A central focus is secure and governed AI adoption, with Microsoft intending to share security and responsible AI frameworks and recommendations. These measures are meant to address data protection, responsible usage and overall enterprise readiness.

Burhan Al Hashemi, Chief Executive Officer of Emarat, said the company wants its workforce to understand, adopt and benefit from emerging technologies in a secure and responsible way. He said the collaboration gives Emarat a structured way to examine how AI can strengthen productivity, decision-making and long-term business value. Kethan Parbhoo, General Manager for Small, Medium Enterprises and Channel in Central Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Microsoft, said AI transformation is ultimately about empowering people and redesigning how work gets done. He added that Emarat is taking a thoughtful approach to building the skills, governance and technology foundations needed for AI adoption.

The MoU also gives weight to skilling and change management, since employee readiness and cultural understanding are seen as essential to the transformation. Microsoft intends to provide training materials, global adoption frameworks and curated learning paths, and may hold educational workshops on AI features and change management. Emarat will lead internal adoption efforts, including staff communications, training coordination and the integration of AI skilling into existing learning and development programmes. The company describes the agreement as positioning it to treat AI transformation as a business-wide shift that connects people, data and governance. The deal also aligns with the UAE's broader goal of embedding advanced technologies across key national sectors.

Articles.Title: Emarat set framework for enterprise AI readiness, workforce transformation supported by Microsoft - www.irishsun.com

stories.Headline: PACOM Looks to AI Agents for Faster Intelligence, Targeting
stories.Summary:
Indo-Pacific Command, known as PACOM, is moving to bring AI agents into its intelligence and targeting work, according to officials who spoke at TechNet Indo-Pacific. The plans were laid out in remarks reported by GovCIO Media & Research on October 28, 2026. Military leaders said adversaries are advancing their own capabilities, which has pushed defense officials to use AI and synthetic intelligence to speed analysis, targeting and decisions. Rear Adm. Jeffrey Buschmann, the command's J2 intelligence director, said AI had moved from a buzzword to a tool that is now built into nearly every process at PACOM.

The command is prioritizing interoperable tools, common data standards and AI-powered capabilities to keep pace with adversaries. Brig. Chris Alder, the Australian Army vice director for intelligence at PACOM, said a common data framework and shared data ontologies would let nations share information. He said that when such a standard is in place, targeting latency falls from minutes to seconds. The command is also exploring agentic AI to automate parts of the targeting cycle, and Alder said officials want a human kept firmly on the loop for critical decisions.

Chief SI officer Scott Brunstetter, whose position was created about 15 months ago, said PACOM is studying SI for warning, targeting, predictive analysis and rapid software prototyping. One priority is a common operating picture intelligence data layer that would pull intelligence from several sources and improve situational awareness across the command. Brunstetter said agentic AI is the next critical step and that the command must reimagine how it works as change accelerates. He also said the command does not blindly trust these tools, and that it wants evidence that helps analysts understand how the technology works.

Scott Buchanan, chief of the Intelligence Information Systems Division at PACOM, argued that clinging to existing systems would be a recipe for failure. He stressed deploying tools that can run without depending on data centers in Hawaii or the continental United States. Brunstetter said smaller, mission-specific AI models could need less computing power and energy while still supporting operations at the tactical edge. Buschmann also pointed to the Navy's long experience with nuclear power as a possible advantage for future operations. The articles do not give dates for when these capabilities will be fielded, so the plans remain at the stage of intent and exploration.

Articles.Title: PACOM Looks to AI Agents for Faster Intelligence, Targeting

stories.Headline: JMU expert urges cybersecurity and awareness amid AI-assisted scams
stories.Summary:
Experts say it is becoming harder to tell real messages from scams, because scammers are now using artificial intelligence to make their pitches more convincing. John Guo, a professor of computer information systems and business analytics at James Madison University, made these points in a WHSV report published on October 28, 2026. He said AI can also be used to make fake phone calls, which adds to the confusion. The article does not describe a single incident, a specific victim, or a specific scam campaign.

Guo said people can look for warning signs that a message is not genuine.
